Latest Update: An Ancient Coffin in a Famous Church Held the Wrong Body for 1,000 Years. Now We May Know Who’s Inside.

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (737 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For more than 150 years, a burial found on the grounds of Westminster Abbey remained a mystery.
  • It has been revealed that if you went only by the inscription carved on the limestone sarcophagus excavated on the North Green at Westminster Abbey in 1869, you’d understandably assume it held the remains of Valerius Amandinus, a wealthy Briton who lived in Roman Britain around 300 C.E.
  • Recent findings suggest that it certainly didn’t help that a written account in 1873 declared the skeleton lost.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For more than 150 years, a burial found on the grounds of Westminster Abbey remained a mystery. Clues from the coffin itself, not to mention the skeleton inside, puzzled experts until Westminster Abbey’s consultant archaeologist, Warwick Rodwell, identified the deceased as a high-ranking medieval monk. He went one step further, determining the bones belonged to Aelfwig, an abbot of the Abbey’s Benedictine monastery, although Rodwell left open the possibility that the occupant was another abbot.

It has been revealed that if you went only by the inscription carved on the limestone sarcophagus excavated on the North Green at Westminster Abbey in 1869, you’d understandably assume it held the remains of Valerius Amandinus, a wealthy Briton who lived in Roman Britain around 300 C.E. Archaeological research isn’t that simple, though. A Latin cross dated to the 10th or 11th century was also carved across the lid, likely when the coffin was reused, so with conflicting symbology muddying the waters, the identity of the person entombed on the Abbey’s grounds remained unknown for generations.

Recent findings suggest that it certainly didn’t help that a written account in 1873 declared the skeleton lost. In 2016, however, conservators found the bones where they had presumably been all along: inside the coffin.

Rodwell worked on the puzzle for years, eventually publishing a study in the Journal of the British Archaeological Association explaining how the evidence led him to two abbots who served at the monastery. His first candidate, Aelfwig, died around 1020, but the second option was Aelfwig’s successor, Wulfnoth, who died 29 years later.

In a recent development, “We have two viable contenders for the occupant of the sarcophagus,” Rodwell remarked in a statement from the Abbey. He ruled out Aelfwig’s predecessor because that abbot left the area and died elsewhere. “We do not know the date of birth of either. But either would fit equally well if we assume the abbot was in his early 20s when the appointment was made and close to 50 when he died. The fact Aelfwig was already a monk of Westminster might favor him.”.

Industry observers note that the sarcophagus’s own history reveals little. The limestone probably came from Oxfordshire, England. But Rodwell wrote that no clues link the sarcophagus to its original burial site or explain why it was later moved, even though the inscription clearly ties it to a Briton who lived about 1,700 years ago. Identification is further complicated by the Anglo-Saxon cross added to the lid centuries later and by Rodwell’s belief that grave goods were stolen in the early 19th century.

To learn more about the man himself, Rodwell worked with James Young Langhorne, a human bone specialist from Pre-Construct Archaeology. They determined that the man was between 35 and 49 years old and stood about 5 feet, 9 inches tall. That contradicts the 19th-century assessment, which described him as a “robust young man” no older than 30 and about 5 feet, 7 inches tall. The analysis also highlighted osteoarthritis in multiple joints, two healed rib fractures, and signs of an old infection in one leg. There was no obvious cause of death.

Radiocarbon dating by the Scottish Universities Environmental Research Centre placed the bones between 987 and 1052 C.E. This confirmed that the sarcophagus had been reused, and the date range matches the Saxon-period cross on the lid. With that range established, Rodwell looked more closely at the possible candidates.

It has been revealed that he concluded the man was an abbot because he was “honored” with burial in a “fine sarcophagus”: his wooden coffin was packed in lime and placed inside the stone casket. To support his theory further, Rodwell wrote that he believes the “prestigious burial” first took place in the eastern arm of the abbey church. The sarcophagus would have been fully buried, with the recut lid serving as a cross-slab in the church floor. Then, after Henry III began rebuilding the abbey in the 1240s, workers moved the sarcophagus into the “newly constructed sacristy courtyard” in 1258.

Today, the sarcophagus is on permanent display in the Abbey’s museum, The Queen’s Diamond Jubilee Galleries.

Tim Newcomb is a journalist based in the Pacific Northwest. He covers stadiums, sneakers, gear, infrastructure, and more for a variety of publications, including Popular Mechanics. His favorite interviews have included sit-downs with Roger Federer in Switzerland, Kobe Bryant in Los Angeles, and Tinker Hatfield in Portland.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thanksgiving asks a lot of us (and our ovens!). From making the turkey to all of the casseroles and sides, don’t even get me started on dessert. You’ve got a lot on your plate, so we’re trying to make the major turkey day a little easier. Appetizers are my favorite part of the meal: little bites that pack so much flavor and fun into the start of the big feast, so you’ve gotta make them count. We’ve got some clever, simple shortcuts to help you whip up appetizers that will impress your guests without adding to your stress.

Recent findings suggest that whether you’re looking for quick and easy last-minute options or want something more elaborate, we’ve got something on this list for you. Need more Thanksgiving hosting ideas? Check out our favorite Thanksgiving side dishes and Thanksgiving cocktails!

Pumpkin Spice Hot Honey Brie Bites.

Sweet and savory with a kick of heat, these pumpkin, Brie, and hot honey bites are the perfect fall appetizer to serve during the holidays. The honey provides the perfect balance for the sweetness of the pumpkin and the savory, melty Brie. Add a bit of fresh thyme and some roasted pecans, and you’ve got yourself a certified crowd-pleaser.

There is nothing better than a soft, homemade dinner roll. These rolls use sweet potatoes to make them even softer and fluffier, similar to our classic potato rolls. These would be a fun alternative to biscuits or Parker House rolls at Thanksgiving or another substantial family meal.

According to recent reports, having multiple Thanksgivings this year? Want to transform your leftovers from one into something incredible for the next? Look no further than this stuffed bread ring—it's gorgeous and super easy, thanks to store-bought crescent roll dough.

With all of the elements of stuffing plus the added flaky and butter benefits of biscuits, this pull-apart stuffing bread just might start a tug-of-war situation at your table when you grab for a slice.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you’ve ever scraped a black fleck off a melted spatula into your pasta and wondered what exactly you just ate, congratulations: You’ve already arrived at the case for nontoxic utensils. Swapping out your plastic-handled, mystery-material kitchen tools is one of the easiest upgrades you can make.

Sources indicate that more difficult is choosing a material to commit to. Walk through any kitchen store and you'll encounter wood, silicone, stainless steel, bamboo, and any number of hybrid constructions. Each has its advocates and its limitations. But after thinking through the tradeoffs and cross-referencing what professionals actually reach for day to day, we landed on a clear answer: Silicone is the best material for a nontoxic utensil set, and a five- to six-piece core collection is all most home cooks need to start.

Latest in this upgrade: We added more information about the pros and cons of each of our winning non-toxic utensil sets.

In a recent development, food-grade silicone is heat-resistant up to around 450°–600°, depending on the manufacturer, which means it’s unlikely to melt against the side of a hot pan or leach chemicals into your food the way that plastic utensils can when exposed to prolonged heat. It's also nonreactive, meaning it won't interact with acidic ingredients like tomato sauce or citrus the way that some metals can. Unlike wood, it's fully dishwasher-safe and nonporous and it won't harbor bacteria or crack over time with repeated washing. And—critically—it won't scratch your enameled cast iron.

According to recent reports, there are some things silicone doesn't do especially well. It can feel slightly grippy or drag-heavy compared to a thin fish spatula, for instance, and some silicone utensils pick up odors over time. (The odor glitch is real—I've had cheaper silicone spatulas that smelled faintly of dish soap for months.) One other issue you might find is that you can’t scrape a pan very effectively with silicone in a situation where you might want to blend fond into a sauce for flavor (that’s a case for keeping a wooden spoon around). But for the vast majority of everyday cooking tasks—stirring, folding, sautéing, serving—high-quality silicone outperforms the competition on the merits that matter most.

Material: Platinum-cured siliconeSet size: 5 pieces (also available in 3- and 10-piece sets)Heat resistance: Up to 425°FDishwasher safe: Yes.

What we love: GIR (Get It Right) makes some of the best silicone utensils on the market. Its tools are made from 100% platinum silicone, which among other things, is a method that keeps odors off the utensils. It also makes them fully heat-safe and more durable than most other sets. That matters more than it might sound: Many budget silicone utensils use a nylon or fiberglass core to add rigidity, which can become a problem if the silicone outer layer ever cracks or peels. With GIR, what you see is what you get all the way through.

The handles are weighted and ergonomic without being bulky, and the heads are thin enough to actually get under food—like a delicate omelet—which is a genuine problem with thicker silicone spatulas. GIR's tools also hold up unusually well over time. The silicone doesn't discolor, doesn't absorb odors the way cheaper versions can, and doesn't degrade with repeated dishwasher cycles.

In a recent development, the brand offers a range of set configurations, but its core five-piece collection gives you exactly what you need without the extras: a spatula, a flip turner, a spoon, a ladle, and GIR's signature spoonula—a hybrid tool that functions as both spoon and spatula that’s particularly useful for scraping the sides of a pan or transferring food cleanly from pot to bowl. The spoonula in particular gets more use in my kitchen than I expected—it's become the default tool for anything that needs to be scraped, scooped, or transferred.

What we'd leave: It's a bit pricier than other silicone sets, but we think it's well worth it.

Good Grips 3-Piece Silicone Utensil Set.

Material: SiliconeSet size: 3 piecesHeat resistance: Not listed on siteDishwasher safe: Yes.

In a recent development, what we love: Oxo's kitchen tools have been a reliable standard for years, and the brand’s silicone utensil line earns that trust at a lower price point. The set includes a ladle, a cooking spoon, and a turner, with flexible edges designed to get every last bit from pans and bowls. The handles are comfortable and grippy even when wet, and the one-piece silicone construction makes cleanup straightforward.

What we'd leave: It's a leaner starting point than our top pick, but that's not necessarily a bad thing—if you're building a collection piece by piece, this is a smart, low-commitment way to start with utensils you'll actually use.

What we love: Wooden spoons are gentle on cookware, they don't conduct heat, and they have a tactile warmth that silicone can't replicate. The Essentials Set, made by a small wood shop out of Kempton, Pennsylvania, includes a large spatula, a stirring spoon, tongs, a medium serving spoon, a ladle, and Jonathan’s signature Original Spootle—plus a jar of their own SpoonWax to keep everything conditioned.

Material: WoodSet size: Wide range; medium set has 7 piecesHeat resistance: Not listed on siteDishwasher safe: No.

Recent findings suggest that what we'd leave: The wood requires more upkeep (and will eventually crack or warp) compared to silicone, but a quick hand-wash and occasional wipe-down with wax takes about 30 seconds. It's not cheap, but it's a premium product. Just keep it out of the dishwasher. For cooks who prefer the feel of wood, Jonathan's Spoons makes some of the most thoughtfully crafted wooden utensil sets available.

5-Piece Stainless Steel Kitchen Utensil Set.

Material: Stainless steelSet size: 5 piecesHeat resistance: 600°FDishwasher safe: Yes.

What we love: Stainless-steel utensils are indestructible and oven-safe to high temperatures, and they look sharp hanging from a rail or stored in a stylish crock. So why make silicone the top recommendation instead? Bare stainless can scratch nonstick and enameled surfaces, so these are best suited for cooks who primarily use uncoated cookware (carbon steel, stainless steel, cast iron). All-Clad's 5-piece set includes a ladle, a solid spoon, a slotted spoon, a turner, and a storage caddy, all crafted from heavy-gauge stainless steel with ergonomic handles long enough to reach into deep pots. The set is heat-safe up to 600°, dishwasher-safe, and backed by All-Clad's limited lifetime warranty. If you're already cooking on All-Clad stainless-steel pans, this is the obvious companion set.

What we'd leave: If you don't have uncoated cookware, this isn't the set for you.

Once you have your core set, it's worth considering what other tools you'd need. Whether you're pescatarian, a deep-fryer, or an avid wok user, there's a tool out there that'll help you achieve your highest cooking goals. None of these need to come from the same brand—this is where building piece by piece, based on what you actually cook, makes more sense than buying a bigger bundle. Here are a few of our favorites.

If crisping salmon skin is your game, a fish spatula is a must. The Lamson Flexible Stainless-Steel Slotted Turner ($53) is a longtime favorite, but Winco’s Fish Spatula ($10) is an inexpensive alternative with a wooden handle that's still flexible enough for delicate fillets.

Medium Stainless Steel Fish Spatula.

Industry observers note that if steak is more up your alley, you can't be without a pair of tongs. Of course it's great for turning the steak in a skillet and holding in steady while you slice, but this tool is also helpful for a boatload of other tasks, like removing corn cobs from a pot of boiling water and shifting sheet pans around your oven. Oxo’s 12" Locking Tongs ($20) with silicone tips are gentle on nonstick and enameled surfaces while still giving you a confident grip.

Whether you're a deep-fry fanatic or a dumpling enthusiast, a spider strainer is a great tool for removing crisped or boiled items from hot pots and pans. We like this stainless-steel version for its sturdiness and extra-long handle.

Open Kitchen by Williams Sonoma.

A from-scratch dressing, a silky cream sauce, or a fluffy whipped cream is made possible because of a good whisk. You can splurge on the editor-favorite Matfer Bourgeat Piano Whisk or opt for a silicone-coated Oxo Good Grips version.

According to recent reports, the same logic that makes a 7-piece cookware set a better starting point than a 15-piece one applies here: More isn't always better, and the average home cook will reach for the same handful of tools repeatedly. A well-considered five-piece silicone set typically covers a large spoon (for stirring sauces, soups, and grains), a slotted spoon (for draining and serving), a flexible spatula (the workhorse for eggs, fish, and pancakes), a turner or solid spatula (for heavier tasks like flipping burgers or moving proteins), and a ladle or tongs, depending on what you cook most.

Sources indicate that with five tools, you can execute most stovetop and baking tasks without reaching for anything else. That remarked, not every set breaks down exactly this way—and that's fine. A three-piece set that covers your everyday tools beats a five-piece set with two pieces you never touch. Think of five as the target, not a hard rule.

Are silicone utensils actually nontoxic?

Recent findings suggest that high-quality, food-grade silicone is considered one of the safest materials for kitchen utensils, with FDA-approved versions specifically tested to ensure they don’t leach harmful substances into food. It's nonreactive, doesn't leach chemicals into food, and is stable at high temperatures. However, the quality of silicone utensils is much more all over the place. Cheaper sets often use filler materials or nylon cores that can degrade over time. Look for utensils made from 100% platinum-cured or pharmaceutical-grade silicone—the kind GIR uses—and you can feel confident about what's touching your food.

How do I take care of my utensils so they last?

Sources indicate that it depends on the material. Silicone is the lowest maintenance—most sets are dishwasher-safe and require no special treatment. Wood needs more attention: hand-washing, drying thoroughly after each use, and oiling periodically with food-safe mineral oil or wax. Stainless steel is virtually indestructible, but hand-washing will keep it looking better longer. Regardless of material, avoid soaking utensils for extended periods and store them somewhere with good airflow rather than sealed in a drawer while still damp.

Do I need to match my utensils to my cookware?

According to recent reports, not exactly—but it's worth thinking about. If you cook primarily on nonstick or enameled cookware, silicone is your safest bet since it won't scratch delicate surfaces. If you cook mainly on stainless steel or cast iron, you have more flexibility and can use metal utensils without worry. Also, you may need a little more leverage to get food off, and metal can help with that. Wood works well across the board but comes with its own maintenance tradeoffs. The most practical approach for most home cooks: Start with a silicone set as your everyday workhorse, then add a stainless fish spatula or tongs as your cooking demands them.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As humanity entered the 21st century and the ravages of climate change became more and more apparent, the push toward electrification (replacing gas-powered cars, furnaces, and stoves with electric versions) really gained steam. At the same time, the electricity supply itself has been getting cleaner. According to Pew Research, solar power accounted for only 0.01 percent of the world’s electricity production back then, but fast-forward a quarter of a century, and that number is now nine percent and rising.

In a recent development, but building out an electrified future isn’t as easy as sticking wind turbines in the ocean and vast solar arrays in the desert and calling it a day. These new forms of renewable energy also need to connect to the grid before they can supply us with that much-needed new power. Expanding the grid’s capacity to meet this ballooning demand was already going to be a tall order as more and more electric cars, ovens, and heat pumps came online. Now, the rise of power-hungry AI data centers has transformed that difficult task into a borderline impossible one for the simple reason that the U.S. may not have enough of the equipment—or the materials to make mentioned equipment—to build the required infrastructure.

In a new study published in the journal Cell Reports Sustainability, researchers at Johns Hopkins University report that critical grid equipment, such as transformers and converters, could become the bottleneck in powering a rapidly electrifying society. According to the researchers, demand for electricity isn’t anything new. In fact, it’s been steadily rising since Thomas Edison flipped the switch on the Pearl Street Station in 1882. But due to the rise of AI data centers, the electricity industry has entered a whole new era of demand growth.

Industry observers note that “When the demand for electricity started to grow faster than expected, it started to amplify all the cracks in the industry,” Yury Dvorkin, a Johns Hopkins researcher and co-author of the study, stated in a press statement. According to Dvorkin and co-author Boyu Yao, electricity demand historically ticked up a percent or two each year. But now, largely because of data centers, demand is projected to grow 21 percent overall by the end of the decade.

If this rapid demand growth persists, it will put considerable strain on supplies of specific materials, including copper, steel, nickel, aluminum, and manganese, needed to build the necessary transformers, which step up or step down the voltage of alternating current on the grid.

“This type of equipment was taken for granted, but without it, you can build a data center or a power plant but it won’t be powered because you cannot connect it to the grid,” Dvorkin mentioned. “By 2030 we’re likely to have transformer shortages even without the most aggressive power demand growth.”.

According to their projections, copper will run short in 2027, followed soon by steel and nickel, which will affect not just grid utilities but wind power infrastructure and electric vehicle charging stations. This shortfall isn’t necessarily news: a study by S&P Global earlier this year found that copper could experience a 10 million metric ton deficit by 2040. This deficit isn’t caused by a lack of copper in the ground, since the planet holds abundant copper resources. Extraction is where the industry is facing a crucial bottleneck.

According to recent reports, “Copper is abundant in the ground, but there’s not enough being extracted to be able to meet the demand,” authors of a copper market analysis wrote for The Conversation earlier this year. That’s because investors want higher and more reliable returns than copper mines currently offer, and the industry faces complex permitting processes and can’t find enough workers.

Industry observers note that this upcoming study suggests that under its baseline scenario, the U.S. might be able to produce enough transformers yet still fall 16 percent short on other grid-related equipment. But with AI data centers supercharging demand, the study’s “high power demand” scenario is more likely. That scenario projects a 15 percent shortage of transformers and a 30 percent shortage of all other equipment. The authors also note that roughly two-thirds of this expected shortage can be attributed to AI data centers.

In a recent development, “Utilities will compete for transformers with the data center industry,” Dvorkin remarked. “Transformers will first be delivered to whoever can pay the highest premium. Will it be a mom-and-pop utility or a big data center corporation?”.

I think we already know the answer to that question.

Tech Report: Where’d You Go, Crêpes Suzette?

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that there’s something simultaneously comforting and dazzling about setting a dessert on fire: Candles atop a birthday cake; the meringue encrusting a baked Alaska; the caramelized fruit in a classic bananas Foster.
  • Crêpes Suzette is a surprisingly simple dish considering its decadent, theatrical reputation.
  • Recent findings suggest that for such a famous dish, though, its appearance on restaurant menus is increasingly rare.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that there’s something simultaneously comforting and dazzling about setting a dessert on fire: Candles atop a birthday cake; the meringue encrusting a baked Alaska; the caramelized fruit in a classic bananas Foster. But chief among them is one whose very name promises something different, something with French sophistication and an air of mystery that demands a moniker all its own: crêpes Suzette.

Crêpes Suzette is a surprisingly simple dish considering its decadent, theatrical reputation. The drama comes from the flames—thin, traditional French crêpes are drenched in a sauce made of orange liqueur, which is then set ablaze (typically tableside in many restaurants), causing the spirits to simmer and the sugars to caramelize. French chef Andrea Calstier, of Michelin-starred La Bastide in North Salem, Latest York, grew up eating them with his family, and in the brasseries of his home country.

Recent findings suggest that for such a famous dish, though, its appearance on restaurant menus is increasingly rare. And for such an iconic French dessert, well, it may not technically be French at all. So where did these flaming pancakes come from? Where did they go? And isn’t it about time we bring them back?

While there are conflicting reports about the original creator of crêpes Suzette, the top candidate is Henri Charpentier, chef at the Café de Paris in Monte Carlo, Monaco, in the late 1800s. But while multiple roads lead back to Charpentier, the path gets murky, contradicted by both general plausibility and Charpentier himself.

Originally, Charpentier claimed credit for the iconic dish in his autobiography, Life à la Henri: Being the Memoirs of Henri Charpentier. In this 1934 volume, he suggested that the dish was a happy accident, tinged with drama. He alleged that as a young man working at the Café de Paris, he had been carrying a platter of crêpes to the Prince of Wales (the future King Edward VII) and stepped too near a chafing dish, setting the crêpes on fire, to the shock and delight of the prince, who proposed naming the newly created dish after his dining companion, a young woman named Suzette. (Frustratingly little information is available on who this Suzette may have been, if she was a real person at all.).

The story has the right theatrical touches for the dish, but it is almost certainly apocryphal, not least because Charpentier himself, in an interview with American writer Elsie Lee for the 1950s “Compleat Imbiber” series, noted that he had developed the dish by taking a beloved childhood fruit crêpe and adding the then-fashionable touches of a liquor-based sauce and, presumably, a flame.

Wherever it came from, though, and whatever Charpentier had to say about it, Suzette’s unwitting legacy has endured for more than a century—her crêpes have remained a household name, even if they have fallen somewhat out of style. While chef Calstier notes that they’re still “served in many restaurants” in his native Marseille and that “French customers…are accustomed to seeing crêpes Suzette in any brasserie,” he admitted that “here in the U.S., they are more difficult to find.”.

Part of the reason may be that, as with many dishes that predate the Edwardian era, it simply went out of fashion. But according to Lucile Plaza, executive chef at Benoit Fresh York, it’s a result of the dish’s inherent service requirements: “True tableside service requires high staffing levels and precise choreography that a busy modern kitchen can’t always support daily,” she states. In London’s West End, fine-dining heavyweights Savoy Grill and The Ritz take this showmanship to the extreme, with portable burners and bottles of Grand Marnier on wooden trolleys.

According to recent reports, but while there are complications to adding an edible spectacle to a restaurant menu, there are benefits, too. Chef Plaza notes that for the kitchen, “Suzette is brilliant because it is the ultimate way to use leftover crêpes. The intense bathing in the hot, rich citrus sauce revives the starch perfectly.” But not every restaurant that serves crêpes Suzette does so with a tableside flourish: In London’s St. John’s Wood, Oslo Court Restaurant, which is famous for its retro menu of classics like steak Diane and sole Veronique (two more of Edward VII's girlfriends, perhaps?), crêpes Suzette are brûléed with a torch in the kitchen rather than set aflame at the table. Adding crêpes Suzette to a menu may only be as hard as a restaurant wants it to be.

Industry observers note that A burst of blue-tinged flame may not be necessary for the dish to achieve its signature caramelization, but it is key to the show—and a major point in favor of the dish’s present-day revival. As the old saying goes, “we eat with our eyes first,” and it’s truer than ever today. In fact, for many diners in the age of social media, it’s the phone that eats first, and that’s where crêpes Suzette has real potential for a modern renaissance. Nearly 400,000 viewers have watched a YouTube video of the tableside crêpes Suzette service at the London Ritz, and more than a million have viewed a TikTok of crêpes Suzette being prepared tableside at Switzerland’s five-star Suvretta House in Saint Moritz.

Recent findings suggest that spectacle is cool again, and whether dining out or cooking at home, we want to feel astonished and excited by the foods we eat. While a tableside flambé may prove logistically complicated at a restaurant scale, the feat is significantly easier to pull off at home—all it takes is a lighter or a match and a little confidence. Chef Calstier, for one, states that crêpes Suzette are a favorite of his wife, Elena, adding, “You can prepare everything in advance and do the flambé in front of your guests to wow them.” Plus, he says, “they don’t require many ingredients, beyond that bottle of Grand Marnier that we all have stashed away somewhere. They’re quite simple to make.”.

Sources indicate that moreover, as delectable as classic crêpes Suzette are, they lend themselves well to upcoming takes and customizations. Chef Plaza’s version at Benoit has a cherry twist: “Replacing Grand Marnier with kirsch is a natural match,” she states. “The dry cherry distillate brings an incredible aroma to the tableside without adding cloying sugar.” Meanwhile, at La Bastide, chef Calstier dishes up a twist that uses French toast instead of crêpes while sticking to the classic flavors and flambé. We asked one of our favorite pastry chefs, Caroline Schiff, author of Daily Desserts: Treats on Repeat, to develop a savory version for us, which she describes as “a cheeky little twist” on the classic. In her take, inspired by French onion soup, crêpes layered with caramelized onions and nutty gruyère are set ablaze with a splash of sherry. “They are at once a novelty and a nod to the classic,” she says.

Charpentier, one imagines, would approve.

Why Weed Is Now a Family Thanksgiving Tradition

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (739 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that getting stoned in America has never been more socially acceptable.
  • The day before Turkey day—dubbed Green Wednesday by the cannabis industry—might soon outpace 4/20 as the busiest day of the year for dispensaries.
  • It makes sense: For many Americans, the fourth Thursday in November is for reuniting with relatives who, were it not for blood, might be the last people you’d ever choose to sit next to on a public bus.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that getting stoned in America has never been more socially acceptable. In the 14 years since Washington and Colorado first legalized recreational cannabis, a majority of states have followed suit by relaxing restrictions as well. While policy has a ways to go, the social stigma attached to the substance has dissipated into a skunky haze. If you’re not convinced, just look at the sheer number of Americans lining up to buy weed each Thanksgiving.

The day before Turkey day—dubbed Green Wednesday by the cannabis industry—might soon outpace 4/20 as the busiest day of the year for dispensaries. News outlets have covered this phenomenon in recent years with varying degrees of sincerity and snark, but the through line is always the same: People are getting high on Thanksgiving not only to improve the meal, but to make spending time with family more bearable—and apparently it’s kind of working.

It makes sense: For many Americans, the fourth Thursday in November is for reuniting with relatives who, were it not for blood, might be the last people you’d ever choose to sit next to on a public bus. Thanksgiving is precision engineered for passive-aggressive ideological bickering and wrenching open old emotional wounds. It’s the day when adult siblings remind each other of their deepest insecurities while loading the dishwasher together, and when drunk aunts across the country engage in the time-honored tradition of casually outing their gay nephews to the table.

While this aspect of Thanksgiving provides plenty of material for movies, comedy specials, and sitcom bottle episodes, the lived reality is often less entertaining. The Reddit threads and advice column queries that crop up around this time each year tend to frame the holiday as a problem to be dealt with—a time for wielding the skills gleaned from cognitive behavioral therapy. Sometimes, in more dire terms, it’s a day one must try to survive. No wonder so many people are opting for a predinner edible.

According to recent reports, but getting high merely as a means to dissociate through it all isn’t what all of these people seem to be stepping outside for. When Lisa Bonos reported on the phenomenon back in 2019, she spoke with several people who found that getting stoned with family members had a transformative impact on their relationships. Weed helped high-strung parents chill out, impart a “cozy atmosphere” for the stoned and sober alike, and most significantly, it dissolved intergenerational communication barriers. As Bonos pointed out, “getting high together can help equalize a historically unequal relationship—at any age.”.

It has been revealed that this is all anecdotal, of course, but there’s research to back it up. Humans have used cannabis for thousands of years socially through ritual and celebration, and the endocannabinoid signaling system plays an crucial role in how humans process social interactions by easing anxiety and fostering feelings of connectedness. Granted, this depends on dose and context.

I don’t mean to suggest that cannabis is a miracle substance that will heal the American family. It goes without saying that a whole lot of stuff is far too painful, complex, or irreconcilable to resolve by passing a joint. Opting for an alternative celebration, such as Friendsgiving, chosen family’s-giving, or DINKs-go-out-to-a-nice-restaurant-instead’s-giving, is for many, the safest way to go.

But for the rest of Americans already imbibing this holiday to deal with more casually dysfunctional matters, it might be time to take the “cousin walk” out of the shadows and invite other cautiously interested members to partake. Since dosage really matters, I’d forgo slathering the Turkey in cannabutter and instead opt for a tin of one of those little low-THC, high-CBD edibles as an option for the inexperienced. Lest we forget when famous New York Times columnist Maureen Dowd ate too much of a THC infused chocolate bar, causing her to hide in a Denver hotel room in fear that she was both dead and wanted by the police.

Recent findings suggest that smoking weed with your family may not lead to a miracle, but at the very least, the odds of getting into a heated debate with your uncle regarding the directional shift of the Overton window are less likely if he’s zooted on the couch, reading the Wikipedia page on pecans. And maybe, just maybe, as Thanksgiving continues to get greener, it might become—for some—a day to look forward to rather than a day to endure.

Bakeries are no longer just a stop along the way—they’re the final destination. According to Yelp’s 2027 Food and Drink Trend report, bakeries are becoming such a hot commodity that people are planning entire trips around viral treats. Yelp searches for “bakeries near me” are up 561% from last year, while searches for a “sweet treat” are up 303%. Treat yo’ self culture is officially here.

It has been revealed that bakery tourism is on the rise, and honestly, I'm not surprised. I, myself, am prone to walking unfamiliar city streets just to get my hands on the town's most beloved pastry. And people are getting pretty specific about what they want. Searches for cardamom buns are up 24%, kouign-amann 67%, and salt bread a whopping 616%.

It’s not just individual pastries getting all the attention, either. Yelp found that searches for “hot and newly introduced bakeries” jumped 359%, while “best gluten-free bakery” rose 113%. Bakeries are also the most-saved type of specialty food shop on Yelp’s My Lists feature. Even New York City's Radio Bakery, which you’ll find below, saw searches increase by 176%. It seems we’re all doing some serious research before our next pastry run.

So which hot spots should you add to your must-visit list? I asked Yelp to do a deep dive into the most-saved bakeries across America to see which ones people are bookmarking. Here's what came out on top.

Sources indicate that this famed Taiwanese bakery opened its first U.S. outpost earlier this year in Pasadena, California, and has already gone viral for its unique cream cheese-filled bagels and flaky pastries.

Sources indicate that what started out as a pandemic-era creation has now morphed into a line-worthy brick-and-mortar. Bad Butter regularly draws block-long lines, with its breads, croissants, and pastries often selling out.

In Santa Ana, California, 61hundred Bread is known for its signature heirloom blue-corn masa sourdough bread, along with Filipino baked goods like pandesal and ube-filled cruffins.

Sources indicate that at this Latest York City French bakery, the jambon-beurre sandwich is the star item. Fresh baguettes and flaky croissants are also among the other reasons locals and tourists flock to the shop.

Located at the Halepuna Waikiki hotel in Honolulu, Hawaii, Halekulani Bakery is known for its signature coconut cake and assortment of pastries.

Located in Los Angeles, California, Out Of Ordi specializes in Korean-style salt bread.

Upcoming York City’s Sunday Morning frequently sells out of its viral cinnamon rolls.

San Diego’s Relic Bakery & Kitchen offers a mix of sweet and savory baked goods, from pies and croissants to breads and danishes.

In New York City, you’ll find Justin’s Salt Bread, voted the city’s best new bakery of the year and known for—you guessed it—its salt bread.

San Francisco’s Butter & Crumble is known for its crumble cakes and laminated pastries, with offerings that rotate seasonally.

According to recent reports, another Honolulu bakery makes the list, although this one comes with a twist. Part bakery, part butcher shop, The Local General Store sells everything from quiche and danishes to sausage and ham.

It looks like my travel schedule just got a little busier (and tastier).

American science is broken. Meet the people fixing it

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3434 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that this is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • The February sun was setting outside her family’s West Virginia home when Rebecca Lindsey found out she was being fired in 75 minutes.
  • “Every week, it was like, ‘This is the week we’re all going to get fired,’ ” says Lindsey, who had worked as a contractor and later a civil servant at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration for nearly 15 years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

The February sun was setting outside her family’s West Virginia home when Rebecca Lindsey found out she was being fired in 75 minutes. Lindsey, who until early 2025 managed the federal government’s climate.gov website, had just begun to think her job might be safe during the second Trump administration.

“Every week, it was like, ‘This is the week we’re all going to get fired,’ ” says Lindsey, who had worked as a contractor and later a civil servant at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration for nearly 15 years. “Every time you would hear the rumor and then it wouldn’t happen, you would think … maybe this is all just talk.”.

Industry observers note that but at 3:45 p.m. on February 27, 2025, Lindsey and around 800 of her NOAA colleagues received a mass termination email saying they no longer “fit the Agency’s current needs.” In June, Lindsey’s sister and the data visualization lead for the project, Mary Lindsey, was fired alongside the remaining climate.gov contractors. The website URL was redirected, hiding the site — and its decades’ worth of climate visualizations, educational tools and extreme weather trackers — from the public.

According to recent reports, the Lindsey sisters decided to fight back. Along with another terminated NOAA employee, they split a $65,000 grant from the nonprofit Surge Climate Talent and introduced a crowdfunding campaign to rebuild and upgrade climate.gov. The site, now called climate.us, notched one million views in its first month.

But as proud as they are of their work, the project is a patch, not a fix. Rebecca Lindsey predicts it would take at least seven employees and $1.8 million annually to resume 80 percent of the old site’s work. “Climate.gov was more than just a website; it was a climate literacy program,” she indicates. To rescue the full mission, they still have a long way to go.

Industry observers note that courtesy of M. Lindsey and R. Lindsey.

According to recent reports, the Lindsey sisters are far from the only tale of makeshift resilience. Over the last year, untold numbers of U.S. scientists and their supporters have rebuilt data dashboards, formed recommendation groups for childhood vaccines and screenings, and doled out research funds for hundreds of stranded early-career scientists. They’ve reconstituted committees to advise space missions, rehomed key reports on climate and Arctic science, and even turned to social media to spread public health alerts in the wake of a massive realignment of the federal science enterprise.

“I don’t think anyone could have foreseen the amount of destruction and deliberate breaking down of norms and infrastructure” over the last two years, indicates Christina Madison, a clinical pharmacist and public health communicator known on social media as The Public Health Pharmacist.

According to recent reports, since January 2025, the second Trump administration has frozen or rescinded billions of dollars in research funding on topics from climate change to vaccine hesitancy and is trying to redirect it — often without congressional approval — to administration priorities such as artificial intelligence and quantum computing. During deliberations for the FY2026 and FY2027 budgets, the White House proposed slashing future science funding by one-third.

“When this was first starting, it really, truly felt like an alternate universe,” notes Sean O’Leary, a pediatric infectious disease researcher at the University of Colorado Anschutz. “The science was always what drove the decision making, and now we’re at a place where it’s not.”.

It has been revealed that in 2025 alone, the federal government shed some 20 percentof its science workforce. And in May 2026, the Office of Management and Budget proposed a sweeping set of rules to expand the authority of federal political appointees in selecting science grants.

Approximate proportion of the scientific workforce who left federal service in 2025.

Yet some researchers see the destruction as an opportunity to rebuild their corners of U.S. science — or even reimagine it, claims Michael Osterholm, an epidemiologist at the University of Minnesota in Minneapolis. “If there’s any good that can come out of what has been a horrible situation, it’s that it’s given us time and provided a pause to think through clearly: Is this the way we want to continue?”.

University of Ottawa ecologist Julien Martin spent a decade building a respected lab that probed how social behaviors affect the evolution of bushy-tailed, cat-sized rodents called marmots. So when the National Science Foundation began its sweeping grant cuts, Martin found himself doing something unexpected: uploading cute marmot videos to OnlyFans, an online video subscription platform better known for hosting pornography.

The effort, called OnlyMarms, netted $6,000 — a mere drop in the funding bucket. But the project went viral, leading outside supporters to launch a cryptocurrency token that earned the lab an additional $150,000. And direct donations, including an anonymous $300,000 gift, gave the lab enough to fund one Ph.D. student’s entire degree.

According to recent reports, “When you see that so much money could be obtained by doing essentially nothing about science, it’s quite shocking,” Martin says. He welcomes the support, but having to spend so much time on non-research tasks has also felt demeaning. “Sometimes, you have to question: Is the science funding broken? Are we just competing for pennies?”.

In 2025, the National Institutes of Health and the NSF canceled or suspended more than 7,800 existing grants, totaling billions of dollars. (Some 5,200 grants were later reinstated.) Each agency issued roughly a quarter fewer grants in 2025 than their previous 10-year averages.

Universities and research centers were hit hard. “It was really dire,” indicates Emily Young, who leads medical research grantmaking at the San Diego-based Prebys Foundation. In phone calls with researchers, many told her they had halted ongoing experiments, such as developing measles vaccines for people with autoimmune disorders.

But the thing that really stood out, Young states, was how the sudden drop in funding was affecting postdocs and early-career researchers. “Young people were going from feeling like they had an avenue for a really promising career … to feeling like they were in a worthless career.”.

Sources indicate that so, in May 2025, the foundation awarded $7 million total in emergency grants to seven local institutions, including San Diego State University, the University of California, San Diego and Scripps Research. The grants targeted more than 80 research programs involving early- and mid-career scientists that were facing hundreds of millions of dollars in lost federal funding.

Larger science philanthropies also stepped into the breach. The Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation gave $55 million total to 30 universities to support 400 postdoctoral researchers. The Alfred P. Sloan and Spencer foundations, among others, partnered to provide 83 quick-turnaround grants of around $25,000 each to researchers whose NSF education grants had been canceled.

Some wealthy universities also offered bridge funding to their researchers; Johns Hopkins University gave awards up to $250,000 to individuals with unexpected funding gaps, and the Yale School of Medicine arranged to fund up to 90 percent of terminated or frozen NIH grants.

After the first bout of funding chaos, science philanthropy Schmidt Sciences unveiled a more ambitious approach: to develop the science themselves. In January 2026, they revealed plans to construct three ground-based observatories and a space telescope larger than NASA’s Hubble by the end of the decade. The space telescope alone will cost hundreds of millions of dollars and provide open-access data to scientists worldwide, with a special focus on exoplanets and transient events like supernovas.

In November 2026, the philanthropy opened its first round of funding for early-career scientists using the observatory system; individual awards will total up to $2.5 million each.

Industry observers note that “Originally, the hope was we would play a more classic philanthropic role,” claims Arpita Roy, an astronomer who directs the Astrophysics & Space Center at Schmidt Sciences. But given the federal funding landscape, she says, “it became pretty clear to us, if we really think these things need to exist in the world … then we need to build them out.”.

While private funding can be a lifeline, Young claims, it’s still a temporary measure at best. “We are not going to fill the vacuum of federal funding,” she says. “There is simply not enough philanthropic resource out there to do that.”.

In 1995, the American Academy of Pediatrics and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention made a consequential decision: Rather than publish independent recommendations for childhood vaccines, as they had since the 1960s, they would glitch one set jointly. Over the next 30 years, a group called the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices advised the CDC, with academy input, to expand its recommendations to include chickenpox, hepatitis A and pneumococcal infections. Cases of the three dropped by more than 90 percent, saving thousands of lives.

It has been revealed that but in June 2025, Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr., an outspoken vaccine critic, fired all 17 members of ACIP and replaced many with vaccine skeptics. Kennedy also dismissed the academy representatives that informed the group.

In a recent development, “Essentially, we had no voice anymore,” recalls O’Leary, the pediatric infectious disease researcher at the University of Colorado Anschutz. He also serves as the AAP’s immunization schedule editor. “So we made a decision to not participate until we could say, ‘OK, this is a body that can be trusted.’ ”.

According to recent reports, in July 2025, the academy and other public health groups sued over the ACIP firings. The committee was unable to meet due to the lawsuit, and over the next six months, the CDC removed recommendations from its childhood vaccination schedule including hepatitis A and B, COVID-19 and meningococcal disease. The American Academy of Pediatrics issued its own schedule including those vaccines in January 2026.

Svetlana Repnitskaya/Getty Images Plus.

The loss of trustworthy federal recommendations leaves “an impossible gap to fill,” O’Leary says. But when it came to stepping in, “from my perspective, there was not an alternative.” The academy has since collaborated with the Vaccine Integrity Project, a new group led by Osterholm, to conduct the scientific reviews that inform vaccine recommendations.

Vaccines weren’t the only childhood health matter to get a shakeup. In April 2025, HHS terminated the Advisory Committee on Heritable Disorders in Newborns and Children, which formulates newborn screening recommendations for genetic disorders, many of which can be deadly or disabling. Currently, some 98 percent of U.S.-born infants are screened at birth.

In a recent development, when the genetics community raised concerns, Cynthia Powell, a retired pediatric geneticist at the University of North Carolina School of Medicine in Chapel Hill, gathered around 15 representatives of professional medical societies to create the Newborn Screening Collaborative. With support from the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics, the group began meeting in early 2026.

Recent findings suggest that while the collaborative cannot give direct recommendations to HHS, it hopes to conduct evidence reviews for states and the small, parent-led advocacy groups that form around rare diseases, Powell states. It looks to focus on conditions that already have treatments under development, like a rare metabolic disorder known as Sanfilippo syndrome type A.

Approximate number of NIH and NSF grants canceled or suspended in 2025. Some 5,200 have since been reinstated.

“This Newborn Screening Collaborative is another effort not to leave a complete void,” says Jewel Mullen, an epidemiologist at the University of Texas at Austin who was lead editor on a May 2025 newborn screening report for the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering and Medicine.

Recent findings suggest that other researchers are filling gaps in awareness about public health threats. A philanthropy-backed group called the Evidence Collective posted about the diarrhea-causing cyclosporiasis outbreak before the CDC’s Health Alert Network did. The collective, made up of more than 30 medical communicators, has more than 10 million followers across social media and notched 11 billion impressions in 2025.

“I don’t think that we will ever be able to fully replace the infrastructure that was there through the federal government,” says Madison, a founding member of the collective. But “there is a concerted effort now to look at: How do we take the momentum that we have with these organizations, and then make it sustainable?”.

Although stopgap measures are succeeding so far, scientists see them as Band-Aids at best. “We’re going to do it for as long as we’re needed,” Osterholm indicates. But “I look forward to the day when we’re not going to be needed anymore.”.

In April 2025, nearly 400 scientists working on the National Climate Assessment, a recurring, congressionally mandated report, received an email that it was being reevaluated and they were being released from their work. One of them — Rutgers University climate scientist Bob Kopp — wasn’t surprised. “I don’t think you have to speculate very far” to know why, Kopp says. He cites a directive in the White House’s 2027 budget request to “stop wasting biological and environmental research resources on climate change.”.

Industry observers note that however, “there was an immediate and deep sentiment by the science community to continue the work,” says environmental engineer Costa Samaras of Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh, who had also been involved with the climate report. He and colleagues asked the American Geophysical Union and the American Meteorological Society to help organize the U.S. Climate Collection, a upcoming set of papers from scientists about climate research, risks and solutions that will keep the public informed until federal assessments resume.

While the work is promising, “a volunteer effort of 170 scientists cannot substitute for a $30 million effort of 600 people,” Kopp says.

Industry observers note that the American Geophysical Union similarly stepped in with crucial financing for the Arctic Report Card, an annual report from NOAA that has provided information about the changing Arctic since 2006. Its editors were blindsided when they found out during a routine meeting in August 2026 that NOAA was withdrawing its support.

AGU’s in-kind offer to support the project just one month later was “tremendous,” claims Twila Moon, a glaciologist at the National Snow and Ice Data Center in Boulder, Colo., who edits the report card. “But [it] is not a kind of model that is sustainable into the future.”.

AGU President Brandon Jones agrees. Nevertheless, at the time, the organization “had this sense of what was moral, what was right, what was ethical,” Jones indicates. And given AGU’s resources, “it seemed like it was our turn to show up and step up and act like the union that we’ve always been.”.

The Planetary Society, a nonprofit space advocacy organization based in Pasadena, Calif., took the lead on several committees that NASA dropped. In January, the agency cited executive orders as it withdrew financial and logistical support from eight groups of space scientists and experts that advised NASA’s planning teams on exploring asteroids, comets and planets.

Industry observers note that “It was pretty well-managed and organized [before], and then really fell apart because of the intrusion of the executive orders,” indicates Jack Kiraly, chief of advocacy at the Planetary Society. The organization now hosts the advisory groups’ websites, documents and meetings. “We’ve basically been having to reinvent this whole system.”.

Chris Gunn, Courtesy of Schmidt Sciences.

Recent findings suggest that climate.us isn’t the only site saving federal data. In November 2024, many environmental organizations “started preparing for the worst,” says Brittany Janis, executive director of the Open Environmental Data Project. Her group and nine others banded together to create the Public Environmental Data Partners, a network of 400 volunteers that archive environmental data and tools they suspected “would probably be on the chopping block.”.

In February 2025, the Environmental Protection Agency deleted a tool called EJScreen, which maps places where people face high levels of risk from environmental burdens such as hazardous waste and ozone. Within 48 hours, the partnership had stood up EJScreen on a new website, using open-source files to reverse engineer and refine the data pipelines. It has since received 1,000 views a month, Janis says.

It has been revealed that nearly $2 million in philanthropic funding has helped the project pay staff, host data and hire engineers. It has restored the Federal Emergency Management Agency’s Future Risk Index, which projects county-level economic losses from climate change; the White House Council on Environmental Quality’s Climate and Economic Justice Screening Tool, which identifies communities overburdened by pollution; and the Department of Homeland Security’s Homeland Infrastructure Foundation-Level Data tool, which maps infrastructure at risk of natural disasters.

Industry observers note that “We should not misunderstand the administration’s closing off of this data [to mean] that they don’t think data is crucial,” Janis says. “They recognize how important it is — and how valuable it is to causes that they disagree with.”.

At the University of Chicago, the Data Mirror Project preserves datasets larger than one terabyte, including those from the U.S. Census Bureau and the National Park Service. The project has a guiding principle: LOCKSS, which stands for lots of copies keeps stuff safe, notes colead Lisa Chinn, who is head of research data services at the university library. An agency doesn’t have to delete its data to create problems, she adds. Firing website staff can lead to wonky links, corrupted files and pages that degrade into Wingdings gibberish.

The thought of losing all that data can be stressful, Janis says, but “there’s a lot of parachutes that have gone out.”.

Industry observers note that even as researchers, volunteers and scientific organizations pick up the pieces of the federal science enterprise, some are already imagining upcoming ways of shaping it. “The world was not perfect in 2024,” claims Rutgers’ Kopp. “Reconstruction is an opportunity to improve upon the way things are done.”.

Industry observers note that to Mullen, the epidemiologist at the University of Texas at Austin, transparency is key. New bodies like the Vaccine Integrity Project and the Newborn Screening Collaborative should make their meetings and deliberations as open as possible, she says, especially when “people think that those with the loudest voices or the biggest wallets are going to be the ones that have the greatest influence behind the scenes.”.

It has been revealed that powell, of the Newborn Screening Collaborative, is hoping for greater efficiency in the disease recommendation process. Previously, it could take as long as three years to bring a condition from an initial vote to a final recommendation; with the collaborative, she hopes it could take one to three months.

It has been revealed that janis, of the Open Environmental Data Project, hopes to develop more creative and flexible data tools for researchers based on their needs. And Madison from the Evidence Collective and Martin of OnlyMarms believe that the science infrastructure needs to diversify its funding sources to prevent future shocks.

“If we really think these things need to exist in the world … then we need to build them out.”.

However, Janis notes that there are inherent risks in having the private sector support public goods such as open information. And Kopp warns that “attempts to replace something that was well-functioning … are not going to necessarily end up with something that is better or even as good as what was there before.”.

At the end of the day, one of the key elements in establishing a new science system is “faith that you will still exist in a year or 10 years or maybe even 20 years,” indicates Katharine Jacobs, an environmental scientist who directed a previous National Climate Assessment under President Obama. Without stable institutional funding, “we are all essentially wasting our time, bashing our heads against the wall, trying to create a system that we can’t support,” Jacobs says.

For the Lindsey sisters, being involved in public service — even outside the government aegis — has been empowering, especially during what they see as an otherwise dark period for science.

In a recent development, they have raised more than $600,000 from individual donations since August 2025. And in February, they received a one-time grant from the Doris Duke Foundation and others that will cover their salaries and benefits until February 2027.

“If we can get the money, I can see us doing this indefinitely,” Rebecca Lindsey claims. She still hopes to retire one day, and she fights off worries that the government might come knocking about their unsanctioned work. But “we had a public that trusted us,” she says about jumping into the fray. “It was a risk worth taking.”.

The 6 Best Metal Detectors for Treasure Hunters and Experts Alike

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

You've probably seen a metal detectorist hard at work at a beach or park with their funky-looking gadget and thought, "I wish I had one of those." It's easy to fantasize about stumbling upon a hoard of buried pirate gold or, more realistically, a lost piece of jewelry, but the reality of metal detecting is this: It's more about the process of searching than the actual find itself.

That mentioned, metal detecting can be a fun and relaxing hobby for anyone to try, especially with friends, and the barrier to entry is low. It’s an activity that gives you an excuse to spend a few hours outside, scouring the sand or dirt for coins or who-knows-what, and you might even find something that really makes it worth your while, though it's best if you don't expect to.

According to recent reports, to determine the best metal detectors for newbies and experts alike, I tested a number of different models on the beaches and in the parks of South Florida, rating their performance, handling, and overall usability across several different terrains. I also consulted with an expert detectorist who helped me understand what factors to consider when making my choices. No matter which of these machines works best for your use case, all of them are great gets.

I selected the best metal detectors after trying a handful of options that came recommended to me by Jeff Lubbert, an expert detectorist who has been tracking down treasures and finding lost rings since the mid-1980s, and a handful of other expert detectorists.

Recent findings suggest that lubbert has used his metal detector in 28 states, one United States territory, five foreign countries, and three foreign territories, where he has recovered items adding up to approximately $980,000. He is president of the Eureka Treasure Hunters Club in Denver, Colorado, and has written articles about metal detectors for outlets like American Diggers. He's also appeared on the TV show Forensic Files.

Sources indicate that to test accuracy, I buried an old spoon and two different coins—a quarter and a penny—8 inches underground to check their level of discrimination and pinpointing. I also used each detector for several hours in a variety of conditions, including in a grassy park and at the beach, in both dry sand and wet sand, and under several inches of surf.

The Minelab Vanquish 560 is a dynamic metal detector that works well on every terrain, including wet sand, and is incredibly intuitive to use. Unlike the slightly cheaper Vanquish 440, my previous top recommendation, the 560 is waterproof to 16 feet, which makes it suitable for wading and underwater use. It also includes a rechargeable battery, a flashlight, and Bluetooth headphone support, making it one of the most fully-featured detectors in this guide, and especially for this price.

While it only has four find modes (including an adjustable “custom” option). That’s are far fewer than you will find on professional-grade detectors like the Minelab Equinox 900, but it's still much more than enough for most amateur metal detectorists.

The Vanquish 560 punches well above its weight, and value-wise, it's the best detector we tested on a per-dollar basis. It may feel like a splurge for first-timers, but you’re getting what you pay for. And it’s an incredibly handsome upgrade for folks looking strong accuracy and some quality-of-life improvements.

Industry observers note that since I primarily spoke with experts and enthusiasts, the Nokta FindX Pro was not remotely on my radar when I first began my research. But it may just be the best option for upcoming detectorists looking to dip a toe into the hobbyist pool. It’s an all-in-one kit, complete with an effective digging tool, a nice duffel bag, and decent headphones—all for less than $200.

Recent findings suggest that while it is not as accurate as my other recommendations, it’s a more than capable VLF detector. I was able to find items at both parks and beaches, though I noticed that its performance really suffered on wet sand and underwater. Its compact frame and adjustable handle make it accommodating to a wider-than-average range of newcomers, including kids and adults.

If you’re interested in the hobby and don’t want to spend too much to try it, the FindX Pro is a great fit for beginners.

Recent findings suggest that while I wasn’t able to get this detector in for my current round of tests, Lubbert recommended the Minelab Manticore for expert detectorists who want the ultimate metal detector experience. He notes it can visualize the ground beneath it in a 2D map, directing you to finds with depths and ID targets. It should work well in any terrain, including underwater, and has the most advanced backlight of any Minelab machine. Plus, with 10 search modes, there are many options for veteran detectorists looking to optimize for a specific type of search.

The price is substantial, but if you’re willing to spend this much money on a detector, I’m confident that it will be worth it.

The Simplex line is often recommended by experts as a good entry point for fresh detectorists. Nokta is one of the two biggest brands in the metal detecting game—the other is Minelab—and the Simplex Lite is a strong, basic VLF detector. I found it had top-notch discrimination, plenty of find modes, and a good coil size that easily found my testing materials and led me to beer cans, aluminum foil, and plenty of other objects on the beach.

It has been revealed that because this is a single-frequency VLF detector, it doesn’t perform as well as the Vanquish 440, especially on the mineralized sand at saltwater beaches. It’s still a very capable machine, though—even more so if you’re searching for a specific type of item, particularly coins and jewelry. Though it offers fewer customization options than its more expensive multi-frequency counterparts, it’s also much easier to pick up and use as a newcomer.

For those who are looking to spend a bit more, you can upgrade to the Simplex Ultra, which adds Bluetooth support and gives you precision detector tools like target ID scale and depth.

Underwater metal detecting is typically the domain of serious enthusiasts, especially if it’s in seawater. If this sounds intriguing, two different experts for metal detector recommendations (including Lubbert) suggest the XP Deus II, a high-end machine that specializes in just that. Expert Stanley Ross, known as the Metal Detector Man, who we spoke with for this article previously, indicates that he uses his Deus II to search for lost rings and other jewelry on the beach all the time.

In a recent development, the Deus II has something called "fast multi-frequency" technology, which allows for superior multi-frequency detection in a variety of conditions, and it's rated for up to 20 meters of water, a massive upgrade compared to our other picks that top out at 5 meters of water resistance. Our other multi-frequency picks use similar technology, but the Deus II offers better and faster response in saltwater conditions, making it easier to pinpoint buried targets without having to pass over the same spot multiple times, especially underwater.In order to use the Deus II underwater, however, you'll need a few accessories, including its waterproof wireless headphones and an underwater remote control. While these upgrades are technically “optional” in the sense that you can easily use the Deus II on land without them, they are virtually required for anything beyond getting your ankles wet.

Sources indicate that both of these additions will increase the price of the overall package considerably, depending on which exact model of headphones you choose. Both the $280 WS6 headphones (which can control the detector, but are not recommended for underwater use) and the $749 remote control have slightly different interfaces, but the remote control is generally recommended for both ease of use and underwater functionality. Because of its high customizability and 12 preset modes, the Deus II isn't quite as beginner-friendly as some of our other picks.

While I haven't yet tested the Deus II for myself, it’s highly regarded among enthusiasts. If you're interested in underwater detecting—whether that's wading around or even diving down—this choice will not disappoint.

Recent findings suggest that the Minelab Equinox 900 is the most feature-rich metal detector I tested. From the second I picked it up, I could tell that it would be a cut above the rest. The build quality is noticeably better than that of other, less expensive models I tested—it just feels more substantial.

Recent findings suggest that its features and performance back up that first impression. The Equinox 900 consistently performed better than its less expensive counterparts as well, pinpointing targets precisely and identifying both their depth and target ID. Though I was able to find my planted targets with every detector, the Equinox 900 directed me precisely to all three, making the process quicker and easier in both dry and wet sand.

It also features a number of settings and tools that improve the detecting experience, including six customizable frequency settings, an easy-adjust handle, and Bluetooth support so you can use wireless headphones. All that customization is incredible if you’re an expert. I personally had more success using the premade settings, but I can see detectorists like Lubbert fine-tuning searches to great effect.

Industry observers note that I was especially taken with its handgrip vibration feature, which gives you a rumbling haptic response when the Equinox picks up a target. It’s a great way to get your attention in a loud area, if you’re hearing-impaired, or if you’re just on a long walk and not paying close attention. Personally, I found it very helpful while roaming some very popular stretches of Miami’s beaches.

It’s worth noting that Minelab lists the Equinox 900 as a bit heavier than the other models we tested, though I personally didn’t notice a difference, even after several hours of sweeping. At more than triple the price of my best overall pick, it’s fair to say that the Equinox 900 is an investment for serious hobbyists. But it is far and away the most effective choice I tested and a worthy upgrade.

Sources indicate that in addition to a decent pair of headphones, it helps to carry a pinpointer when using your metal detector. These precise, short-range auxiliary detectors assist you with determining the exact location of a find after picking something up with your detector’s large coil.

This one, from Minelab, is relatively expensive, but fully waterproof with five sensitivity levels, and it works very well. It also features ferrous discrimination, which allows it to tell if a target is made of ferrous metals like iron or non-ferrous metals like gold, silver, or copper. It isn’t strictly necessary but is an extra feature you’ll enjoy using in trash-filled parks.

Recent findings suggest that we tested and loved the Minelab Vanquish 440, a slightly cheaper version of our current best overall pick, the Vanquish 560. It was recently replaced with a new and improved model, the Minelab Vanquish 460, which is also a strong choice. We ultimately chose to recommend the 560 because it offers a more robust set of features and works well over more types of terrain.

While shopping for a metal detector, you need to take into account a number of key factors, particularly the type, coil size, weight, and extra features like backlight and frequency customization. Weight and build quality also make a big difference, especially when you use these devices for hours at a time. It was initially hard to weigh these distinct traits, but after testing these machines myself, the features worth springing for became clear.

If you’re going to shop for a hobby-grade metal detector, it’s vital to understand how they work. This is fairly technical equipment, so manufacturers will cater their products primarily to veterans who already have a bit of knowledge, which may be intimidating to new people.

According to recent reports, most metal detectors have a round head called the “search coil,” which is the actual detector itself. It has two parts, the transmitter coil and the receiver coil, which work in tandem to produce an electromagnetic field that shoots down into the ground wherever you wave it. When the field hits metal, it triggers another magnetic effect in response, which the coil picks up. Depending on the device, that signal may be able to tell you how deep an object is buried, based on the strength of the response.

Most of the detectors I recommend can determine what kind of metal they’re reading by measuring the object’s “phase shift,” or the time it takes for the object to react when the coil changes its magnetic current. This function, called “discrimination,” can sometimes help you figure out if your quarry is worth digging up before you go to the trouble of getting your digging tools out. However, as Lubbert notes, discrimination is not always reliable, and it’s generally best to err on the side of digging if you think you’ve found something worthwhile.

In a recent development, the first thing to look at before buying a metal detector is where you blueprint to use it, as some detectors are better equipped to scan specific types of terrain. For example, if you live near the coast and plan to sweep your local beach, you may want a different model than someone looking under hard soil in local parks. Though there are many kinds of detectors, I focused on the two most frequently used by novices and veteran hobbyists.

Industry observers note that the physical size of the metal detector coil is important, too. If you don’t sweep the coil over an object, you aren’t going to get a ping, so bigger is better. Under most conditions, Lubbert recommends looking for a coil that’s at least 11 inches in diameter.

In a recent development, that mentioned, Lubbert advises that smaller coils have their uses, especially in wooded areas, since it’s easier to get between twigs, grass, and weeds with a more compact head. Larger coils can theoretically detect objects that are deeper underground, but they’re also more susceptible to electromagnetic interference from the environment. He recommends having both a compact coil and a large coil option if you proposal to scan a wide range of environments.

In general, all of my recommendations here seem relatively light on paper—the heaviest weighs only a few pounds. Keep in mind, though, that you could be waving this device around with one arm for hours at a time. Even a few ounces can greatly impact how swiftly you tire out.

Recent findings suggest that mid-range and high-end metal detectors tend to feature backlit displays, which come in handy when searching in low-light conditions. (Some high-end models even come with flashlight functions). Though not a universal feature, I consider this essential for all but the cheapest options.

According to recent reports, high-end metal detectors grant you a degree of customization through advanced settings, allowing you to set a specific level of discrimination that, when properly used, can help you identify relics and coins in a variety of environments. You need to know what you’re doing to take full advantage of these do-it-yourself search modes, but there are guides online to help you learn as you go.

According to recent reports, lastly, most metal detectors I researched and/or tested feature built-in batteries that last for hours on a full charge. That noted, some models—including one of my picks—use disposable batteries instead. There are advantages and disadvantages to both: Disposable batteries can be replaced promptly, but you need to keep spare cells on you. It comes down to your preference, so go with what feels right.

Industry observers note that “Make each swing of the detector take about 2 seconds and overlap your swings so that the coil covers all of the ground,” Lubbert indicates. “Wear headphones, as it helps you hear those deep target whispers.”.

It has been revealed that lubbert also noted that detectorists should be happy with what they find, and that you should expect 95 percent of your digs to result in trash. When that happens, be cool, and make sure to dispose of it properly.

According to Lubbert, a dedicated detectorist should have a pinpointer, proper recovery tools like a shovel, and a pouch to store trash and treasure separately.

Based on my testing experience and to echo his point above, I found headphones to be a must-have when using a metal detector, as the built-in speakers are difficult to hear, especially on a crowded beach.

It has been revealed that finding a legal place to use your metal detector is not as easy as you might think. It’s illegal to use a detector in U.S. National Parks and historic battlefields. Many cities ban using them on public property or require you to apply for a permit beforehand. Make sure to check your local city and county laws to determine if and where you may be allowed to use a metal detector and if you’ll need a permit to do so.

And, of course, if you strategy to use your detector on private property, you should obtain permission from the owner, or else you might dig up a lawsuit instead of treasure.
