Industry observers note that "We can do all things, we don't have to do one versus the other," Duffy mentioned in the Fox News Sunday interview. "I don't think that is the answer. The answer is let's do everything that's going to keep Americans safe, whether it's with immigration or it's with air travel.".

Industry observers note that meanwhile on the Senate floor, the energy permitting overhaul bill faces a key test Monday evening​, with a vote scheduled to limit debate on a substitute amendment that represents the most recent version of the bill. Votes on a number of President Donald Trump's judicial nominations are also lined up this week.

According to recent reports, on the other side of the Capitol, the House floor schedule i​ncludes several labor-related bills. ​One of the measures, introduced by Sen.-elect Kevin Hern, R-Okla.,​ would set standards for the way labor law applies to franchise operators.

New member orientation is also continuing, and committees in both the House and Senate will be holding hearings throughout the week as the outgoing Republican committee chairs aim to get through priority items on their agenda before the end of the Congress.

Latest Update: Earth's Atmosphere Took Three Deep Breaths of Oxygen Before the Oceans Caught Up

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1456 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Earth formed about 4.5 billion years ago, along with the rest of the planets.
  • According to recent reports, earth is one substantial system.
  • It has been revealed that cyanobacteria used sunlight to split water molecules apart.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Earth formed about 4.5 billion years ago, along with the rest of the planets. Life appeared somewhere between about 4.28 and 3.8 billion years ago; it's difficult to determine clearly. An oxygen atmosphere is a more recent development for Earth, in geological timescales, and understanding how that happened is a significant part of understanding the present-day Earth.

According to recent reports, earth is one substantial system. The atmosphere, the oceans, and life itself are all parts of the system. In some respects, they can be studied in isolation. But when trying to understand Earth and its long history, they need to be understood together. The system changed significantly when life changed. Somewhere around 2.4 billion years ago, cyanobacteria appeared, and they brought a upcoming trick with them: photosynthesis.

It has been revealed that cyanobacteria used sunlight to split water molecules apart. That did two things: it generated their chemical energy, and it released free oxygen into water, which eventually found its way into the atmosphere. That was a monumental stage of Earth's development that eventually led to an ozone layer, letting life flourish on the surface. The oxygenation of the atmosphere also led to complex life like us.

Recent findings suggest that but this all happened a long time ago. At first, the oxygen didn't accumulate in the atmosphere, and figuring out how it all played out isn't simple. Scientists know that the oxygenation history of the ocean and the atmosphere are coupled, but there are many questions. Some researchers argue that the atmosphere's oxygenation took place in different stages, one of which was the Great Oxygenation Event (GOE), while others have argued that the process was smoother. The debate continues.

New research in The Innovation shows how Earth's atmosphere was oxygenated in three distinct steps, and that the deep ocean lagged behind in each case. In the last of the steps, deep ocean oxygenation lagged behind by 600 million years.

The research is titled "Stagewise oxygenation of the Earthâs atmosphere and oceans," and the authors are Haiyang Wang and Chao Li, geochemists at the Chengdu University of Technology.

It has been revealed that "Earthâs surface oxygenation was a protracted, multi-step process," the authors write. "It is widely accepted that atmospheric O2 rose through three major steps, each closely linked to key evolutionary innovations.".

Industry observers note that the oceans and the atmosphere are linked, and during the quest to understand Earth's oxygenated atmosphere, researchers used the geological rock record to understand ocean chemistry. The well-known banded iron formations are a part of this. They record the ocean's oxygen levels. The atmosphere doesn't hold an ancient record, so the ocean's geological record was used as a proxy for the atmosphere's evolution and oxygenation, too.

So scientists largely think that three stages of rising oxygen created the modern atmosphere: the GOE about 2.4 billion years ago, the Neoproterozoic Oxygenation Event about 800 to 540 million years ago, and the Paleozoic Oxygenation Event about 400 million years ago.

The researchers reiterate the understanding that ocean and atmospheric oxygenation are coupled. Research highlights that on billion year timescales, episodes of rising atmospheric oxygen precede the same episodic rise in ocean oxygenation, "whereas on shorter, million-year timescales, their redox states could diverge, exhibiting negative coupling," they write.

"Here, we synthesize geochemical, sedimentological, and palaeobiological evidence to reconstruct this coupled and dynamic atmosphere-ocean oxygenation history and to reassess its timing, mechanisms, and ecological consequences," the authors explain.

This work hinges on new geochemical proxies that give researchers a clearer picture of what happened so long ago.

"Recent advances in geochemical proxies, most notably sulfate triple-oxygen isotopes (Îâ²17O), provide new constraints on atmospheric oxygenation, complementing and in some cases revising interpretations from traditional ocean redox proxies," the authors explain.

Sources indicate that the researchers say that this sulfate (SO4)offers a cleaner way to understand the oxygenation of the atmosphere. That's because of the isotopic composition of atmospheric oxygen, which is recorded when sulfate forms. It has a deficit of the isotope oxygen-17. So the sulfate can be used to track the rise of atmospheric O2, putting dates on each rise in atmospheric oxygen.

It has been revealed that they found that the GOE is unchanged, sitting between 2.4â2.1 billion years ago. But this work changes the dates of the second and third oxygen rises.

The second, the Neoproterozoic Oxygenation Event was 1.3â1.0 billion years ago instead of 800 to 540 million years ago. The Paleozoic Oxygenation Event was 0.42â0.36 billion years instead of 0.44â0.41 billion.

The researchers found something else, too. The previous dates for the Neoproterozoic and Paleozoic events still record something. But instead of dating atmospheric oxygen, they date the delayed oxygenation of the deep ocean. They lagged behind the oxygenation of the atmosphere by about 200 and 30 million years, respectively.

This graphic illustrates the results from newly introduced research into the oxygenation of Earth's atmosphere that highlights how Earth's O2 rose unevenly: shallow seas first, then the atmosphere, and much later the deep ocean. During a 2-billion-year transition, atmosphere and ocean O2 sometimes diverged despite long-term rise. Ocean oxygenation was highly variable, with extreme spatial heterogeneity over time. Image Credit: Stagewise oxygenation of the Earth's atmosphere and oceans. Wang and Li 2026, The Innovation.

On shorter timescales, the link between ocean and atmospheric oxygen is still the defining feature in this work. But it highlights that a change in one could've pushed the other in the opposite direction. The researchers think that what seems like a signal of rising oxygen levels is actually a drop. When a pulse of oxygen enters the ocean, it oxidized organic carbon and sulfide in the oceans. The organic carbon becomes CO2, and the sulfide becomes sulfate. The more organic carbon and sulfide there was in the ocean, the more it depleted atmospheric oxygen.

Sources indicate that over longer, billion year timescales, the atmophere is oxygenated as photosynthesis continues. But on shorter timescales, it can't keep up.

It has been revealed that "Earthâs surface oxygenation history reflects a dynamic and nonlinear interplay among atmospheric O2 evolution, land and ocean redox buffering, and ecological innovation," the authors write. "Overall, the trajectory from localized Archean oxygen oases to the globally well-oxygenated surface environments of today underscores how atmosphere-ocean oxygenation both governsâand is reciprocally shaped byâthe evolution of life.".

In a recent development, this figure demonstrates the evolution of Earth's atmosphere-ocean redox states through time and space. (A) Before 2.4 Ga: atmosphere and oceans were largely anoxic, with oxygen restricted to localized, shallow-water oxygen oases. (B) From 2.4 to 1.0 Ga: atmospheric O2 remained low; oxygenated waters were confined to the ocean surface, and oxygen oases developed primarily along continental shelves. (C) Between 1.0 and 0.41 Ga: atmospheric O2 increased but fluctuated, while oxygenated waters progressively penetrated to greater depths, with shelf environments continuing to host oxygen oases. (D) Since â¼0.41 Ga: atmospheric O2 approached near-modern levels; deep oceans became pervasively oxygenated, whereas mid-depth waters developed oxygen minimum zones (OMZs) that waxed and waned (solid curves) in response to high organic matter export and oxygen consumption. DOC, dissolved organic carbon. Image Credit: Wang and Li 2026, The Innovation.

Industry observers note that it all happened in stages, as the different elements fed back on one another. This work indicates that during Earth's long path to an oxygenated atmosphere, the ocean and atmosphere didn't change in lockstep on shorter timescales. "Throughout the 2-billion-year oxygenation transition, atmospheric and oceanic oxygen levels were episodically decoupled on shorter timescales, superimposed on a long-term trajectory toward global oxidation," they write.

Industry observers note that the pair of researchers acknowledge some of the weakness in the evidence that paints this picture. The record of oxygen isotopes in sulfate is coarse, not exquisitely detailed. Beyond one billion years ago, the levels aren't well-constrained. So it's still more open to interpretation. There may be other steps in the path to oxygenation that aren't clear yet.

According to recent reports, understanding how life and the planet co-evolved together is a monumental task. Scientists know it happened, but all of the details are difficult to detect. But if it happened here, it almost certainly happened on any other habitable worlds.

"These deep-time perspectives illuminate the co-evolution of life and Earthâs surface environments and provide a conceptual framework for evaluating planetary habitability," the authors write.

Earth’s Soil Is Worth $325 Trillion – so Why Is Nobody Protecting It?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (797 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Saharan dust helps nourish the Amazon, showing why scientists argue that protecting soil requires countries to look far beyond their own borders.
  • It has been revealed that nearly everything we eat depends on the thin layer of soil covering Earth’s surface.
  • Estimates cited in a study published in the European Journal of Soil Science suggest that up to 40 percent of the world’s land is already degraded, putting US$44 trillion in annual economic output at risk.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Saharan dust helps nourish the Amazon, showing why scientists argue that protecting soil requires countries to look far beyond their own borders.

It has been revealed that nearly everything we eat depends on the thin layer of soil covering Earth’s surface. This vital resource also filters water, stores carbon, and supports ecosystems that sustain life. Yet despite its importance, soil remains without a dedicated international treaty to protect it.

Estimates cited in a study published in the European Journal of Soil Science suggest that up to 40 percent of the world’s land is already degraded, putting US$44 trillion in annual economic output at risk.

In a recent development, binding international agreements protect the atmosphere, biodiversity, and the high seas. Soil, an estimated US$325 trillion (A$473 trillion) natural asset, receives fragmented protection through agreements on climate change, biodiversity, and desertification.

It has been revealed that the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification focuses on drylands, while other agreements address individual functions such as carbon storage or biodiversity. None provides comprehensive, binding protection for soil as a planetary system.

The paper’s authors, University of Sydney soil scientists Dr. Quentin Styc and Professor Alex McBratney, argue that this gap partly reflects a misunderstanding of the resource itself.

“We have spent centuries classifying soils according to their different properties, uses and locations. But in doing so, we’ve lost sight of the bigger picture,” stated lead author Dr. Styc, from the university’s School of Life and Environmental Sciences and Sydney Institute of Agriculture.

According to recent reports, consider the connection between the Sahara Desert and the Amazon rainforest. Each year, around 27.7 million metric tons of Saharan dust cross the Atlantic, delivering roughly 22,000 metric tons of phosphorus to the Amazon. This natural fertilization replaces nutrients lost through flooding, helping sustain one of the world’s most biodiverse ecosystems.

Erosion, pesticide contamination, and microplastics can also spread across borders, while soil degradation can contribute to climate change and food insecurity far from the affected region.

In a recent development, “Soil doesn’t stop functioning at national borders. What happens to soil in one country can have profound consequences for ecosystems, economies and food security on the other side of the world.

“We have international treaties to protect the ocean and atmosphere. Yet the soil beneath our feet, which is fundamental to human civilization, remains without equivalent protection.”.

For Styc and McBratney, these links mean soil must be understood and protected as one interconnected global system.

Sources indicate that “These connections demonstrate why soil security cannot be achieved by countries acting independently,” Dr. Styc stated.

Sources indicate that “We need to think about soil in the singular, just as we increasingly talk about one ocean rather than separate oceans. It’s a change in language that reflects a much bigger change in how we understand our responsibility for the planet.”.

In a recent development, A proposal for international protection is already taking shape. Aroura, a global soil security think tank established at the University of Sydney, has outlined an eight-stage pathway toward a Global Convention to Secure Soil, targeting adoption in 2032. The proposed convention would coordinate international efforts while allowing countries to develop strategies suited to their environmental and economic circumstances.

Industry observers note that in October 2025, the International Union for Conservation of Nature approved a resolution calling for a binding international legal instrument on soil security. Ocean governance offers a model for what cooperation could achieve. After decades of negotiations, an international agreement protecting marine biodiversity beyond national jurisdictions entered into force in January 2026.

“When environmental damage crosses borders, international cooperation needs to match the scale of the problem. We cannot solve a planetary challenge with a patchwork of disconnected policies,” Dr. Styc said.

Industry observers note that aroura brings together an international panel of leading experts in soil science, economics, law, and social science to develop the scientific evidence and policy frameworks needed for a convention. It hosted the Third Global Soil Security Summit at the University of Sydney from October 20 to 23, 2026.

“Soil underpins our food systems, biodiversity, water security and climate resilience, yet it remains largely invisible in international environmental governance,” noted co-author Professor McBratney, a leading international soil scientist who was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society in 2026.

“Through Aroura, we are working to build the scientific and policy foundations for a global convention that recognizes soil as a shared responsibility. We have the knowledge and the tools. What we need now is international commitment.”.

Reference: “One Soil, One Planet, No Treaty” by Quentin Styc and Alex McBratney, 3 November 2026, European Journal of Soil Science. DOI: 10.1111/ejss.70448.

Funding was received from the Australian Research Council.

NASA’s Voyager 1 Just Made History One Light-Day From Earth

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1505 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • NASA’s Voyager 1 has made history after 49 years in space, reaching an astonishing 16.1 billion miles from Earth, where even light takes 24 hours to bring its signals home.
  • NASA’s Voyager 1 has reached a remarkable fresh milestone, becoming the first spacecraft to travel one light-day from Earth.
  • It has been revealed that A light-day is the distance light travels in one day, approximately 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NASA’s Voyager 1 has made history after 49 years in space, reaching an astonishing 16.1 billion miles from Earth, where even light takes 24 hours to bring its signals home.

NASA’s Voyager 1 has reached a remarkable fresh milestone, becoming the first spacecraft to travel one light-day from Earth. After more than 49 years in space, humanity’s most distant spacecraft is now so far away that even light takes a full 24 hours to reach it.

It has been revealed that A light-day is the distance light travels in one day, approximately 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers). Voyager 1 officially reached that distance at 2:16 a.m. PST (5:16 a.m. EST) on November 18.

According to recent reports, the extraordinary distance means that communicating with the spacecraft now requires immense patience. Scientists at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) in Southern California, which is managed by Caltech, received a radio signal from Voyager 1 early Thursday, exactly 24 hours after the spacecraft reached the milestone. Although the signal traveled at the speed of light, it still needed an entire day to cross the enormous distance separating the probe from Earth.

“Traveling a light-day is a singular feat for a spacecraft, but Voyager is so much more than a distant traveler. The Voyager mission would be remarkable just for what it contributed to planetary science with the Grand Tour of the outer planets,” mentioned Joe Westlake, director, Heliophysics Division at NASA Headquarters in Washington. “But it went on to become central to NASA’s fleet of heliophysics missions offering insights into the star that we all revolve around, the Sun.”.

Sources indicate that because distances in space are so enormous, astronomers often measure them using the time it takes light to travel between locations. In a vacuum, light moves at approximately 186,000 miles (299,000 kilometers) per second, making it the fastest known way for information to travel.

It has been revealed that consider a beam of sunlight passing Earth. It would reach the Moon in approximately 1.3 seconds and take about four hours to arrive at Neptune. From Neptune, that same beam would need another 20 hours to reach Voyager 1.

For an even larger comparison, a light-year, the distance light travels over an entire year, measures approximately 5.88 trillion miles (9.46 trillion kilometers).

Sources indicate that despite the historic achievement, Voyager 1 is at the moment experiencing a technical problem. NASA engineers have not received science or engineering data from the spacecraft since November 14. However, the probe continues to transmit a carrier signal, the radio signal normally used to send that information back to Earth. By detecting this signal and combining it with calculations of Voyager 1’s trajectory, engineers were able to verify that the spacecraft had reached the one light-day mark. They are continuing to investigate why the expected data are not arriving.

Voyager 1 and its companion, Voyager 2, began their extraordinary journeys in 1977. NASA debuted the twin spacecraft during a rare alignment of the outer planets that made it possible to explore multiple worlds on a single mission.

Operated by JPL, the Voyagers became the third and fourth spacecraft to visit Jupiter and Saturn. They also delivered the first high-resolution images of these planets, revealing extraordinary latest details about the giant worlds and their moons.

In a recent development, voyager 2 continued farther along its unique route, becoming the first spacecraft to closely examine Uranus and Neptune, the two distant planets known as ice giants. Today, both probes are traveling through interstellar space, making them the only human spacecraft to have ventured beyond the Sun’s protective bubble. Their instruments continue monitoring magnetic fields and other conditions influenced by the Sun at extraordinary distances.

“Voyager 1 crossing the light-day threshold is yet another historic feat on an extraordinary voyage of discovery,” mentioned Dave Gallagher, JPL director. “Above all, this milestone stands as a testament to the exceptional teams who built, programmed, and fly these spacecraft today, and who have overcome countless challenges to keep them connected to Earth across the vastness of space. As NASA pushes toward newly introduced frontiers in human and robotic exploration, Voyager and the people behind its success continue to inspire us to reach farther and dream bigger.”.

It has been revealed that the spacecraft are carrying more than instruments designed to explore the cosmos. Each Voyager also holds a Golden Record, a gold-plated copper phonograph record containing images and sounds representing life on Earth. The records were created as messages for any advanced civilization that might encounter the probes in the distant future.

It has been revealed that “Nearly half a century after leaving Earth, the Voyager mission continues to push the boundaries of human exploration. Its epic journey reflects the vision of Ed Stone, the Caltech physicist and JPL director who guided the mission for decades, and the curiosity and tenacity of generations of scientists and engineers who have carried that vision forward,” mentioned Ray Jayawardhana, president, Caltech. “Beyond its immense contributions to science, Voyager also captures something profound about the human spirit. We may never know where its journey will ultimately lead, but it will venture on, an enduring affirmation that humanity was here and we yearned to explore.”.

Voyager 1 is currently traveling at roughly 38,000 mph (61,155 kph). In 2012, it became the first spacecraft to cross the boundary of the heliosphere, the enormous region surrounding the Sun that is filled with particles and magnetic fields generated by our star.

According to recent reports, this protective region helps shield the solar system from cosmic radiation arriving from elsewhere in the galaxy. Beyond its outer boundary lies interstellar space, an environment that scientists had never directly explored with a spacecraft before Voyager 1 arrived. Voyager 2 crossed the same boundary in 2018, following a different path.

Recent findings suggest that although both spacecraft are now beyond the heliosphere, the Sun’s effects extend much farther than scientists once understood. By measuring conditions in this distant environment, the Voyagers are helping researchers investigate how far the Sun’s influence extends into the space between stars.

Recent findings suggest that “The Voyagers are revolutionizing our understanding of interstellar space, a previously unexplored region outside the heliosphere,” said Linda Spilker, Voyager project scientist at JPL. “One big surprise is the extent to which our Sun continues to affect interstellar space, all the way out to Voyager 1. Where does the Sun’s influence end and pristine interstellar space begin? Perhaps Voyager may endure long enough to answer that question.”.

According to recent reports, maintaining spacecraft that have operated for nearly half a century presents enormous engineering challenges. Over the years, the Voyager team has developed inventive solutions to problems involving aging components, including clogged thrusters and a malfunctioning computer.

One of the greatest challenges is the spacecraft’s steadily shrinking supply of electrical power.

Earlier in 2026, engineers took a calculated risk by shutting down three devices aboard Voyager 1 and replacing their functions with three alternatives that require less energy. This approach is helping the spacecraft conserve its remaining power and extend the useful life of its nearly 50-year-old radioisotope thermal generator.

The generator works much like a nuclear battery. Rather than relying on sunlight, which is extremely weak at Voyager’s distance, it produces electricity using heat released as plutonium undergoes radioactive decay.

As that process continues, the amount of available electrical power gradually decreases. Both Voyager spacecraft lose approximately 4 watts of power each year, forcing engineers to make increasingly careful decisions about which systems can remain active.

NASA expects the latest power conservation measures to allow both probes to operate their current collections of scientific instruments until at least the summer of 2027, when they will celebrate the 50th anniversaries of their rolls out.

It has been revealed that even after nearly five decades, NASA maintains regular contact with Voyager 1. Communication is handled by the agency’s Deep Space Network, a worldwide system of powerful radio antennas at three facilities that supports missions exploring the Moon and more distant regions of space.

The immense separation between Earth and Voyager 1 now makes even a simple exchange of messages a lengthy process. A command sent from Earth requires approximately 24 hours to reach the spacecraft. If Voyager 1 immediately sends a response, that signal takes another 24 hours to return.

In other words, a complete exchange of signals now requires about 48 hours, even though those signals travel at the speed of light.

“We listen to Voyager 1 every day and send commands to the spacecraft weekly. It just takes a little longer to communicate than it used to,” stated Suzanne Dodd, Voyager project manager at JPL. “Even traveling at the speed of light, signals now take 24 hours to reach the spacecraft and 24 hours to reach us. One day in the future, when it can no longer communicate with Earth, Voyager 1 will become humanity’s silent ambassador to the stars.”.

  • Recent findings suggest that winter will be here before you know it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that winter will be here before you know it. Easily one of the most laborious and hated chores of that season is shoveling the snow. Not only that, it can be dangerous. Beyond the strain it puts on your back, the American Heart Association claims it can increase the risk of a cardiac event for those with heart challenges, and the cold weather can hide symptoms that otherwise would give you pause. That’s why the best electric snow shovels not only make the task easier, but safer, too, for those at risk.

According to recent reports, of course, you should not mistake these for full-blown snowblowers. Because of their compact size and throwing range, electric snow shovels are best used for small homes with shorter walkways and fewer steps. Like their larger counterparts, they use augers to scoop up snow (no more than 6 to 8 inches, ideally) and launch it up to 25 feet through the air so you don’t have to bend or lift as you dig out after a storm.

Recent findings suggest that they also work well as supplemental tools for clearing out outdoor stairs, walkways, patios, decks, and anywhere else a snowblower may not be able to reach. If that sounds like it could help you out of a blizzard-induced jam this winter, we can steer you toward the best electric snow shovels that can make the chore as painless as possible.

Toro Power Shovel 60-Volt 12-Inch Electric Snow Shovel.

As a top name in yard tools, we are interested to see what Toro’s take on simple snow removal is.

Ego Power+ EGO POWER+ 12-Inch Electric Snow Shovel.

Ego has several models of electric now shovels. This one has adjustable fins to let you guide the direction of the snow you remove.

It has been revealed that we leaned on our personal experience with snow removal machines and conducted extensive research to inform our selections. Specifically, we looked at each machine’s clearing area, weight, battery life, and throwing distance. Because snow removal needs vary from property to property, we included larger models that can clear up to 6 inches of snow from two- to four-car driveways, along with lighter electric snow shovels that are easy to lift and maneuver in smaller areas, such as walkways and patios.

Though we still include one corded model as our best budget pick, we primarily focus on cordless models because for most people these days, the convenience of battery power beats having to drag a cord around on a cold day.

Most electric snow shovels max out with a fairly narrow clearing width and low clearing depth, potentially forcing you to do multiple passes to clear a proper path. This Earthwise model is an exception.

With a broad clearing width of 16 inches and a depth of 8 inches, it’s capable of clearing paths through deeper snow. And since it launches snow up to 32 feet away, you can use this machine to clear small driveways along with your walkways, deck, and patio.

On the other hand, this electric snow shovel is quite heavy. It has wheels, though, which make it easier to push and maneuver. It’s a tradeoff, but one that pays off if you live in an area that routinely gets 6 to 8 inches of snow in a night.

You may notice that our best overall is a bit cheaper than our best value pick. This is because we felt the wide clearing width and the fact that it has wheels to support your efforts made this a solid choice for many people.

According to recent reports, though higher in price than some of the other models on our list, there’s a lot that you get for the price, namely power and run time. With a larger battery than most, this electric shovel from Greenworks runs longer on a single battery than any other cordless electric snow shovel out there.

According to recent reports, it packs a good amount of power with a large 80-volt 4.0-amp-hour battery powering a brushless motor; you’ll get about 45 minutes of run time on a single charge. This snow shovel clears a 12-inch path through up to 6 inches of snow, then blows it 25 feet away, making it ideal for uncovering a large area after a light snowfall.

Just remember that with great power and runtime comes great weight. With the battery loaded, this machine weighs more than 19 pounds, so moving it around for 45 minutes can turn into a real workout.

If you want the most clearing power possible from an electric snow shovel, Earthwise is your brand. This corded model can carve a 16-inch-wide path through snow up to 8 inches high, which is significantly more than what you can expect from other brands. It’s also significantly more powerful, moving up to 430 pounds of snow per minute.

Sources indicate that for reference, most of our other picks move around 300 pounds per minute. As a result, it can handle deeper, slushier snow than most electric snow shovels. It also has a longer throwing distance than most corded or cordless electric snow shovels out there.

At 16 pounds, it’s pretty heavy, but like other heavy models, it has a pair of wheels so you can push it most of the time. In short, it offers the best snow removal capability of any machine this side of a snowblower.

Ryobi makes several types of cordless electric snow shovels, but this model is a head attachment for its Expand-It 40-Volt String Trimmer that you can swap in when the snow starts falling. The advantage here is that you aren’t limited to just one tool; you can swap in a variety of attachments to run on the same primary unit and battery. This makes a lot of sense if it only snows a couple of times where you live, and you only need a snow thrower infrequently.

It has been revealed that during our testing, we were impressed with this tool’s performance. In mere minutes, we were able to clear a wide path through 8 inches of snow (more than the max height of 6 inches this model is rated for) on a patio outside our office. It was not fresh snow, either; it was densely packed after sitting for several days. There were times when the shovel head froze up while trying to push through too much at once, but this was rapidly rectified by pulling back and pushing through again. The snow flies quite far, too, for such a small toolhead, at least 10 to 15 feet by our estimation.

Being able to fling snow that far is a good thing because this thrower can only send the snow straight forward (some models have adjustable fins that allow you to send it to either side). You need to be strategic about the direction you push to avoid creating more work for yourself if you have a long path to clear.

According to recent reports, we must admit, too, that while this electric snow shovel makes the job easier than a manual shovel, it does take a bit of strength to operate, especially since it doesn’t have wheels to help you stay balanced and moving. You can move it along the ground, but you may need to lift it slightly if the snow is packed or icy at the lower levels, and it doesn’t come with a shoulder strap to help you do that. If you aim to greatly reduce the physical strain of snow removal, models from our list that feature wheels and directional fins may be a better option.

Sources indicate that overall, if you already have the Ryobi 40-volt-compatible string trimmer, adding this attachment to your arsenal would be a good move if you only need to clear snow from a small driveway, walkway, deck, or patio. The 40-volt, 4-amp-hour battery will give you up to an hour of power, which is more than enough for a small job like that, and buying into this multitool system will keep it from being a tool that just sits in the toolshed or basement for most of the time.

The lightweight design of this cordless electric snow shovel makes it a great option if other electric snow shovels are too heavy for you to manage. Whereas most electric snow shovels weigh around 18 pounds, this one weighs just 13.5 pounds.

In a recent development, along with being lighter, the Snow Joe electric snow shovel also has a dual-handle design that allows you to operate it while standing up straight, taking pressure off your back. Despite its lighter weight, it can still clear a foot-wide path of snow up to 6 inches deep. The Snow Joe does have a shorter runtime than most, which limits it to lighter-duty snow removal, such as clearing walks, decks, and patios.

With its two 20-volt rechargeable batteries, the Worx electric snow shovel is both versatile and powerful. It can clear a path a foot wide and up to 6 inches deep and throw snow up to 25 feet, so it's suitable for clearing tighter spaces.

The two-battery design gives you the option to mix and match larger-capacity 20-volt Worx batteries to increase this shovel’s run time for larger jobs, such as clearing small driveways. It also comes with a dual charger, so you can charge both batteries simultaneously for a shorter turnaround time.

Another plus is that this model's batteries are compatible with other 20-volt Worx yard machines, making it a great option if you’ve already bought into the Worx product line.

Industry observers note that we’d be remiss if we didn’t point out that this whole category of yard machines has some limitations. Most electric snow shovels can only handle snow depths up to 6 inches—8 inches if you’re lucky—and lack the power to handle heavier slushy snow. They are ideally suited to powdery snow on walkways, patios, decks, and maybe a small driveway. If you see heavy snowfalls regularly or have a large number of driveways and parking spaces to clear, get a snowblower before you buy an electric snow shovel. For massive jobs, go with a gas snowblower. An electric snowblower works for small to moderate-sized driveways.

According to recent reports, when push comes to shove, we recommend looking for a cordless electric snow shovel rather than a corded one. Having the freedom to move without worrying about a cord makes the whole shoveling or snowblowing process much easier. That mentioned, if you’re on a tight budget or only need to clear a short walk or a small patio or deck that’s near an outdoor outlet, you can get by with a corded model.

Much like a snowblower, electric snow shovels are rated by how much snow they can move. The wider the shovel, the fewer passes it takes to clear an area. Most electric snow shovels move a 10- to 16-inch-wide path of snow. A small, narrow shovel is lighter and more nimble, making it useful for creating pathways. Wider, larger models are better equipped for clearing a patio or driveway, but are also heavier and more difficult to maneuver in tighter spaces.

Electric snow shovels can handle snowbanks around 4 to 8 inches high, depending on their clearing depth. Technically, you can remove deeper snowfall with these machines, but you’ll have to make more passes to do so.

For an electric snow shovel to be useful, it should be able to propel the snow far enough that it’s off the deck, walkway, or driveway that you’re clearing. Most electric snow shovels launch their snow between 20 and 30 feet, which is on par with entry-level, corded electric snowblowers, but shorter than cordless and gas snowblowers that can throw snow a distance of 40 feet or more. With that in mind, consider the route you plan to take while clearing, and make sure you’re moving the snow somewhere out of the way so it can sit until spring arrives.

It has been revealed that electric snow shovels process and throw snow like a snowblower, so you won’t need to bend over and scoop up snow as you would with a shovel. However, you should still look for the lightest possible option. While you won’t have to lift and throw snow as you would with a conventional snow shovel, you have to hold it upright and apply some force to push it through the snow. At the very least, you should look for a shovel that you can lift easily whenever you need to clear steps or multiple levels of patio.

According to recent reports, electric snow shovels typically weigh between 10 and 20 pounds. As you might expect, more powerful shovels that can move more snow and feature large batteries tend to be heavier than smaller, narrower models. Some large electric snow shovels have a set of wheels mounted to the rear of the base for standing upright on their own, so you can maneuver the machine with minimal lifting.

According to recent reports, similar to standard snow shovels, electric models come in both straight and curved handle varieties. A curved handle allows for standing more upright while operating the machine, putting less strain on your lower back and decreasing the risk of injury. A straight handle gives you more leverage for lifting loads of snow, but since an electric snow shovel has an auger that lifts and blows the snow for you, it’s not an advantage for electric models.

According to recent reports, electric snow shovels operate similarly to single-stage snow blowers. The shovel end of the machine has an auger that’s powered by an electric motor. As you push the shovel through the snow, the rotating auger collects snow, mashes it up, and then propels it through a shoot that throws the snow off to the side.

According to recent reports, the average electric snow shovel can churn through about 300 pounds of snow per minute. That means a snow shovel with a 12-inch wide intake and a clearing depth of 6 inches can remove about 4 inches of powdery snow from a 1,000 square foot driveway in about 20 minutes.

Just keep in mind that a shovel’s snow-clearing ability varies depending on certain conditions, such as the heft of the snow itself.

Industry observers note that it’s never a bad idea to have a standard snow shovel around. While the electric snow shovel can reach most spaces that a standard push-behind snowblower can’t, it may not always be able to clear hardened snow or wet slush.

Plus, a manual shovel ensures that you can always dig out in an emergency, like when you’ve lost power after a snowstorm.

Scientists Shine Upcoming Light on One of the Greatest Mysteries in Modern Physics

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (796 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The search for more efficient power grids could benefit from understanding a hidden rivalry inside copper-based superconductors, where a mysterious quantum state appears to compete with superconductivity.
  • When researchers used a pulse of light to temporarily suppress superconductivity in a copper-based material, a mysterious quantum state emerged.
  • According to recent reports, these materials, known as cuprates, were discovered in 1986, a breakthrough that earned Bednorz and Müller the Nobel Prize in Physics the following year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The search for more efficient power grids could benefit from understanding a hidden rivalry inside copper-based superconductors, where a mysterious quantum state appears to compete with superconductivity.

When researchers used a pulse of light to temporarily suppress superconductivity in a copper-based material, a mysterious quantum state emerged. As superconductivity returned, that state faded. The experiment offers upcoming evidence in a decades-old debate about how certain materials can carry electricity without losing energy.

According to recent reports, these materials, known as cuprates, were discovered in 1986, a breakthrough that earned Bednorz and Müller the Nobel Prize in Physics the following year. Their ability to become superconducting at relatively high temperatures has made them especially promising for future technologies, including more efficient power grids, medical equipment, and quantum computers. Yet nearly 40 years later, scientists still do not fully understand what makes their remarkable properties possible.

One of the biggest uncertainties involves the pseudogap, a poorly understood quantum state that appears in cuprates. Scientists have long debated whether it helps superconductivity emerge or competes with it.

“The pseudogap is one of the greatest mysteries in condensed-matter physics. Understanding how it interacts with superconductivity is essential if we want to explain why these materials can carry electricity without energy loss at unusually high temperatures,” indicates Fabio Boschini, a professor at INRS and specialist in ultrafast spectroscopy of quantum condensed matter.

Boschini, who led the research, holds the Canada Research Chair in Quantum Materials’ Dynamics and is a recipient of an Alfred P. Sloan Research Fellowship.

In a recent development, to investigate the relationship between the two states, his team used a pulse of light to briefly suppress superconductivity and then tracked how the material’s electrons behaved as it recovered. The researchers used time- and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (TR-ARPES), a technique that allows scientists to observe rapid changes in the electronic properties of materials.

The experiments took place at the INRS Énergie Matériaux Télécommunications Research Centre, using the TR-ARPES endstation at the Advanced Laser Light Source (ALLS).

The measurements revealed electronic states that had remained hidden from conventional techniques. For the first time, researchers directly observed a temporary pseudogap induced by light. When superconductivity was suppressed, the pseudogap emerged in its place. As the material regained its superconducting properties, the pseudogap gradually faded.

“Thanks to the unique capabilities of the TR-ARPES system at the ALLS laboratory at INRS, we were able to directly observe what happens when superconductivity temporarily disappears and then re-emerges. It is a bit like uncovering missing frames from a film that scientists have been trying to piece together for decades,” says Dario Armanno, a PhD student at INRS and first author of the study.

Published in Nature Physics, the findings support the idea that the pseudogap and superconductivity compete rather than cooperate. This challenges the long-standing hypothesis that the pseudogap acts as a precursor, or an earlier state that helps superconductivity develop.

The project also involved international collaborators, including the Center for Computational Quantum Physics at the Flatiron Institute in New York.

In a recent development, “The pseudogap and superconducting states in cuprates are among the most complex phenomena to reproduce theoretically. Our study reveals that they compete with one another and provides new insight into their behavior when both are excited simultaneously,” said Olivier Gingras, Associate Research Scientist at the Flatiron Institute’s Center for Computational Quantum Physics.

Although the work is fundamental research rather than a demonstration of a new technology, a clearer understanding of these competing quantum states could help guide the development of next-generation superconductors and more energy-efficient technologies.

Industry observers note that “This research is essential to advancing the quantum technologies of the future. It contributes to the training of highly qualified personnel in a field that is critical to Canada’s technological sovereignty and to the implementation of its National Quantum Strategy,” indicates François Légaré, Director of the INRS Énergie Matériaux Télécommunications Research Centre.

Reference: “Light-induced asymmetric pseudogap below the critical temperature in cuprates” by D. Armanno, O. Gingras, F. Goto, J.-M. Parent, A. Longa, A. Jabed, B. Frimpong, R. D. Zhong, J. Schneeloch, G. D. Gu, G. Jargot, H. Ibrahim, F. Légaré, B. J. Siwick, N. Gauthier, A. Georges, A. J. Millis and F. Boschini, 20 October 2026, Nature Physics. DOI: 10.1038/s41567-026-03446-6.

The work at ALLS was supported by the Canada Foundation for Innovation’s (CFI) Major Science Initiatives Fund. We acknowledge support from the Alfred P. Sloan Foundation, the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada (NSERC), the Canada Research Chairs Program, the Fonds de recherche du Québec – Nature et technologies (FRQNT), the Québec Ministry of Economy, Innovation and Energy, PRIMA Québec, and the Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation’s EPiQS Initiative.

Tiny Grains of Sand Act as Cosmic Speedometers for Alien Winds

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (998 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Weâve managed to take high-resolution orbital images of many worlds across our solar system, and many of them with an atmosphere have one feature in common - sand dunes.
  • Earth and Mars, the two most commonly thought of planets with sand dunes, arenât the only ones.
  • Understanding why this is vital requires looking at how wind actually moves sand in the first place.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Weâve managed to take high-resolution orbital images of many worlds across our solar system, and many of them with an atmosphere have one feature in common - sand dunes. Scientists have been using the size and orientation of these dunes for decades to act like a weather vane, figuring out which way the wind blows on these other worlds. Unfortunately, weather vanes arenât good at telling the full windy story - they canât tell you how fast the wind is going. However, according to a latest paper published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences by researchers at Stanford, sand dunes can.

Earth and Mars, the two most commonly thought of planets with sand dunes, arenât the only ones. Weâve also seen them on Venus, Titan, and, surprisingly, Comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko. Each is made up of different materials, but all share a crucial characteristic - their âsandâ consists of small grains of similar particles, which could be blown around by wind.

Understanding why this is vital requires looking at how wind actually moves sand in the first place. When air is moving across a dune, individual grains stay stationary until the wind itself reaches a critical speed known as the transport threshold. Once it rises above that, the grains begin bouncing across the ground in a movement known as saltation. Each time a grain crashes back to the surface, it kicks up other surrounding grains into the air, creating a self-sustaining cascade of moving sand.

Fraser talks about whether Martian dust storms are dangerous.

In a recent development, what was unclear to scientists was whether these motions were primarily driven by violent dust storms that were relatively rare, or moderate winds which are much more common on the other worlds where dunes have been seen. It might seem counter-intuitive that a comet would have âwindâ, but a 2017 study showed that the âripplesâ ESAâs Rosetta probe found on the comet's surface were created by localized vapor flows caused by extreme day-night temperature cycling.

It has been revealed that solving the mystery of what type of wind causes these shifting sands was the focus of the paper. Lead author M. Colin Marvin, a PhD student in the Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences at Stanford, collected wind speed data and detailed grain-size measurements from twenty-four different dune fields spread all over the world. From the Coral Pink Sand Dunes State Park in Utah to the ancient, hundred-meter-tall dunes in the Namib Sand Sea in Namibia, the researchers found a remarkable similarity.

Across every terrestrial site, the most sand was moved when the wind was slightly above the speed required to start moving it. And, crucially, the same relationship also held on a Maritan sand dune. The process didnât require the odd violent gale to get sand moving, just every day wind speeds common throughout the globe. For example, a dune made of sand 0.2 mm across (about the width of two pieces of paper) is mostly moved by winds blowing at only 26 kilometers per hour 10 meters above the ground.

Fraser talks about the Dragonfly mission, which will land next to dunes on Titan.

According to recent reports, with that data set in hand, the researchers then turned to simulations. Using a tool called ReSCAL, they grew virtual dunes from flat sand beds using different wind speeds. As part of that process, the team confirmed that, as long as a world has plenty of loosely bound grains of sand and winds that grow rarer as they grow stronger, dunes will largely be formed by the wind speeds that correspond directly to the grain sizes that compose them.

Industry observers note that despite the challenges of finding individual sand grain size from orbit, this technique is useful on more than just Earth. Curiosity has already drilled into the Stimson formation, a layer of sandstone that used to be a windblown dune billions of years ago. Another upcoming interplanetary mission â Dragonfly â is expected to touch down on the surface of Titan, where there are dunes of hydrocarbons, sometime in the 2030s.

Combining the grain size measurements from these missions with the math laid out in the new paper will provide scientists with a rough indication of the history of wind speed in the area. There will also undoubtedly be other missions to other dune-ridden planets - Venus comes to mind as a potential target. And from now on, scientists will be able to read a major part of a worldâs geological history directly written into its sand.

Stanford - Scientists discover sand dunes can reveal wind speeds on Earth and beyond.

These are the Thanksgiving sides recipes that Eater editors have vetted as being worth the space on our holiday tables.

Every year, my sister and I have a stuffing-off. Not that we’re all that competitive (we are), but she insists on having her signature mushroom and sage stuffing, and I insist on making the best stuffing. My recipe is just an old Gourmet magazine version of sausage cornbread stuffing with a bunch of fennel, but what makes it exceptional is my own riff on what is so often overlooked as filler when it comes to stuffing (or, depending on where you’re from, dressing): the bread cubes. I take the full loaves of Whole Foods’ signature cornbread, slice them into cubes, stick them in a low oven (around 200 degrees) for a few hours, and eureka! It’s a stuffing that delivers again and again.

Recent findings suggest that why are the store-bought loaves the key? I’m not quite sure. My hunch is that they’re just dense enough, un-fresh enough, and mass-produced enough to dry out easily, and the store’s recipe strikes some unicorn balance of flavor that compliments the fennel without making the dish overwhelmingly sweet. — Lesley Suter, brand director.

I keep coming back to this deeply savory, unexpected side dish when the weather turns cold. Its varying textures, ample acidity, and subtle sweetness are a welcome addition to any spread of holiday sides. Cabbage and bacon might be a familiar pairing, but the miso paste and Dijon that are swirled into the reduction offer a pleasant and welcome surprise to the palate. An added bonus: Jesse’s videos are some of the most relaxing and soul-soothing I’ve seen on the internet; it’s as if he invented food ASMR himself. Let them regulate your blood pressure this holiday season when that one in-law’s antics start to send you over the edge. — Nat Belkov, deputy brand director.

Nobody says they crave a salad at Thanksgiving, but I promise you they do, especially once the heaviness of everything else starts to set in. At the very least, I crave a salad at Thanksgiving, and the kind of salad I desire in an instance like this is something crunchy and bright and which tastes nothing like anything else on the table. Thus, some combination of citrus and fennel is generally my go-to. The citrus lends a brightness that pairs well with the cranberry sauce that’s inevitably on my plate, and I like the licorice sweetness of fennel amid the savoriness that dominates the spread; plus, I think it goes well with the celery that’s in other dishes.

While more complex takes on this kind of salad exist and sound delicious, I find the most pared-down versions easier to slot into my day of cooking. This salad is usually my very last task before we sit down to eat. Sometimes, I don’t even announce that it’s happening, so it seems like the “just threw this together,” afterthought touch that surprises you with how essential it ends up being. — Bettina Makalintal, senior reporter.

Tauba Auerbach, Salad for President by Julia Sherman.

Recent findings suggest that tauba Auerbach’s Brussels sprouts salad recipe in Julia Sherman’s book Salad for President is a pleasing salad with lots of crunchy textures and punchy flavors that’s become a go-to of mine for the holidays. Thinly shaved Brussels sprouts serve as the base of the salad, while lemon-marinated, toasted almonds add bite to the equation. The dressing adds tartness with sherry and cider vinegars, which is a nice juxtaposition against the season-sweet apple pieces. Don’t skip the pickled mustard seeds if you have the time, as they add another dimension of flavor. — Dianne de Guzman, regional editor, Northern California/Pacific Northwest.

Industry observers note that this is less of an elaborate recipe, and more of a plea: Please don’t bring steamed green beans to Thanksgiving dinner (or any holiday, for that matter). They’re hardly offensive, but I’ve always found them to taste a bit ghostly and one-note. Instead, I like this simple but impactful recipe of garlicky green beans. High-heat oil, garlic, and ice cubes at-the-ready will give you crispy green beans with a welcome, garlicky char to liven up the usual parade of sweet potatoes and all the beige classics. — Francky Knapp, staff writer.

According to recent reports, I have become the Sweet Potato Bringer at our family’s large, outdoor potluck Thanksgiving, mostly because I am the only one who must have them (or it’s not Thanksgiving, obviously). Every year, I bring a sweet potato casserole with essentially the same elements: mashed sweet potatoes — slow-roasting them in the oven lends a deeper flavor — brightened with things like orange juice or cinnamon applesauce; some sort of pecan-y crumbly brown sugar topping; and blistered marshmallows. It’s all very satisfying but can become somewhat formulaic, which is why, a couple years ago, I kicked it up a notch with Epicurious’s s’moresy take on the classic: In this recipe, the sweet potato mixture gets added earthiness from maple syrup and unsweetened cocoa powder, while the pecan topping’s punch-up is the addition of crushed graham crackers (you can buy them gluten-free to be more inclusive). It’s not a dramatically different flavor from the original, meaning the eternal crowd-pleaser lives on. — Nicole Fellah, dining editorial manager.

Mitchell Davis, Cook and Eat Better.

If I am having a holiday party with a spread, The Cheese Thing will be on the table and will be decimated promptly — my repeat guests have come to expect and crave it. The Cheese Thing defies explanation; what can be stated is that it’s very much a personal blog recipe, its name coined by Mitchell Davis and then surfaced more broadly on the internet by Bon Appétit back in 2018. On its surface, it just sounds like a sort of wonky baked ziti. It is the ultimate comfort recipe; cubes of cheese melt into the crevices of penne pasta, melding with a super-simple sweet and buttery tomato sauce. I absolutely shower it in salt, cracked pepper, and fluffy Pecorino, and sometimes bake extra cheese onto the top. I’d consider it a side because it lacks main-course energy and is ideal for a potluck or buffet, but there’s no doubt that it could serve as an entree on a chilly night for two, four, or however many people fit on your couch. — Hilary Pollack, deputy editor.

Two Overlooked “Forever Chemicals” Linked To More Than Double the Risk of Liver Cancer

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (925 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, two little-studied “forever chemicals” have been linked to substantially higher odds of liver cancer in a new University of Southern California (USC) study.
  • According to recent reports, the association was especially strong among people genetically predisposed to fatty liver disease.
  • Researchers analyzed blood samples from 223 people who later developed hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), the most common form of liver cancer, and 223 matched controls.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, two little-studied “forever chemicals” have been linked to substantially higher odds of liver cancer in a new University of Southern California (USC) study. People with the highest blood concentrations of either chemical had roughly two to two-and-a-half times the odds of developing the disease compared with those with the lowest concentrations.

According to recent reports, the association was especially strong among people genetically predisposed to fatty liver disease. Published in Environmental Health Perspectives, the findings suggest that inherited susceptibility may influence how environmental chemical exposures affect cancer risk.

Researchers analyzed blood samples from 223 people who later developed hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), the most common form of liver cancer, and 223 matched controls. The samples were collected an average of 7.8 years before diagnosis as part of the Multiethnic Cohort Study (MEC), which has tracked more than 215,000 participants in California and Hawaii since the 1990s.

Of the 12 per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) measured, two indicated significant associations with liver cancer: perfluoroheptanoic acid (PFHpA) and perfluorononanoic acid (PFNA).

Recent findings suggest that “The concerning thing about our results is that the strongest associations were not in the most studied legacy PFAS,” said lead author Jesse Goodrich, PhD, assistant professor at the Keck School of Medicine of USC. “They are among the newer PFAS, and we don’t have much information about their effect on human health.”.

In a recent development, the researchers also examined whether inherited susceptibility to metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), commonly called fatty liver disease, influenced cancer risk. They found that the association between PFHpA exposure and liver cancer was considerably stronger among participants with high genetic susceptibility to MASLD. No statistically significant association was detected among those with low susceptibility.

Industry observers note that “Our study indicates that genetic differences in how the liver processes fats may play an notable role in determining susceptibility,” Goodrich said. “You have this one-two hit: first, your genes and then PFAS impacting this pathway.”.

Industry observers note that PFAS exposure may disrupt liver fat metabolism, contributing to the fat accumulation associated with MASLD. Over time, the condition can progress to inflammation, scarring, and cancer. MASLD is an increasingly key driver of HCC, which has a five-year survival rate below 20%.

“PFAS have been linked to an increase in fat accumulation in your liver, and over time, that can actually increase the risk of liver cancer,” Goodrich said.

According to recent reports, PFAS are found in products such as nonstick cookware, food packaging, stain-resistant fabrics, and firefighting foams. Many resist degradation and persist in the environment for decades. These chemicals have been detected in drinking water across roughly half of U.S. water systems, while an estimated 99% of the global population has detectable PFAS in their blood.

Most regulatory attention has focused on older compounds such as perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) and perfluorooctanesulfonic acid (PFOS). PFHpA was developed as an alternative to these chemicals, which were phased out of many applications because of health and environmental concerns.

“PFOA and PFOS have received much of the scientific and regulatory attention, however, they represent only a small part of the PFAS family,” mentioned senior author Vaia Lida Chatzi, MD, PhD, professor at the Keck School of Medicine. “Our findings show why we need to look beyond those legacy compounds. We can miss notable associations with liver health if we study only the chemicals we already know best.”.

The PFHpA finding also supports results from an independent National Cancer Institute study published two months earlier. However, these observational studies cannot establish that PFAS exposure causes liver cancer.

Industry observers note that identifying people with both elevated PFAS exposure and high genetic susceptibility could eventually help guide earlier liver cancer screening. Reducing exposure may also offer a potential prevention strategy, although its effect on cancer risk remains uncertain.

“Our study actually provides something that is actionable,” Goodrich mentioned. “You can make lifestyle and diet changes and there are certain types of water filters you can put in that can reduce exposure. And if you have the information on genetic susceptibility, that could also provide additional evidence for things that you could do to mitigate risk.”.

The study is the first publication from a USC Norris Comprehensive Cancer Center research program supported by a $3.4 million federal grant to investigate PFAS and liver cancer.

Recent findings suggest that “This first paper from our NIH-funded study is an notable step. Drawing on the diverse Multiethnic Cohort, it adds to the evidence that some PFAS may be associated with liver cancer,” remarked senior author V. Wendy Setiawan, PhD, professor at USC. “We hope this work will help build the evidence needed to reduce harmful exposures and inform prevention efforts for diverse communities.”.

The team intends to investigate additional environmental exposures to better understand how chemicals encountered throughout life may contribute to cancer.

In a recent development, reference: “Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances, Hepatic Lipid Metabolism Genes, and Hepatocellular Carcinoma: Evidence of Gene–Environment Interactions in a Multiethnic Cohort” by Jesse A. Goodrich, Hongxu Wang, Adelynn Paik, Sihao Han, Brittney Baumert, Joseph Romano, Razieh Moghadam, Shiwen Li, Tanya L. Alderete, Syam S. Andra, Robert O. Wright, David V. Conti, Lida Chatzi and Veronica Wendy Setiawan, 6 November 2026, Environmental Health Perspectives. DOI: 10.1021/EHP.6c00546.

This research was supported by the National Cancer Institute under award numbers R01CA300355 and U01CA164973, and by the National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences under award numbers U2CES026555, U2CES026561, U2CES030859, and P30ES007048.

#168770. Breaking: This is the First Time Astronomers Have Seen One of These Stellar Mergers

Breaking: This is the First Time Astronomers Have Seen One of These Stellar Mergers

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1867 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that binary stars are common in the Milky Way.
  • Astronomers know that in some situations, binary stars share common envelopes (CEs).
  • It has been revealed that it all begins with common envelope evolution (CEE), a critical stage in the evolution of binary stars.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that binary stars are common in the Milky Way. Up to 40% Milky Way stars are binaries, though there's a lack of absolute certainty. Sirius, which is the brightest star in the night sky, is actually a binary star.

Astronomers know that in some situations, binary stars share common envelopes (CEs). It means that a body of gas surrounds both stars, but the gas doesn't move with either one separately. These envelopes are transitory; the CE creates drag that slowly draws the planets together, sometimes ending in an explosion. But it's difficult to predict when that will happen, and when astronomers should observe a particular binary star to learn more about it.

It has been revealed that it all begins with common envelope evolution (CEE), a critical stage in the evolution of binary stars. No two stars in a binary system are the same. One evolves and puffs up, overflowing its Roche lobe. Mass begins to pile up on its companion. That process becomes unstable, and the two stars become engulfed in a common envelope of gas.

It has been revealed that the common envelope exerts a powerful drag on both stars, and they're drawn closer together. After that, the CE is ejected and the two stars are left behind in a compact binary. The pair of tightly-bound stars can remain as a compact binary, or they can merge and cause an explosion, called a luminous red nova(LRN). Whether they merge and explode, or whether they remain as a compact binary, depends on how soon the CE is ejected. If the CE isn't dissipated soon enough, the continued drag forces the stars closer together until they merge and erupt.

It has been revealed that this simple graphic shows how common envelopes evolve. At first, on star fills its Roche lobe. Then, the companion is engulfed and both stars orbit one another inside the common envelope. Then, either the common envelope is ejected and the stars remain as a binary, or the common envelope isn't ejected, and the stars are forced to merge. Image Credit: By Philip D. Hall - Own work, CC BY-SA 4.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:Redirect/page/55287112.

This is a coarse overview of the process. Astronomers know it can happen, and they'd like to learn more about it. But they need to observe them, and that's tough to do. Not only are they difficult to predict, but they're also relatively rare.

It has been revealed that observations with the JWST and other telescopes have found one CE situation where a main sequence star a little less massive than the Sun spiralled into its CE partner, a puffy supergiant star, and erupted as a LRN. This happened in our neighbouring galaxy, Andromeda. The observations and details are in upcoming research in Nature titled "An inspiral of a star inside a common envelope with its giant companion." The first author is Viraj Karambelkar, a NASA Hubble Fellow at Columbia University in New York.

"The formation of compact stellar binaries requires rapid orbital tightening of their progenitor binary stars," the authors write. "This is theorized to happen via Common Envelope Evolution, when the stars orbit in a loosely bound, shared convective envelope, triggering an inspiral due to frictional drag.".

That much is known by astrophysical theory. But nobody's observed the end of the inspiral and the eruption yet. "Here, we present observations of ATâ2025abao, a transient eruption in the Andromeda Galaxy," the researchers write.

Astronomers have lots of observations of ATâ2025abao with multiple telescopes because it's been experiencing brightness changes for several years and has attracted their attention. They've become familiar with ATâ2025abao and now simply refer to it as 'Bao'.

âStellar mergers are very, very difficult to observe in real time because they are hard to predict,â remarked first author Karambelkar. âHowever, we noticed something unusual was going on in 2023 and continued to monitor the system to see what it would do. Then, in 2025, it erupted! Webb observed Bao only 47 days after the starsâ eruption peaked, the earliest ever follow-up of an event like this. The telescopeâs data helped us characterize what the system looked like before, during, and immediately after the merger, which is absolutely mind-blowing.â.

Sources indicate that stars in these situations orbit each other for thousands of years with little change, and that was true of ATâ2025abao. But once they contacted each other, things changed. Other stars in CEs take thousands of orbits before they merge. But this one was different from other CE binaries. The pair merged after only 7 orbits (about 7 years.).

Observations go back as far as 2018, and between then and early 2025, the star gradually brightened in optical light. After that, it gradually faded in optical light, but its infrared light continued to brighten. Then, in October 2025, it erupted. It brightened by 100 times in the r-band over a period 25 days, and its temperature jumped to about 8000 Kelvin. Then, for about 80 days it plateaued and cooled down to about 3000 Kelvin. The JWST observed it during this period, only 47 days after its peak.

It has been revealed that âWe thought an outburst from a such an extended star would take years,â mentioned co-author Nadia Blagorodnova, an associate professor at the University of Barcelona in Spain. âOne day, its brightness started rising and within a week, it peaked!â.

Recent findings suggest that âWhen a companion star begins to interact with the outer surface of the primary star, it produces a subtle effect â a slow brightening, which we clearly saw in Baoâs data,â mentioned co-author Kishalay De, an assistant professor at Columbia University in Newly introduced York. âAs the companion continues its orbit, it keeps peeling off the primary starâs outer layers, and that gas flows away into the surrounding space.â.

Recent findings suggest that this was when the CEE began. The primary star engulfed the companion star in a common envelope, and drag stole its momentum, forcing it to spiral inward. This is when the JWST saw the destructive merger.

This is the finding chart for AT 2025abao. It was captured by the Asiago 67/92cm Schmidt telescope on 7 November 2025, when the light was at is maximum. M 31's (Andromeda) spiral disk is just visible on the left of the image. The zoomed-in panel shows the transient. Image Credit: Reguitti et al. A&A, 709, A25 (2026).

In a recent development, since the transient has been in the watchful eyes of astronomers for so long, they have detailed spectroscopy from it. The SPHEREx near-infrared space observatory played an important role, catching the star in its survey. "In July 2025, the source was serendipitously observed during its rapid optical fading by the first sky survey of the SPHEREx mission, providing a precise glimpse of the stellar photosphere during this phase," the researchers state. That let them determine the masses of the stars, but only with some help from simulations.

As in a lot of astronomy research, simulations played an notable role here. In this research, the authors worked with different models of CEE until the outcome of one matched the JWST's detailed observations of the star and its surrounding dust, shed by the primary star over hundreds of years.

It has been revealed that that work revealed that the primary was seven times more massive than the Sun, with a radius 350 times larger. It was also 18,000 times brighter than our star. âIt was an absolute beast of a star, completely outshining its companion in the data,â said co-author Karel Temmink, a Ph.D. student at Radboud University in Nijmegen, Netherlands, who led the simulations.

Recent findings suggest that the modelling also revealed the smaller star's true nature. It had only about 0.7 solar masses, one-tenth as massive as the other star. Its radius was much smaller and it was also much dimmer.

The astronomers called the pair Massive Bao and Little Bao, and when Little Bao was engulfed, there was a massive explosion. Only more observations will reveal what the resulting star, now simply called Bao, looks like.

It has been revealed that these artist's illustrations help explain what happened with ATâ2025abao and its common envelope evolution. The first panel shows the quiescent phase, when the stars are surrounded by a common envelope. The brightness was consistent during this phase. The second panel shows the stars brightening in the precursor stage. The companion star experiences drag and begins to spiral toward the primary star. In the third panel, there's a sudden bright eruption, as the companion spiralled and the common envelope is ejected. The JWST observed this. Then, in the final panel, months after the eruption, gas from the starâs ejected envelope freely expanded at the poles, but not at the equator, where previous ejecta from the more massive star was concentrated. Image Credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Leah Hustak (STScI); Science: Viraj Karambelkar (Columbia).

According to recent reports, "The 2025 eruption of ATâ2025abao displays the defining hallmarks of Luminous Red Novae, a class of transients established to arise from impulsive energy injection into a common envelope during the merger of a star with its companion," the authors write. But it's different from all other known LRN. It's progenitor is unambiguously an evolved AGB star with an extended convective envelope.

"In contrast, all known LRN progenitors have primary stars on the main sequence," the researchers explain. But classical CEE theory claims that the primary star should be an AGB star.

"Thus, ATâ2025abao provides the first view of a classical CEE progenitor system continuously monitored from its onset through its culmination," the authors explain.

Watching a common envelope evolution in real time like this is a first in astronomy. Astronomers have had to perform a sort of forensic astrophysical study of transients like this in other cases, trying to reconstruct what happened thousands or even millions of years ago. Even with powerful telescopes and computer simulations, and with detailed theoretical frameworks to guide their work, that's tough to do.

According to recent reports, but this work opens a fresh window into CEE and how efficient it can be. And it's just in time to help with a potential flood of upcoming transient detections. Only a few dozen luminous red novae have been detected, but the Vera Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time will detect hundreds of them, possibly thousands. The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope will also detect some LRN and CEE, but probably far fewer.

This work lays the foundation for understanding some of what those surveys will find. In a few years time, astronomers should have a much clearer understanding of common envelope evolution and luminous red novae.

"This end-to-end characterization using multi-survey observations demonstrates a path towards mapping the landscape of CEE outcomes with upcoming surveys," the authors write.

  • These days, Jessica Yih spends a lot of time talking to women about testosterone.
