💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the dairy industry’s “Milk.
  • It has been revealed that “When children and adolescents have access to sufficient, high-quality food, they grow taller, within the constraints of genetic factors,” Manon Stephan, an economic historian at Germany’s University of Tübingen, said in a statement.
  • To test that idea, Stephan and colleagues at Tübingen and the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology examined 18,457 bones from 783 sites in 45 countries.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the dairy industry’s “Milk. It does a body good” slogan has some historical backing, at least in Europe. That’s one of the more surprising takeaways from a large study that used ancient skeletons to track how well people lived across Europe and Asia over the past 7,000 years. The researchers based their analysis on one telling measurement: human height.

It has been revealed that “When children and adolescents have access to sufficient, high-quality food, they grow taller, within the constraints of genetic factors,” Manon Stephan, an economic historian at Germany’s University of Tübingen, said in a statement. “Therefore, height enables us to draw conclusions about living standards.”.

To test that idea, Stephan and colleagues at Tübingen and the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology examined 18,457 bones from 783 sites in 45 countries. In the study, published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, the team estimated people’s heights from their long bones. They then tracked how average height changed in each region and compared those changes with shifts in population density and technology.

In China, men were taller 7,000 years ago, averaging 5 feet 10 inches. Over time, however, their height steadily declined, reaching a low of just 5 feet 3 inches on average in the 19th century. Chinese women’s height also declined, though less drastically, falling from an average of 5 feet 2 inches 7,000 years ago to 4 feet 10 inches in more recent times.

Sources indicate that trends like these would be nearly impossible to trace through written records alone. “In many parts of the world, any written sources that would allow us to draw conclusions about economic development appear quite late on our timeline and are patchy in their distribution,” Stephan noted. “That’s why we rely on bones.” The bones in question came from 22 Asian and 23 European countries and were taken from the graves of commoners in both densely populated and rural regions.

Recent findings suggest that in Europe, by contrast, the trends went in a different direction. Around 5,000 years ago, men in northern Europe averaged just 5 feet 4 inches. However, the study authors wrote, as pastoralist peoples migrated from the steppes of Eastern Europe and western Siberia, they brought with them more advanced dairy farming and the genetic trait of lactose tolerance. This led to greater consumption of dairy products, which the study identifies as a leading factor in increased height. Average heights in northern Europe continued to climb into the early Middle Ages, but sometime between 500 and 1000 C.E., they began to decline, a trend that lasted until the end of the 19th century.

Women’s heights followed a similar pattern. China and Japan experienced the steepest declines, while Europe saw a rise, though a less steep one than among men.

Sources indicate that the authors wrote that “human stature is a valuable indicator of nutritional status and health.” Reconstructing this indicator offers insight into which societies provided better health and nutrition to their people. Surprisingly, technological progress did not prove to be a major factor in improving either.

Industry observers note that “Our study also confirmed that technological progress does not automatically lead to greater height,” stated Jörg Baten, a professor of economic history at the University of Tübingen. “In China, for example, latest, higher-yielding rice varieties and other innovations were introduced in the 11th century [C.E.]. While the higher yields enabled the empire to remain the dominant power, they did not subsequently lead to a better standard of living for the general population. Instead, population density increased: People had more children because this was seen as a form of security in old age. This meant, however, that each individual had not more to eat, but less. And importantly the quality declined, for example, in terms of high-quality protein.”.

Europe’s findings on technology mirrored Asia’s. Improved technology helped support denser populations, but it didn’t increase average height or necessarily improve the nutritional value of food.

According to recent reports, going forward, the authors hope to link more of these changes in height to shifts in social conditions or developments in agriculture. “This requires further research,” noted Mark Hudson, an archaeologist at the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology. “However, the statistical data reveal trends and provide clues as to when these changes occurred.”.

He covers stadiums, sneakers, gear, infrastructure, and more for a variety of publications, including Popular Mechanics. His favorite interviews have included sit-downs with Roger Federer in Switzerland, Kobe Bryant in Los Angeles, and Tinker Hatfield in Portland.

Industry observers note that in an increasingly fire-prone western North America, Jennifer Grenz, an ecologist and member of the Lytton First Nation, looks at fire with a holistic eye. She considers her work with landscapes recovering from catastrophic wildfire to be “deliberately unfocused,” spanning soil microbial ecology, restoration ecology, invasion biology and historical biology.

Grenz analyzes historical ecological records, like how Indigenous people have shaped and cared for ecosystems over time, to paint a comprehensive picture. “I’m interested in how those histories leave ecological legacies and hints of the stewardship of the past,” says Grenz, who leads the Indigenous Ecology Lab at the University of British Columbia in Canada. “What changed on the land that made it more vulnerable?”.

Grenz spends time with many kinds of specialists, such as archaeologists, anthropologists and Indigenous elders who provide oral histories.

In a recent development, moving forward, her lab will examine ecology below ground, including soil, microbial communities and root networks. The goal is to understand the role of underground ecology in critical topics like carbon sequestration, climate change, biodiversity and sustainable management.

Recent findings suggest that “My motivation is in our interior Salish Territories in the southern interior of British Columbia, where my ancestors rest and where my people are,” Grenz says. “The responsibility I feel to them and to our Tmícw, which means our lands, [is] to not take us back to the past, but to show that we have the deep knowledge to help us move forward.”.

In this case, it’s your temperature controls. These devices tend to be a bit pricier than conventional thermostats, but it’s an upgrade that can pay for itself over time thanks to increased energy efficiency.

It has been revealed that using a companion app on your phone, you get intuitive and nuanced controls, including the ability to customize temperature schedules remotely. That comes in handy when, let’s say, you want to warm up the house earlier than usual if you head home from work early. You’re also able to track your usage with monthly energy reports, which can help you bring down your bills.

Recent findings suggest that for the past few months, my colleagues and I have been steadily testing smart thermostats throughout in our homes, including models from Google Nest, ecobee, and Honeywell Home. These are the models we tried, plus a few more we recommend based on our research and reviews. We’ve also included some expert advice on what to consider before you buy.

The ecobee covers the standard lineup of smart thermostat features, with climate control and money-saving that are commonplace among any of the top options, but sets itself apart with a wider range of smart features.

Industry observers note that it doubles as a security base for your home security, serving as the arming and disarming mechanism. It also features a built-in air quality monitor that alerts you to poor air quality and sends reminders when you need to replace air filters in your furnace.

The ecobee comes with a separate smart sensor for precision control, allowing it to fine-tune the temperature in the rooms where you spend the most time. Though it comes with a single sensor, you can purchase more to add that precision throughout the house.

It also provides free Eco+ Software which works on your smartphone and generates energy reports that further maximize your energy savings.

It has been revealed that the smart thermostat also comes with a host of standard smart features. After connecting to a Google assistant or Alexa, the smart speaker built directly on the thermostat itself can take voice commands and even play music. It also comes with a three-year warranty from date of purchase.

Each purchase comes with a full converter kit as well, so if you aren’t currently in a home with a C-Wire, you can add one by following the kit instructions.

According to recent reports, for a smart thermostat that better fits a tight budget, Amazon has its own option that comes with many of the same energy-saving features at a lower overall price tag. Through the connected app, the thermostat tracks and reports your energy usage and peak time periods throughout the week and month.

Through Alexa, you can also set home, away, and sleep temperatures that you can schedule throughout the day and week in order to further maximize savings on your energy bill and optimize your air conditioning to your exact schedule. You can also set the temperature remotely from your phone through the Alexa app.

Beyond the controls, by using an Amazon product, the company will pass along potential rebate and saving opportunities that you could take advantage of by owning a smart thermostat.

As for upfront costs, the device is designed specifically for easy DIY installation so there is no need to hire an HVAC technician unless you want one.

The Honeywell T9 is a great choice if your primary concern is reducing energy use and lowering your bills. You need to pair it with one of Honeywell’s smart room sensors to take advantage of the thermostat’s full functionality, which is an extra hurdle, but the sensor only costs about $30, so it’s a short one.

It has been revealed that one of the key ways the T9 saves money is through virtual fencing. Using your phone’s GPS, the thermostat automatically switches between home and away mode as you come and go. So, when you leave your house, energy usage is reduced across the board.

According to recent reports, honeywell also provides monthly usage reports that point out areas where energy can be reduced for a lower upfront cost. Adding more room sensors can increase the accuracy of those reports, giving you more chances to optimize your heating and cooling system.

The Honeywell T9 doesn’t have the same wide spectrum of features as our other recommendations, but it’s core functionality is very solid.

The newest generation of the Google Nest Thermostat has impressed our team as an easy-to-install, easy-to-use option that reduces energy use and is compatible with most HVAC systems. Like previous models, the smart thermostat builds a schedule, learns your temperature preferences, and reduces energy when it isn’t needed.

Recent findings suggest that reviews Editor Danny Perez installed the Nest in his own home and absolutely fell in the love with nearly every aspect of it. “To say I like this thermostat is an understatement: It lights up when I pass by to show me the interior temps, as well as local weather and humidity (it’s nice to know my presence is acknowledged, not gonna lie),” writes Perez.

Beyond the basic features, Perez also pointed out how much he likes the actual display and design of the thermostat. “Sure, other thermostats and window a/c units have similar smart features, but they don’t blend into my home the way the Google Nest thermostat does. It’s a versatile option, compatible with multiple smart home assistants. Like other models, it’s Energy Star-certified, which means that using one can help you save even more money through local rebates.

It has been revealed that while the smart thermostat is great for easy scheduling and reading, it lacks the learning software of the Google Nest or the virtual fencing adjustments that many other smart thermostats have. That stated, it’s also considerably cheaper.

Most smart thermostats aren’t compatible with baseboard heating and cooling systems. This Mysa unit is the rare exception, and designed specifically to work with electric baseboards. Combine that with compatibility across every major smart home system, and the Mysa becomes one of very few thermostats with such capabilities.

It has been revealed that while the compatibility alone makes this a tempting choice, it also has many of the same high-end smart features as the competition. This includes virtual fencing, so when you head out for the day, the thermostat automatically reduces energy use.

Another key feature is its temperature monitor. Unlike many other devices, which only provide you with degrees, the Mysa smart thermostat also measures and reports humidity levels.

Recent findings suggest that traditional thermostats only require power through the four classic wires while smart thermostats typically require low- voltage power all day in order to run the display screen and some basic functions. This low-voltage power comes from an additional fifth wire called the “common” wire or C-Wire. The biggest potential concern you may have with installation is if your home lacks this wire.

It has been revealed that if this is the case, it’s probably time to step away from your weekend home project and call an HVAC technician. While installing a common wire isn’t an incredibly difficult undertaking if you’re somewhat handy, it’s one that likely requires the expertise of a trained professional.

Industry observers note that some smart thermostats include installation kits that provide equipment and step-by-step instructions for adding a C-Wire to your current wiring. This can be a helpful addition to the handier among us, and may circumvent the need for an HVAC technician entirely, though you may want to keep one waiting in the wings if anything goes wrong.

Once you've wired and installed your smart thermostat, you can connect it to other devices in your home via Wi-Fi or occasionally Z-Wave. Most units are compatible with many major smart home ecosystems. While they’re compatible with many systems, I would still take a moment to check and make sure that a thermostat works specifically with the smart home setup you use at home.

Along with scheduling heating or cooling programs from the convenience of your phone, there are a handful of features that set smart thermostats apart from their traditional counterparts. Most smart models automatically adjust the temperature based on peak usage and some automatically respond to outdoor temperatures and set ideal temperatures indoors.

Other models use geofencing, or virtual fencing technology. This creates a radius around your home and detects how close or far away your smartphone is from it. With this, the smart thermostat eases energy use when you aren’t home, and ramps back up as you reenter the virtual boundary.

Recent findings suggest that several smart thermostats we cover use external sensors to expand the reach of temperature readings. Setup is typically no more complicated than placing the sensors around the house and syncing them up with the rest of the system.

In a recent development, they’re great for maintaining different temperatures in rooms, like keeping bedrooms and bathrooms warm and offices and laundry rooms cool. More precise temperature control also increases the potential for saving energy. Smart thermostats that include sensors as part of their systems often come with one, though some models require purchasing sensors separately.

The Popular Mechanics Gear Team has tested several of these recommendations over the course of several months, including the ecobee Smart Thermostat Premium and the Google Nest Learning Thermostat. We installed these smart thermostats in our homes, set them up, and used them to keep ourselves warm and cool, as the seasons demanded. We gave them our seal of approval based on ease-of-use, installation process, programmable features, and how well the devices integrated with our smart home assistants, mobile devices, and tablets.

Sources indicate that we also prioritized options that were highly compatible with other smart devices and offered convenient features for everyday use. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Dor Minzer remembers sitting in an undergraduate computation class at Tel Aviv University. He was intrigued by his professor and soon found himself pulled into a fresh world: the mystifying intersection of math and computation, first laid out by Alan Turing during World War II. Working with the professor, Minzer became deeply interested in the limitations of what computers can and can’t do.

Sources indicate that “My part is actually to prove not only do I not know how to do it, but I can prove that it’s impossible,” Minzer says. “You have to really be curious.”.

It has been revealed that minzer’s hard work has paid off. In 2018, he proved a theoretical computer science problem called the 2-to-2 games conjecture. It asks whether computers can efficiently distinguish games where almost all rules can be satisfied from those where almost none can be satisfied, when the rules have a strict structure.

Industry observers note that in September, Minzer and his two graduate students at MIT posted a 95-page milestone paper on the unique games conjecture, which builds off the 2-to-2 conjecture. The paper wasn’t quite ready, but they published to get ahead of a press release from OpenAI, describing its proof for the same problem, slated for only days later. It’s a situation that many mathematicians have found themselves in this year as AI companies flood the field with findings at lightning speed.

It has been revealed that minzer states it’s critical to remember that math, and all the research and contemplation behind it, is very human. “It’s a human activity,” he says. “Research is sort of a living organism, a living body.”.

Minzer teaches his own students now. Some days, he talks to his class and gets the sense that nobody is paying attention. But other days, he gets a few students that participate. They have ideas, they’re excited, and they remind him of his own days as a graduate student.

Recent findings suggest that “I feel like now I feel like I’m passing the torch,” he notes. “Before you have a Ph.D. adviser, you’re like a latest person in a dark room. There are infinite places to go. Your Ph.D. adviser is the person that holds your hand and says, ‘Okay, let’s walk here.’”.

The Secret Reason Why Ancient Roman Concrete Is So Remarkably Strong—And How One Engineer Has Recreated It

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.
  • The Pantheon, Rome’s unreinforced concrete dome, constructed around 118 to 125 C.E., still stands intact to this day.
  • For decades, researchers credited the inclusion of volcanic ash from Pozzuoli, a city in Naples, Italy, for the unique strength in the mix; others claimed that lime, a calcium oxide or calcium hydroxide binder created from heating limestone, was the key ingredient.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.

The Pantheon, Rome’s unreinforced concrete dome, constructed around 118 to 125 C.E., still stands intact to this day. The Aqua Virgo, part of the ancient Roman system of aqueducts, was built in 19 B.C.E., yet still supplies Roman fountains, including Trevi, today. Is it any wonder that ancient Rome still draws our global admiration?

For decades, researchers credited the inclusion of volcanic ash from Pozzuoli, a city in Naples, Italy, for the unique strength in the mix; others claimed that lime, a calcium oxide or calcium hydroxide binder created from heating limestone, was the key ingredient. Massachusetts Institute of Technology’s Admir Masic, a civil and environmental engineering professor, thought there must be more to the story.

Sources indicate that masic established a lab at MIT with the specific goal of researching ancient Roman concrete. First and foremost a chemist, he says he knew there was something beneath the surface of Roman concrete potentially lending it strength. His team of researchers, from MIT, Harvard, Italy, and Switzerland, discovered that ancient Roman concrete gets its strength—and therefore its incredible longevity—from its inherent self-healing properties. As cracks form, the surrounding material somehow fills them back in, over and over.

According to recent reports, scientists commonly suspected that ash, and not lime, was the hero of the Roman concrete-making process, because the Romans were the first to add volcanic ash to the mixture. This hydration-based method gives the mixture additional strength and makes it possible to build in all seasons.

But it didn’t explain the self-healing quality. Another mystery was in the concrete’s apparent crystalline phases, known to take shape only at high temperatures—at least 80 degrees Celsius (or about 176 degrees Fahrenheit). Yet, the Romans wouldn’t have exposed their concrete mixture to those sorts of temperatures.

In a recent development, then, researchers discovered calcium aluminate hydrate being used as a binding agent in ancient Roman concrete, which only created further intrigue. This is where the mystery of self-healing gained its first substantial clue—trying to learn where the calcium came from, Masic indicates. So his team’s focus shifted to the overlooked role of lime, which is primarily composed of calcium compounds.

Masic notes that modern concrete, when mixed with lime, volcanic components, and water, creates a homogeneous mixture—quite unlike ancient Roman concrete, which is studded with tiny, distinct white particles. “How is it possible that every construction site would make this heterogeneous material even though they put so much effort [into] making it very standard in terms of ingredients [and] how to mix it?” Masic wondered.

Industry observers note that the research team decided to investigate the mechanical, structural, and chemical properties of these particles, dubbed “lime clasts,” which were present in every sample they analyzed, Masic claims. It led the team to realize “that lime clasts are not an error in mixing, or sloppy mixing, but they are the root of a very specific way of mixing mortars.” Not present in modern concrete, but ubiquitous in the ancient Roman version.

Originally, researchers believed that the Romans added water to the lime mixture to make a slurry. This “slaking” creates a homogeneously structured mixture. However, the presence of the lime clasts didn’t fit into this model.

What the Romans actually did was “hot mixing,” which introduces a novel series of chemical reactions. They ground the stone into tiny pieces of calcium oxide and mixed them with volcanic ash and a dry aggregate. Finally, they added water. “This is where the reaction of calcium oxide with water happens, and the entire mix gets hot, [which] releases energy, and creates hot spots up to 200 to 250 degrees Celsius,” Masic explains.

While lime and the ash formed the basis of the mixture, the constellation of millimeter-scale, mineral particles embedded throughout the mortar turned out to be the secret outcome of the hot mixing process. The key to hot mixing is that it doesn’t dissolve all of the lime clasts. Instead, they get systematically embedded into the concrete mix, creating a reservoir of calcium. When the concrete is exposed to water, the calcium spontaneously expands, creating a protective layer of nanoparticles that fill in the cracks before they can spread. Voila, self-healing concrete. Masic’s team published their findings in the journal Science Advances.

The team’s own recreation of Roman concrete healed a crack within two weeks. A modern concrete mixture didn’t heal at all, allowing water to flow through the crack. Eventually, water seepage like this destroys the integrity of modern concrete structures.

According to recent reports, roman self-healing concrete allows the mixture to last longer and requires less maintenance and less newly introduced material for construction—which also reduces emissions during concrete production. Standard cement production, the solid binder in concrete, accounts for about 8 percent of global CO2 emissions today.

In a recent development, our world actually has various forms of self-healing concrete, such as bioconcrete, in which bacterial spores activate and produce calcium carbonate to fill in cracks. However, the high costs of modern methods keep the industry from using them widely, says Masic. Meanwhile the ancient Roman method offers “self-healing at an extremely competitive price,” he says.

Now that we know the secret, should we return to making concrete this way?

In fact, Masic co-founded a company in 2021, that uses lessons he has learned from studying ancient Roman concrete. Today, DMAT is creating a concrete additive “that increases the lifespan of concrete structures by 50 percent and reduces CO2 emissions to 40% of traditional concrete,” according to MIT’s Climate Portal. As of August 2026, their material is part of underground water tanks, road barriers, and pavement in Italy and Switzerland. DMAT also plans to expand to U.S. infrastructure projects.

Manasee Wagh contributed to this story.

Tim Newcomb is a journalist based in the Pacific Northwest. He covers stadiums, sneakers, gear, infrastructure, and more for a variety of publications, including Popular Mechanics. His favorite interviews have included sit-downs with Roger Federer in Switzerland, Kobe Bryant in Los Angeles, and Tinker Hatfield in Portland.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that lightning hit Apollo 12 twice in its first minute in 1969.
  • The Apollo 12 moon mission lifted off at 11:22 a.m.
  • Recent findings suggest that lightning had struck the rocket.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that lightning hit Apollo 12 twice in its first minute in 1969. The crew still landed next to Surveyor 3, whose camera later sparked controversy.

The Apollo 12 moon mission lifted off at 11:22 a.m. EST on November 14, 1969, into a dark, rainy sky over Florida. Thirty-six seconds later, the commander saw a bright flash, and many of the spacecraft’s electronics went offline.

Recent findings suggest that lightning had struck the rocket. Sixteen seconds after that, a second event knocked out the spacecraft’s guidance system.

The crew still landed on the Moon five days later, right next to a robotic probe that had been sitting there since 1967.

What they brought back from that probe started a story that has never quite gone away: that Earth germs had survived on the Moon.

Industry observers note that the crew was commander Charles “Pete” Conrad, command module pilot Richard Gordon and lunar module pilot Alan Bean. Their mission was NASA’s second Moon landing, four months after Apollo 11.

Later crews carried living cargo on purpose, like the tree seeds an Apollo astronaut flew around the Moon in 1971.

A NASA photo reveals a bolt between the clouds and the ground 36.5 seconds after liftoff, when the vehicle was about 6,000 feet up. The first event took the spacecraft’s three power-generating fuel cells offline.

The Saturn V rocket that was guiding the launch was not affected and kept flying normally. The spacecraft on top of it was another matter.

In a recent development, in Mission Control, a young engineer named John Aaron was watching the spacecraft’s systems. His data turned to garbage during both events.

Industry observers note that aaron had seen similar readings in a test a year earlier. He concluded that a unit called the Signal Conditioning Equipment had suffered some upset and gone offline, and that a seldom-used switch needed to be moved from Normal to Auxiliary.

He told Flight Director Gerry Griffin, and the call went up to the crew through capcom Gerald Carr. Bean remembered that the switch was on his panel and flipped it. Several seconds later, Aaron had good data on his screen again.

Once Conrad understood what had happened, he radioed Houston: “I think we need to do a little more all-weather testing.”.

In a recent development, for about two and a half hours in Earth orbit, the astronauts and Mission Control checked that every system still worked. Then Carr told them they were go to leave for the Moon.

On November 19, Conrad and Bean landed the lunar module Intrepid in the Ocean of Storms, about 950 miles west of the Apollo 11 site.

Recent findings suggest that they came down about 535 feet from Surveyor 3, an uncrewed NASA lander that had been on the Moon since April 1967. It is the only time Apollo astronauts landed near another spacecraft and touched it.

In a recent development, on their second moonwalk, on November 20, the two men walked into the 650-foot-wide Surveyor Crater. They cut off the probe’s 17-pound TV camera and also collected its motorized scoop, pieces of cable, aluminum tubing and glass.

Engineers wanted the camera to see how its gears, motors, optics, metals and lubricants had held up.

Scientists were most interested in the cable, because biological organisms had been trapped inside it, and they wanted to know if any had survived two and a half years on the Moon.

After splashdown, the camera went to NASA’s Lunar Receiving Laboratory in Houston. Sampling for microbes began on January 8, 1970.

Industry observers note that A team took 33 samples from 11 locations inside the camera body. One sample, a bit of polyurethane foam used as insulation between the aluminum plates of a circuit board, grew a colony of Streptococcus mitis, a bacterium that commonly lives in the human mouth.

Sources indicate that the result was published in 1971. It gave rise to the idea that Earth bacteria had survived the vacuum and the extreme temperatures of the Moon, and that idea has circulated ever since.

The broader question is still studied today, as in research on whether Earth microbes can survive in hidden pockets on the Moon.

Sources indicate that decades later, John Rummel of East Carolina University, Judith Allton of NASA’s Johnson Space Center and Don Morrison reviewed the case. They tracked down the 16mm films of the sampling and watched them.

Industry observers note that their review, now hosted by NASA, lists several problems. No viable microbes were found in 10 of the 11 sampling locations inside the camera, or in 32 of the 33 samples.

Sources indicate that none were found in the Surveyor cables or in any Apollo lunar samples, and a test camera that had stayed on Earth never yielded S. mitis.

S. mitis is not a spore former, and microbes like it are much more vulnerable to heat, even in a vacuum. NASA’s Manned Spacecraft Center, now Johnson Space Center, estimated that the camera reached a maximum temperature of about 158 degrees Fahrenheit (70 degrees Celsius).

According to recent reports, there was also no negative control to check whether the sampling itself added microbes. And S. mitis was one of the organisms found on the crew during routine microbial testing.

In a recent development, the films showed technicians in short-sleeved scrubs, with their arms exposed. Just before the foam was sampled, one worker leaned his upper body into the laminar-flow hood and examined the side of the camera where the foam was.

Morrison concluded that his breath could have contaminated the foam. Because the foam was the last sample taken, nobody could check whether nearby surfaces had been contaminated too.

“The general scene does not lend a lot of confidence in the proposition that contamination did not occur,” Morrison wrote.

It has been revealed that the review does not prove where the bacterium came from. What it indicates is that the claim of survival on the Moon rests on a single sample taken under weak controls.

The authors used the case as a warning for future missions that bring material back from Mars and other worlds.

In a recent development, contamination should be avoided but anticipated, and a microbial inventory should be taken before launch. Other scientists have since proposed a Moon lab to screen samples for alien microbes.

Sources indicate that their summary also admitted something about the story’s staying power. Just because scientists do not believe it, they wrote, does not mean it is going to go away.

The information was obtained from NASA’s account of the Apollo 12 launch, its mission summary and the review of the Surveyor 3 microbe claim.

Industry News: A meteorite older than Earth crashed through a Texas woman’s roof and landed near her daughter’s bed

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (888 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The 4.5-billion-year-old meteorite that pierced a home in Spring, Texas is now on free display at the Houston Museum of Natural Science.
  • According to recent reports, on the afternoon of March 21, 2026, Sherrie James heard a thunderous boom at her home in Spring, Texas, north of Houston.
  • Eight months later, that rock is on display at the Houston Museum of Natural Science, in a free exhibition called Fall To Earth that opened on November 6.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The 4.5-billion-year-old meteorite that pierced a home in Spring, Texas is now on free display at the Houston Museum of Natural Science.

According to recent reports, on the afternoon of March 21, 2026, Sherrie James heard a thunderous boom at her home in Spring, Texas, north of Houston. A rock from space had just come through her roof.

Eight months later, that rock is on display at the Houston Museum of Natural Science, in a free exhibition called Fall To Earth that opened on November 6.

Industry observers note that on the day it fell, it pierced an upstairs bedroom and came to rest near her daughter’s bed. It was a meteorite about 4.5 billion years old, dating back to the birth of the solar system.

James was not the only one who noticed. People across Texas heard a low boom and felt their houses shake, under clear skies, according to the museum.

Recent findings suggest that NASA’s analysis says the meteor became visible 49 miles above Stagecoach, northwest of Houston, at 4:40 p.m. Central Daylight Time. It moved southeast at about 35,000 miles per hour and broke apart 29 miles above Bammel, just west of Cypress Station.

In a recent development, the space rock that entered the atmosphere weighed about a ton and measured about 3 feet across, NASA estimates. When it broke apart, it released energy equal to 26 tons of TNT. That created a pressure wave that reached the ground and caused the booms.

More than 180 eyewitnesses reported the fireball, from as far away as Dallas-Fort Worth, Austin and Rockport, the museum noted.

According to NASA, the Geostationary Lightning Mappers on the GOES weather satellites also detected it, and Doppler weather radar revealed meteorites falling to the ground between Willowbrook and Northgate Crossing.

Radar has helped track falls before, as researchers showed when they found that weather radar systems can detect meteorite falls.

Recent findings suggest that at first, nobody knew what had hit the house. The Ponderosa Fire Department initially looked into whether the object might be debris from an aircraft.

It has been revealed that its unusual weight and appearance soon pointed to something else. Most of the original space rock burned up before it reached the ground, but some pieces survived.

By late October 2026, 19 meteorite fragments had been recovered around the Houston area, according to the museum.

Researchers at Rice University have proposed naming the meteorite “Houston” as part of its formal classification, which still needs approval from the Meteoritical Society.

According to recent reports, it is not the first time a meteorite has hit a home in the United States. A similar rock crashed into a man’s house in Georgia.

Recent findings suggest that within 24 hours of the fall, experts and enthusiasts were finding small chunks on public property, Rice University stated. That is rare: meteorites seldom land in a major city, and samples are seldom collected so soon after landing.

Rice scientist Bidong Zhang walked 23,000 steps searching but found no samples himself. Two other searchers, David Gonzales and Marc Fries, found several pieces and donated them to Rice.

Those samples became the first meteorite tested and catalogued by Zhang’s new Rice Astromaterials Research and Exploration lab, known as RARE.

The analysis confirmed that the Houston meteorite is a chondrite, a type of stony meteorite. Its oxygen isotopes matched what scientists call high-grade H chondrites.

But there was a mystery. Chondrites usually contain small round grains called chondrules, and the Houston meteorite had none.

The scientists found clues in a mineral called feldspar, which was in an unusual sodium-rich form. That suggests the rock was heated to nearly 1,100 degrees Celsius (about 2,000 degrees Fahrenheit) while it was still part of its parent asteroid, hot enough to melt the chondrules.

At some point after that, a high-speed impact likely broke up the asteroid and set the meteorite free. “We think this meteorite was impacted in space,” Zhang said. “It truly is a unique specimen.”.

Some results are still unexplained. The levels of one oxygen isotope varied within the samples, when scientists would normally expect them to be fairly consistent, and the team notes more work is needed.

Industry observers note that the museum calls it one of the most remarkable, documented meteorite falls in recent Texas history. Because the rock dates to the birth of the solar system, it offers scientists a rare chance to study material older than Earth itself.

Sources indicate that “A 4.5-billion-year-old fragment of our solar system’s original formation crashed through the roof of a Houston-area home,” said Carolyn Sumners, vice president of astronomy at the Houston Museum of Natural Science. “That’s not something you expect to happen in your own neighborhood.”.

Industry observers note that james sees it in a more personal way. “That little thing has traveled by planets and stars, there’s no telling how far it’s come,” she remarked. “So, it’s very exciting. I just feel blessed it came to see me.”.

Fall To Earth is free and open to the public at the museum, at 5555 Hermann Park Drive in Houston.

The information was obtained from the Houston Museum of Natural Science, Rice University and NASA’s fireball report.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Webb’s fresh view of Cassiopeia A reveals how dust from a supernova can preserve clues to what happened inside the star before it exploded.
  • Today’s Image of the Day from the James Webb Space Telescope reveals a cloud of debris left behind by an exploded star.
  • Bright orange strands form a loose ring, with wisps of green along the edges and patches of pale blue scattered through the cloud.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Webb’s fresh view of Cassiopeia A reveals how dust from a supernova can preserve clues to what happened inside the star before it exploded.

Today’s Image of the Day from the James Webb Space Telescope reveals a cloud of debris left behind by an exploded star.

Bright orange strands form a loose ring, with wisps of green along the edges and patches of pale blue scattered through the cloud.

The debris stretches about 10 light-years across.

This is Cassiopeia A, the expanding wreckage of a massive star.

The light from its explosion reached Earth more than three centuries ago.

Astronomers are now using dust in the wreckage to investigate a much shorter span of time, possibly just a few hours in the life of the star.

Cassiopeia A lies about 11,000 light-years away in the constellation Cassiopeia.

From Earth, the debris appears roughly circular. Within that outline are strands, knots, and clouds of material that took different paths to get there.

Some came from deep inside the star and were hurled into space when it exploded. Other material had already escaped while the star was alive.

One of the features astronomers examined is a structure nicknamed the Green Monster.

Sources indicate that it contains dust rich in magnesium silicates and traces back to material shed before the explosion. Two other regions contain debris expelled in the blast.

One is dominated by silica dust and the other by carbon dust. A single image brings those different pieces of the star’s history into view.

As the blast expanded, it pushed into gas around the star. That encounter produced a second shock wave, called a reverse shock, that traveled back through the outward-moving debris.

As the shock encounters clumps of material, it heats them.

Warm dust gives off infrared light, which Webb’s Mid-Infrared Instrument can detect.

The orange, green, and blue in the image represent infrared light rendered in colors our eyes can see.

The shapes are what first draw the eye, but the chemistry comes from examining how the dust emits light at different wavelengths.

Different kinds of grains leave different signatures. With Webb, astronomers can examine individual clumps that would have blurred together in earlier observations.

Some of those clumps are roughly the size of our solar system.

Late in a massive star’s life, nuclear fusion can take place in several layers at once.

It has been revealed that one layer may be hot enough to fuse oxygen while another, farther out, fuses carbon. Material circulates within each of these layers.

Recent findings suggest that under some conditions, that motion can carry material across the boundary between them until the layers begin to mix. Astronomers call this a shell merger.

A team led by Tea Temim of Columbia University found signs of that mixing in dust across much of Cassiopeia A.

The Webb observations build on X-ray measurements from NASA’s Chandra observatory and the Japan-led XRISM mission.

Together, the observations support the idea that the oxygen- and carbon-burning layers were already mixing when the star’s core collapsed.

That process may have begun mere hours before the explosion.

NASA’s retired Spitzer Space Telescope helped the team decide where to look.

In a side-by-side comparison of Spitzer and Webb images, the older view catches the broad sweep of the glowing debris.

Webb resolves that same patch into narrow threads and individual knots. That difference matters when two clumps close together in the sky contain different kinds of dust.

By studying them separately, astronomers can trace where those differences occur across the remnant.

Some of the material scattered by supernovae can later become part of other stars and planets.

If two layers mixed before the blast, they could change the mixture of elements the explosion sent into the galaxy.

The dust still glowing in Cassiopeia A gives astronomers a way to connect what the star released with what was happening deep inside it just before it came apart.

Image Credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Tea Temim (Columbia University), Rick Arendt (UMBC), Dan Milisavljevic (Purdue University). Image processing by Joseph DePasquale (STScI).

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, senate Democratic leader Charles E.
  • ANALYSIS -- “Life moves pretty fast,” that famed 20th-century philosopher Ferris Bueller once said.
  • Sources indicate that in 2024, Democrats were consigned to the political wilderness.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer poses in his office on Nov. 9 for a group photo with incoming members of his caucus: from left, Ohio's Sherrod Brown, Texas' James Talarico, Iowa's Josh Turek, Michigan's Abdul El-Sayed, North Carolina's Roy Cooper, Illinois' Juliana Stratton, Latest Hampshire's Chris Pappas, South Carolina's Annie Andrews, Minnesota's Peggy Flanagan, Maine's Troy Jackson and Kansas' Adam Hamilton. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

ANALYSIS -- “Life moves pretty fast,” that famed 20th-century philosopher Ferris Bueller once said. “If you don't stop and look around once in a while, you could miss it.”.

Sources indicate that in 2024, Democrats were consigned to the political wilderness. Republicans had captured the White House, flipped the Senate and held the House. President Donald Trump had completely altered the party coalitions as he led the ascendant GOP to victory.

Recent findings suggest that now, just two years later, Democrats are on the rise. A historic midterm tsunami has swept them into such commanding Senate and House majorities that some are questioning whether Republicans will ever be in charge again. And if Texas is blue, how does the GOP have any chance in the Electoral College again?

A big takeaway from the midterm results should be that there’s very little permanence in our politics.

What may have looked like a newly introduced GOP coalition was really more of a Trump coalition, and it crumbled in the face of economic frustrations, affordability concerns and the president’s unpopular policies.

With Trump’s negative job approval rating weighing them down, Republican candidates suffered losses among virtually all demographic groups – including by wide margins among constituencies thought to make up the GOP’s core.

In a recent development, trump or the Republicans finished ahead among male voters by 4 points in 2018, 8 points in 2020, 14 points in 2022 and 12 points in 2024, according to the exit polls. Men went for Democratic candidates by 4 points (51 percent to 47 percent) this cycle. Meanwhile, Republicans lost even more ground among women. While Kamala Harris finished ahead of Trump by 8 points in 2024, that margin grew to 21 points for Democratic candidates this year.

It has been revealed that trump closed the gap among Hispanic voters to just 5 points behind Harris two years ago. This year, Hispanic voters nationwide supported Democratic candidates by 32 points (65 percent to 33 percent). Even white voters shifted significantly. They backed Trump or  Republican candidates by 10 points in 2018, 17 points in 2020, 18 points in 2022 and 15 points in 2024. And yet Democrats edged out Republicans by a point (50 percent to 49 percent) on Nov. 3.

Recent findings suggest that voters without a college degree were supposed to be a key cog in Republicans’ new populist coalition. But they went from +13 (56 percent to 43 percent) for Trump in 2024 to backing Republican candidates by just 1 point this year. Meanwhile, the gap among voters with a college degree went from 14 points for Harris in 2024 to 30 points for Democrats this cycle.

Industry observers note that republicans had closed the gap among young voters aged 18 to 29 from 35 points in 2018 to just 11 points in 2024. But younger voters supported Democratic candidates this year by 50 points (74 percent to 24 percent). Not to mention Democrats flipped voters aged 45 to 64 for the first time in nearly two decades.

According to recent reports, white evangelicals appear to be one of the only groups that didn’t shift toward Democrats. They supported GOP candidates 82 percent to 17 percent. But they only made up 17 percent of the electorate, according to the exit polls, which is down from a very consistent 25 percent for more than a decade. So there was still a problem with that group of voters, but it was more about turnout than persuasion.

While there was an unmistakable leftward shift this year, the results should not be considered a permanent party realignment any more than 2024 was. While Democrats did extremely well in Texas this year, they still haven’t won the Lone Star State in a presidential race in 50 years. So maybe it’s wise for everyone to take a deep breath.

Recent findings suggest that if you take this year’s election results and match them with the Senate seats on the ballot in 2028, there doesn’t appear to be a viable path for Republicans back to the majority. But there wasn’t a particularly viable Democratic path to the Senate majority at this point two years ago. And if the Alaska election goes their way, they will end up winning Senate races in seven states that were initially rated Solid Republican.

If one party starts to get too comfortable, voters have a way of bringing politicians back down to earth. If Democrats come to Congress and push too far to the left or become too defined by their most extreme members, they will squander the opportunity they earned this year.

The dramatic demographic swings should be evidence that many voters are not beholden to either party and are open to switching allegiances, particularly in a time of economic uncertainty.

At the same time, if Republicans don’t go through some time of reflection and instead triple down on the policies that led to the blue wave, they risk cementing some of the shifts that started this cycle. It just won’t be thick cement.

Weight-loss drugs have become more common, but not everyone has access

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A study of more than half a million privately insured adults found that where patients received care was linked to whether they filled a prescription for weight-loss drugs.
  • Semaglutide and tirzepatide are sold as Wegovy and Zepbound, and the two weight-loss drugs can seem to be everywhere.
  • Only 8.5% of eligible adults in the study filled a prescription for either drug within six months.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A study of more than half a million privately insured adults found that where patients received care was linked to whether they filled a prescription for weight-loss drugs.

Semaglutide and tirzepatide are sold as Wegovy and Zepbound, and the two weight-loss drugs can seem to be everywhere.

Only 8.5% of eligible adults in the study filled a prescription for either drug within six months. Patients were more likely to fill one if they received care in areas where more residents had a college degree.

This gap grew as the drugs became more common.

According to recent reports, private insurance was held by every one of these patients. Coverage alone was therefore not enough to make access equal.

The study was led by Minh Trung Le, a research data analyst at Boston University School of Public Health.

Recent findings suggest that he was based in the school’s Department of Global Health. Le worked with Andrew Stokes, an associate professor of global health at the school.

Recent findings suggest that insurance billing records were used for the analysis. Such records can show a pattern in who received a prescription. The cause of that pattern cannot be shown by them.

Stokes remarked insurers pay for these drugs far more readily when a patient has diabetes.

He called people with overweight or obesity “a population that has been left behind.”.

According to recent reports, the records were drawn from a national database of insurance claims. More than 175 million people are covered by that database.

From it, Le and Stokes selected adults between the ages of 18 and 64. They first met the study’s eligibility criteria between July 2021 and June 2025.

Clinical guidelines decide who qualifies for the drugs. The bar is a body mass index, or BMI, of at least 30. A BMI of at least 27 is also accepted alongside a weight-related condition.

High blood pressure and sleep apnea are two examples.

Recent findings suggest that people with type 2 diabetes were excluded from the study. People on Medicare or Medicaid were left out as well, along with those without insurance. That left 512,389 patients.

The researchers checked whether patients filled a prescription for semaglutide or tirzepatide within six months of first meeting the study’s eligibility criteria.

Recent findings suggest that ozempic and Wegovy are the brand names of semaglutide. Tirzepatide goes by Mounjaro and Zepbound.

Recent findings suggest that versions labeled for diabetes are at times prescribed for obesity. These prescriptions were included in the count.

The clinics were compared through the ZIP code of each patient’s health care provider. Each ZIP code was looked up in the Census Bureau’s American Community Survey.

The survey reports how many residents hold a bachelor’s degree or higher. On that basis, patients were split into four equal groups.

Among patients diagnosed in the summer of 2021, 1.9% were prescribed one of the two drugs within six months. For patients diagnosed in the spring of 2025, that share had risen to 16.6%.

Even then, about five of every six eligible patients had no prescription after six months.

Recent findings suggest that semaglutide was approved for weight management by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration in June 2021. Tirzepatide got the same approval in November 2023.

It has been revealed that both belong to a class called GLP-1 drugs. In clinical trials, drugs in this class have helped people lose weight. They have also protected the heart.

Both drugs were in short supply at times during the study. When semaglutide was scarce, tirzepatide prescriptions rose quickly. The reverse was seen when tirzepatide was scarce.

Sources indicate that le and Stokes took that as a sign that doctors swap one drug for the other. By the second half of 2024, tirzepatide had become the more prescribed of the two.

In a recent development, at first, prescription rates were about the same in all four neighborhood groups. The rates began to differ in late 2022.

By spring 2025, 21.7% of patients seen in areas with the highest share of college graduates filled a prescription. In the other three groups, the share ranged from 14.4% to 15.2%.

The results were then adjusted for age, sex, race, BMI and other illnesses. The number of doctor visits was taken into account as well.

Industry observers note that between 2021 and 2023, odds of a prescription were 15% lower in the least educated group. The most educated group served as the benchmark. For 2024 and 2025, that figure reached 35%.

It has been revealed that among men, the neighborhood gap was wider than among women. The overweight range indicated the widest gap of any BMI category. Odds in the least educated group were 40% lower there.

For the most severe obesity category, the difference shrank to 10%.

Recent findings suggest that le and Stokes offered a possible reason. More illnesses tend to be on record for patients with severe obesity. An insurer’s approval rules may be easier for them to meet.

By the spring of 2025, 20.7% of women were prescribed one of the drugs. Among men, the figure was 11.9%. After the same adjustments, men had less than half the odds that women had.

Age was linked to prescriptions too. Adults ages 35 to 54 had about twice the odds of adults ages 18 to 24.

Black patients and Hispanic patients each had 11% lower odds than white patients. About a third of the records had no race or ethnicity listed, though. Those two estimates may be shakier as a result.

According to recent reports, as BMI rose, so did prescriptions. Even so, most patients in the most severe obesity category went without one. Only about one in five of those diagnosed in the spring of 2025 got a prescription.

Earlier research suggests that early treatment can prevent or ease later complications, Le and Stokes wrote.

Among patients who first qualified in summer 2021, 1.9% filled a prescription for either drug within six months.

By spring 2025, that share had risen to 16.6%. Even then, about five in six eligible patients had no recorded fill within six months.

In a recent development, the forms for that approval are filled in by the staff of the clinic. Fewer of those forms may be handled by a clinic where staff are few.

Cost was named second. Different amounts are charged to patients by different employer health looks for the same drug.

In a 2026 study, 8,914 privately insured adults who had started semaglutide were followed by other researchers.

After accounting for other factors, researchers found that patients who paid more than $168 per 30-day supply were 9 percentage points more likely to fall short of the study’s refill target than those who paid $21 or less.

Recent findings suggest that A review of approval rules and of patient costs was requested by Le. He also asked for help with approval forms for clinics that are short of staff.

Recent findings suggest that payment programs that reward clinics for quality targets were mentioned in the paper as well. If prescribing rates were made a target, a short-staffed clinic could be penalized for the shortage, not its care.

The ZIP code of the clinic was held by Le and Stokes for each of the 512,389 patients.

Sources indicate that the income and the schooling of each patient were not held by them. The study therefore cannot assign the gap to the clinics or to the patients.

Semaglutide and tirzepatide are sold to some people by direct-to-consumer sellers and no insurer is involved.

It has been revealed that sales of that kind are not recorded in claims and were not counted by the researchers. Which groups of patients buy the drugs in this way is not known.

A diagnosis had already been given by a doctor to every patient in the study.

Diagnosis codes are applied unevenly and milder obesity is often left unrecorded, Le and Stokes wrote. Some adults who were eligible may have been missed for that reason.

Sources indicate that more than 60 data sources are combined in the database that was used. It was still not described by the authors as a match for all insured Americans.

Industry observers note that the cause of the neighborhood gap has not been found. Insurance rules, prescribing habits and patients’ awareness of the drugs were listed by the authors for future studies.

Records of direct-to-consumer sales were also suggested by them, to show who is missing from the claims.

The full study was published in the journal Health Affairs Scholar.

The 8 Best Home Generators Are a Massive Investment. These Deliver Reliable Power During an Outage.

💡 Key Takeaways
