📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An eye tracker in a VR headset can determine how hard people are concentrating by reading how pupil size changes.

According to recent reports, A person’s concentration level during a difficult mental task highlights up in the eyes. Pupils open wider and blinks come faster, and a VR headset with an eye tracker inside can record both.

Recent findings suggest that A team in England asked whether a virtual reality headset could use those signals to tell when a person with chronic pain is working too hard. The answer was mostly yes for healthy volunteers, and not yet for the patients.

Jordan Tsigarides of the University of East Anglia‘s School of Health Sciences led the study, which was part of his Ph.D., with colleagues at UEA and the University of Southampton.

In a recent development, virtual reality is already used as a drug-free way to ease pain, he mentioned. His goal is a headset that changes what it demonstrates, based on how a patient is coping.

“Imagine putting on a VR headset that can recognize when you’re becoming mentally tired or overwhelmed and automatically adjust the experience to suit you,” Tsigarides said in an interview with Earth.com.

“On a difficult day, it might simplify an activity or guide you through a calming environment.”.

The study tested only whether the headset could read the effort. It didn’t treat anyone’s pain.

Between March and June 2025, 84 adults put on a consumer VR headset with built-in eye tracking and played a memory game.

Half had lived with musculoskeletal pain for at least three months, most often rheumatoid or psoriatic arthritis, osteoarthritis or fibromyalgia.

The other half were healthy university students and staff. They were younger on average, 35 years to the patients’ 58.

Recent findings suggest that letters appeared one at a time on a gray panel, each for three-quarters of a second. At the easiest level, a player pressed a button when a letter matched the one just before it. At the hardest, the match was four letters back. The whole session lasted under 20 minutes.

According to recent reports, players found it hard, and stated so. Their own ratings of effort kept climbing through the top level, even after their scores had stopped getting worse.

Pupils widened as the levels got harder, by about a fiftieth of an inch (half a millimeter) at most, which is less than the thickness of a credit card. Blinks came more often too.

Both changes demonstrated up in people with chronic pain and in people without it, and pain and fatigue scores made no difference to either one.

“What fascinated me was that people’s eyes responded to mental effort in remarkably similar ways, whether or not they lived with chronic pain,” Tsigarides told Earth.com.

A plain average of pupil size told a computer almost nothing. A simple model that used average pupil size alone to sort the easiest level from the hardest guessed right 56 percent of the time in healthy volunteers.

In a recent development, in patients it managed 51 percent, which is barely better than chance. The pattern was in the way the pupil changed second by second, not in its size.

Industry observers note that machine learning models that read the full, second-by-second trace did much better, at least in healthy volunteers. Tested on people they had never seen, the best models picked the easy level from the hard one with 88 percent accuracy.

In the chronic pain group, the same models managed 58 to 65 percent.

Age didn’t explain the gap. When the team matched volunteers and patients by age, or adjusted for it, the patients’ eyes were still harder to read.

The two groups also differed in education, medication and other illnesses, and the authors stated a sample of 84 can’t untangle all of that.

In a recent development, the patients were a varied group. Nearly all had two or more long-term conditions, and 45 percent took opioids. A quarter had dry eyes or another eye problem. None of those factors, on its own, predicted whose eyes the models misread.

“Rather than expecting one algorithm to work for everyone, we may need headsets that learn how each individual responds,” he said.

Industry observers note that one result was encouraging. People with chronic pain rated their motivation above 90 out of 100 at every level of the game, the same as the healthy group. Motion sickness scores were low in both groups, and pain scores didn’t rise during the session.

Tsigarides holds an honorary chief medical officer role at Revolve Labs Ltd, a company that helped fund his Ph.D. The paper discloses both.

Virtual reality for pain has so far been a fixed experience, Tsigarides stated: everyone gets the same woodland walk or the same puzzle, however they feel that day.

His earlier work tested VR therapy in people with fibromyalgia, and he stated this study is a step toward a version that adjusts itself.

Everyone was measured once, on one day. The researchers can’t say whether a patient’s eyes behave the same way on a good day and a bad one, and Tsigarides notes investigating that question comes next.

“Someone’s ability to concentrate might be very different on a good day compared with a day when their pain or fatigue is particularly severe,” he stated.

The team also wants to move from a letter-matching game to the kind of calming scenes a real therapy uses, where changing light levels will complicate the pupil readings.

In a recent development, all of the models in this study were run afterward on a desktop computer rather than live inside the headset. None was tested on an outside group of patients.

Industry observers note that tsigarides told Earth.com he hopes early adaptive systems can be tested within a few years. Whether a headset that reads mental effort and responds to it actually eases anyone’s pain is a trial that hasn’t been run.

The full study was published in the journal Scientific Reports.

Breaking: One of the world’s rarest fish lives in a single cave in Death Valley National Park, and earthquakes have left it on the verge of extinction

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (914 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, devils Hole pupfish live in just one cavern of Death Valley National Park.
  • One of the rarest fish on Earth lives in just one place: a water-filled cavern in the Nevada desert called Devils Hole, part of Death Valley National Park.
  • Recent findings suggest that the National Park Service announced the newly introduced figure in November.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, devils Hole pupfish live in just one cavern of Death Valley National Park. Earthquakes are rapidly pushing this fish towards extinction.

One of the rarest fish on Earth lives in just one place: a water-filled cavern in the Nevada desert called Devils Hole, part of Death Valley National Park. In the spring of 2025, after two earthquakes shook its tiny home, biologists counted only 38 of them.

Recent findings suggest that the National Park Service announced the newly introduced figure in November. Divers and surface counters found the 137 Devils Hole pupfish during a survey on October 10, nearly double the 77 seen in the spring of 2026 and about double the 69 recorded in the fall of 2025.

Devils Hole is a cave about 12 feet wide and more than 500 feet deep. The bottom has never been mapped. The water stays at a constant 92 degrees Fahrenheit (33 degrees Celsius).

Pupfish have been found as deep as 66 feet, but they feed and spawn only on a shallow rock shelf near the surface, where algae grows.

Recent findings suggest that the species has been isolated there for 10,000 to 20,000 years, longer than any other pupfish in the Death Valley system. The region’s caves keep other long records too, like a Nevada cave that reveals 580,000 years of climate swings.

Sources indicate that it is the only naturally occurring population of the species, which was listed as endangered in 1967. Biologists from the National Park Service and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service have counted the fish almost every spring and fall since 1972, with scuba divers in the cavern and counters at the surface.

One of the fish’s main threats can come from thousands of miles away. Large earthquakes as far away as Japan, Indonesia and Chile have made the water slosh in Devils Hole like water in a bathtub, according to the park.

According to recent reports, waves can splash as high as two meters (about 6.5 feet) up the walls and sweep the shelf clean. The park calls it a tsunami in the desert, although it is tiny next to the ocean tsunamis that substantial earthquakes can unleash.

That is what happened in the winter of 2024 to 2025. Two earthquakes, one in December and one in February, set off waves that moved algae, organic material and fish eggs off the shelf.

Recent findings suggest that the spring count in 2025 found 38 fish. One year earlier, the official spring count had recorded 191.

On July 29, 2025, just 21 minutes after a magnitude 8.8 earthquake struck Russia’s Kamchatka Peninsula, waves rippled through Devils Hole, nearly 4,000 miles away. Those waves were only about 10 inches high and removed just some material from the shelf.

Then, after an earthquake in Panama on October 9, 2026, nearly 3,000 miles away, biologists at first saw signs of stress in the fish. On a later visit, they found them in healthier condition.

Recent findings suggest that the team had prepared for a crash like this for years. Pupfish eggs from Devils Hole had been collected regularly to build a backup population at the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service’s Ash Meadows Fish Conservation Facility.

Recent findings suggest that in 2025, biologists added captive-raised fish to the wild population for the first time. Between March 2025 and February 2026, scientists released 72 of them into Devils Hole. They also gave the fish extra food while the algae grew back.

Recent findings suggest that the fish live an average of only 10 to 14 months. Because of that, biologists believe most of the 137 fish counted this fall hatched and grew up in Devils Hole itself.

“It’s exciting to see Devils Hole pupfish numbers increase so significantly over the past year,” noted Death Valley National Park Superintendent Mike Reynolds.

“These results reflect the dedication of our scientists and conservation partners working to protect this extraordinary species. While challenges remain, we’re encouraged by this progress and committed to its long-term survival.”.

Sources indicate that the pupfish has survived human threats before. In the late 1960s, a farming operation drilled large wells in the Ash Meadows area, and the water level in Devils Hole began to drop toward the shelf the fish need.

Biologists even hung a floating, artificially lit shelf in the cave as a substitute. The fish never used it.

In a recent development, A federal court halted further pumping in 1971, and the fight reached the U.S. Supreme Court. Its 1976 decision in Cappaert v. United States recognized the water right of Devils Hole as part of a national monument and limited pumping so the natural shelf would stay underwater.

Until the mid-1990s, spring surveys counted more than 200 fish. In the early 2000s, spring counts averaged about 90, and in 2013 the number fell to 35. The cause of that long decline has not been determined.

The new count is an encouraging step, but the park states the population naturally fluctuates and remains highly vulnerable.

It calls continued monitoring, research and habitat management essential if one of the world’s rarest fish is to keep its foothold in a single desert cave.

The information was obtained from the National Park Service’s fall 2026 count announcement, its spring 2025 update, its report on the Kamchatka earthquake and its Devils Hole page.

Industry observers note that rep.-elect Mark Teixeira reacts after drawing the worst chip during Tuesday’s lottery for newly elected members of Congress. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

As far as birthdays go, Rep.-elect Shannon Taylor was having a pretty good one.

Crowded into a room in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday morning with the rest of her freshman class, the Virginia Democrat walked up to a table with a wooden box and reached in.

“This is so nervewracking,” she said, before pulling out a chip with a “1” printed on it.

Her prize was a coveted one — first choice of office space. Every two years, incoming members of the House play a game of chance to see who can land the best real estate and who will be relegated to less desirable corners of the Capitol complex.

The room broke out in raucous applause and a standing ovation. Her new colleagues started singing “Happy Birthday.”.

Not everyone was so lucky. Rep.-elect Mark Teixeira, R-Texas, pulled number 105 — the very last one. The former MLB player raised his arms in a mock celebration.

“Lets all hope for the luck of the Taylors,” said Rep.-elect Brent Taylor, R-Tenn., only to emerge with number 81.

The newly-elected members got their turn in a random order, walking up one by one to a table where deputy executive director of House Office Buildings Kornell Rancy kept watch over the box of chips.

In a recent development, rep.-elect John Cowan, R-Ga., was the first to pick a number. The first neurosurgeon to be elected to Congress, Cowan wore his white doctor’s coat as he pulled number 11 out of the box.

“I wanted to do something where I’m just representing health care providers around the country,” Cowan mentioned.

In a recent development, as returning members lay claim to more desirable offices made available by those who resign, retire or lose elections, the space they’ve abandoned is left for the newcomers, who are on the Hill this week for orientation. Many of them will end up in the Longworth Building, where suites can be awkward or cramped.

Not all offices are created equal, and the calculus has changed over the years. The previously undesirable Cannon Building just underwent a budget-busting renovation that lasted more than a decade, with a spacious courtyard opening earlier this year. But the coveted Rayburn Building still retains its prestige, despite repeated and dire warnings from the Architect of the Capitol about its crumbling infrastructure.

“You’re welcome,” said Rep.-elect Amish Shah, D-Ariz., after pulling a disappointing number 94.

Prior to the lottery, Rep.-elect Trever Nehls, R-Texas, was hoping for the best but had a backup plan in case his number said otherwise.

Industry observers note that “If I don’t pick number one, I’m going to offer one of these cigars as a trade to whoever gets it,” he stated, pointing to three of them sticking out of his jacket pocket. He’s preparing to take over the seat currently held by his twin brother Troy, who shares a fondness for stogies.

Recent findings suggest that the office space lottery dates back to 1908, when members of the 60th Congress received their first office assignments after the completion of what would be named the Cannon Building. A House page drew names and numbers from a box, and members selected their offices from a chart, according to House Office Buildings executive director of facility operations Joe Yates, who kicked things off Tuesday with a history lesson.

The lottery now is a little more modern, with members poring over virtual office layouts and doing walkthroughs of spaces on laptops.

“If somebody had to get 105, I’m glad it was me because I am here to serve, and I’m serving my freshman class by picking the worst office,” Teixeira mentioned. “This is low on my priority list.”.

Some members confirmed their lucky draws themselves, while others let Yates break the news.

“Come visit me,” noted Rep.-elect Chris Gober, R-Texas, after pulling number 2 from the box.

After the lottery itself, members huddled with their staff to strategize about the next steps — how to leverage their numbers and select the best suites left on the list, while also exploring layouts, paint colors and carpeting.

It has been revealed that “First and foremost, a good layout, so we can do good work, and people can be comfortable in doing the work, and then a convenient location. Very utilitarian,” said Rep.-elect Scott Wiener, D-Calif., of his priorities.

It has been revealed that “We’ll get a decent Longworth office,” noted Wiener, who drew pick 43. “Cannon would have been ideal, but I’m happy with any office.”.

Rep.-elect Manny Rutinel, D-Colo., was hoping to replicate the good luck of some of his colleagues. “I’m going to do the Shannon Taylor and Sam Forstag. It’s eyes closed, behind the back,” he stated of his moves, reaching into the box. But it wasn’t enough, and Rutinel pulled number 69.

“These are not red numbers, these are not blue numbers. These are the remaining numbers, and there ain’t that many,” remarked Rep.-elect Johnny Garcia, D-Texas, who was among the last few people to pick. He emerged with number 75.

And when Rep.-elect Joe Strada, R-Fla., the last of the incoming members to draw, walked up to the table, the whole room cheered.

“Wouldn’t it be crazy if I picked number 1?” he joked, pulling out the last chip in the box.

Isabel Angelo spends her days searching the cosmos for exoplanets and signs of extraterrestrial intelligence. But Angelo’s head isn’t in the stars. It’s buried under mountains of 0s and 1s — data from space telescopes old and new.

It has been revealed that to piece together a fuller picture of what’s out there (alien megastructures around nearby stars, perhaps?), Angelo and her colleagues at the SETI Institute in Mountain View, Calif., are turning to machine learning models. These tools are analyzing the troves of telescope data for anomalies — things that look “weird” in space that we don’t know how to explain yet.

According to recent reports, most of the space weirdos will probably turn out to be total normies — a comet, a newborn star or a star surrounded by lots of gas and dust. “These are things that I would expect [the models] to find,” Angelo indicates. “But the goal is to find something that’s not even in any of these categories.”.

In the meantime, Angelo keeps her whimsy and wonder for space alive by remembering historic moments, like the reveal of the first portrait of a black hole in 2019. The scientists “put all of these telescopes all over the Earth. They wait for the Earth to rotate. They do all this math to construct this one image,” Angelo notes. “I can’t believe how creative and innovative we have to be to learn about space. It’s such a specific and really fun challenge.”.

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (836 w)

What you just touched can change how the next thing feels

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (836 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A study in rats found that frontal brain activity helped predict how an earlier vibration would bias judgments about the next one.
  • What you feel right now depends partly on what you felt a moment ago.
  • A region of the frontal cortex represented both the current and previous vibrations, and its activity helped predict how the previous vibration biased the rats’ judgments.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A study in rats found that frontal brain activity helped predict how an earlier vibration would bias judgments about the next one.

What you feel right now depends partly on what you felt a moment ago. In rats trained to judge vibrations, the primary sensory cortex mainly tracked the current vibration.

A region of the frontal cortex represented both the current and previous vibrations, and its activity helped predict how the previous vibration biased the rats’ judgments.

The study was carried out by neuroscientists at SISSA, the International School for Advanced Studies in Trieste, Italy.

“Perception is often thought of as a direct mapping of the external world,” explained Mathew Diamond, a cognitive neuroscientist at SISSA.

Recent findings suggest that “Yet what we experience depends not only on what is happening now, but also on what happened moments ago. In short, every percept is constructed against a backdrop of recent experience.”.

Scientists call this effect serial dependence, and it’s easy to picture. “Imagine feeling a vibration with your fingertip (for instance, from the cell phone) and then feeling a second vibration shortly afterward,” Diamond noted.

Sources indicate that “The second stimulus will not be experienced as an independent event; instead, perception is systematically biased by prior inputs. The brain, in effect, carries traces of the recent past into the present.”.

“Perception is not a photograph of the world. It is more like a film, in which the experience of each frame is influenced by those that came before.”.

Psychologists have known about the effect for a long time. Where the brain does the mixing, and how, has been much harder to work out.

Sources indicate that theories of “predictive processing” propose that the brain constantly combines incoming signals with expectations built from experience. What nobody had clearly shown was the neural machinery that brings the two together.

Recent findings suggest that to find it, Diamond’s team trained rodents on a simple touch task. On each trial the animal felt a stimulus and had to decide whether it was weak or strong.

Meanwhile, the researchers recorded the activity of hundreds of neurons.

The animals’ judgments were consistently pulled by the previous trial. After a strong stimulus, the next one was more likely to be judged weak.

After a weak one, the next was more likely to be judged strong. A medium-strength touch could feel faint or firm depending on what had come right before it.

“The key finding emerged from comparing two cortical regions,” stated lead author Iacopo Hachen.

“Activity in the primary sensory cortex mainly reflected the stimulus right now being processed, a direct representation of the ongoing input.”.

Sources indicate that “By contrast, neurons in a frontal cortical area carried information about both the current stimulus and recent sensory history. There, neural representations of the present were embedded within a context established by the past.”.

The first stop for touch signals in the cortex, in other words, stayed true to the present. The frontal region carried the present and the recent past together.

The frontal region also helped predict the animals’ choices.

When its activity rose or fell from one trial to the next, the animals’ judgments shifted in step.

“Variations in this frontal-cortex activity predicted corresponding variations in perceptual judgments from one trial to the next, suggesting that while the sensory cortex faithfully reports the ongoing input, the frontal cortex integrates that input with recent experience to shape perception,” Hachen explained.

One region reports what is happening, and the other decides what it means given what just happened.

The researchers also identified a possible mechanism at the level of individual cells.

Fast-spiking neurons played a prominent role in how the frontal region represented both vibrations. Their firing patterns suggest they may be inhibitory neurons.

In a recent development, there was also an unexpected finding. While a touch was happening, the frontal neurons encoded it as an ongoing sensory event.

Once the animal committed to its answer, the code switched to a different, memory-like format. That stored version lasted and went on to bias the next decision.

In other words, the brain doesn’t just keep a recording of what happened. It rewrites the experience into a new format as it moves from perception into memory.

That rewritten trace then colors the next moment.

The authors see the work as evidence for a basic principle of how the brain works. Perception comes from a constant back-and-forth between new sensory evidence and traces of the recent past.

Industry observers note that “Our findings suggest that the brain does not treat each moment in isolation. Instead, the recent past becomes part of the neural representation of the present, a unitary construct that mirrors our experience,” Hachen concluded.

Understanding this exchange could help explain how prediction normally supports behavior, and how it might go wrong in neurological and psychiatric disorders.

The study is published in the journal Science Advances.

The quilted, lined interior provides much-needed insulation, and the cotton canvas shell is durable and hard-wearing. The corduroy collar gives it bonus points for style (not to mention a real throwback look). You can never go wrong with Levi’s.

Yeti isn’t the name most closely associated with outerwear, but the brand has been expanding. First, with its upcoming line of iPhone cases, and lo and behold, Yeti jackets are now a thing. This down jacket is surprisingly light, and like most of its coolers, tumblers, and ramblers, is supremely insulated. $400 is a little pricey for a down jacket, but in typical Yeti fashion, well worth the extra dough.

Corduroy is more of a fall staple, but it still works well as a layering option into early winter. The Piston Trucker Jacket from Reigning Champ features a stylish waist cut, a plush, textured feel, and an adjustable bottom-tab hem for a more customized fit. Layer a simple flannel underneath or add a hoodie for extra warmth. If you choose the latter, though, you may want to size up. And like most, if not all, of the outerwear on this list, this one only gets better the more you wear it.

Patagonia has winter wear down pat, and if you’re looking for something in the fleece department, its upcoming Retro-X Fleece Jacket is calling your name. It gives off an old-school fleece vibe, but it feels even warmer than it looks, thanks to its NetPlus 100% postconsumer recycled nylon made from old fishing nets. It also features zip-up hand-warmer side pockets, mobile Y-Joint sleeves, and an internal wind flap to keep you protected from the elements.

Sources indicate that if you’re really looking to go fancy (and warm), Overland’s array of sheepskin jackets will have you looking and feeling like Rocky training in Siberia, or at least its vintage-inspired sheepskin bomber jacket will. It boasts a convertible notch-to-stand-up collar with two buckle straps, adjustable waist straps for a more form-fitting fit, and four total pockets with plenty of storage. You won’t have to layer up with this one—and like most of our favorite outerwear, it only gets better with age.

  • Sources indicate that A few hours after sunset, the house-shaped constellation Cepheus stands on the point of its roof in the northern sky, above the Little Dipper.
  • Glowing at magnitude 4.3, Kurhah is not one of the stars in the house’s outline, but lies within the boxy base.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

November 22: Flat-floored lunar crater Schickard.

Sources indicate that A few hours after sunset, the house-shaped constellation Cepheus stands on the point of its roof in the northern sky, above the Little Dipper. Cepheus is home to several lovely double stars, including Xi (ξ) Cephei, also known as Kurhah.

Glowing at magnitude 4.3, Kurhah is not one of the stars in the house’s outline, but lies within the boxy base. You can find it about midway between Alderamin (Alpha [α] Cep) and Iota (ι) Cep, the western and eastern points in the house’s box, respectively. Kurhah’s two components are separated by just under 8” — once you find the star in binoculars or your finder scope, any telescope will split them. The pair consists of a brighter magnitude 4.4 primary, which glows white, and a fainter magnitude 6.5 secondary, which appears to many observers as yellow.

Industry observers note that if you happen to have a large telescope, you may want to give a nearby deep-sky treasure a try: planetary nebula NGC 7139 sits just 2° west-southwest of Kurhah, but it requires a large scope (8 inches at least) to spot, as this bubble of gas glows at magnitude 13.3. If available, an Oxygen-III filter will help bring it out by dimming the nearby stars.

In a recent development, sunrise: 6:54 A.M.Sunset: 4:38 P.M.Moonrise: 3:37 P.M.Moonset: 5:52 A.M.Moon Phase: Full*Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.

Sources indicate that full Moon occurs at 9:54 A.M. EST on November 24, bringing us our second Super Moon of the year. A Super Moon occurs when the Moon reaches Full phase close to perigee, its closest point to Earth, making our satellite appear larger and brighter than average. The November Full Moon is also called the Beaver Moon. A few hours earlier, before dawn, the Full Moon passes through the Pleiades star cluster (M45) in Taurus, occulting several of its bright stars.

This is an easy event to watch, visible to the naked eye — or you can get a closer view with binoculars or a telescope (just note that you may want a Moon filter if available, as our satellite is so big and bright). The timing of the event will depend heavily on your location; note that it begins right around sunrise along the East Coast, so observers there may only see the Moon approaching the famous group of stars.

According to recent reports, the 5th-magnitude star Celaeno (16 Tauri) disappears behind the Moon’s leading edge just moments before 6 A.M. CST, followed minutes later by 4th-magnitude Taygeta (19 Tau). Next to vanish is 4th-magnitude Maia (20 Tau) just before 6:20 A.M. CST, followed rapidly by Sterope (21 Tau) a few minutes later. The latter two may be difficult to catch from the Midwest without optical aid, as sunrise is fast approaching. If you are using binoculars or a telescope in this region, make sure to put them away several minutes ahead of sunrise from your location. Celaeno reappears around 6:40 A.M. CST, 15 minutes or so before sunrise.

For specific timings from your location, visit the International Occultation Timing Association at http://www.lunar-occultations.com/bobgraze/index.html.

#168684. Your home may be full of wildlife you’ve never noticed

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1159 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Your home may be full of wildlife you’ve never noticed

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1159 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A survey of indoor spaces across the U.S.
  • Homes across the United States and Canada are full of wildlife.
  • A continent-wide survey has found nearly 2,100 species of wild organisms living indoors, mostly insects and spiders, plus centipedes, snails, fungi, and many animals most people have never heard of.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A survey of indoor spaces across the U.S. and Canada recorded nearly 2,100 species, from familiar house spiders to an alligator in a garage.

Homes across the United States and Canada are full of wildlife.

A continent-wide survey has found nearly 2,100 species of wild organisms living indoors, mostly insects and spiders, plus centipedes, snails, fungi, and many animals most people have never heard of.

One record is an alligator that turned up in somebody’s garage.

Sources indicate that this is the largest study of indoor wildlife so far. Nearly all of it is built from photos taken by ordinary people.

The study was led by researchers at North Carolina State University and Colorado State University.

Over 60 co-authors contributed, including museum curators, university entomologists, and independent experts from across North America and Europe.

Ecologists have spent decades cataloging life in rainforest canopies and on the deep sea floor. The places where most of us spend most of our time have received far less attention.

“While researchers have focused significant attention on a variety of natural ecosystems – from rainforest canopies to the deep sea – we know remarkably little about the ecosystems of manmade, indoor environments,” said lead author Bradley Allf from Colorado State.

“Our goal with this work was to treat the indoors, at the continental scale, as an ecosystem that we wanted to explore as ecologists,” he explained.

Earlier surveys of indoor life either covered much smaller areas or relied on DNA traces, which can’t always pin down exactly which species was present.

This is the first survey of indoor life spanning the United States and Canada.

The team released a citizen science project called Never Home Alone on iNaturalist, a website where people share photos of the living things they come across.

Participants were asked to photograph wild organisms in their homes, offices, and other indoor spaces. The rule for “wild” was simple: anything that was neither a pet nor a potted plant.

Submissions came from at least five continents. This study focuses on North America.

About 3,000 people contributed 23,782 observations, from every US state and every Canadian province. Most were taken in homes, but some came from offices, schools, and airports. The records cover almost three decades, from 1996 to 2024.

Every observation was checked by specialists. Dozens of experts identified each organism as precisely as they could.

“This work underscores the value of natural history expertise and the ability to identify species, which is a skillset that is less common among biologists than it once was,” Allf said.

About 95% of the observations were arthropods, the group of animals with jointed legs and hard outer skeletons. Insects made up 60% of all records, mostly beetles, flies, moths, wasps and ants, and true bugs.

It has been revealed that spiders accounted for 30%. Animals with backbones made up only 4%, most of them reptiles and mammals.

The rest included fungi, plants, earthworms, snails, small crustaceans, and even single-celled organisms.

Eight species were recorded more than 200 times each.

In order, they were the Asian lady beetle, the brown marmorated stink bug, the house centipede, the varied carpet beetle, the long-bodied cellar spider, the triangulate combfoot spider, the bathroom moth fly, and the eastern parson spider.

“The organisms we found ranged from Asian lady beetles – which were the most commonly found species – to an alligator that unexpectedly turned up in one person’s garage,” Allf mentioned.

“But one of the things that was striking was how common predator species were – including hundreds of different spider species.”.

Half of the top eight are hunters, and some of them do useful work.

“One study participant noted that they view jumping spiders as working animals, because the spiders play an active role in reducing the population of flies and other pests that they don’t want in their home.”.

Senior author Rob Dunn from NC State pointed out that most people share their homes with these animals every day and have no idea what they are.

“Another thing that is striking about this work is that most people could look over a list of the most commonly found species and wouldn’t know what most of those animals even are – and yet they are around us, all the time,” he remarked.

“For example, I suspect most people are unfamiliar with comb-footed spiders, but we have more than a thousand observations of this family of spiders.”.

He sees this as a fairly recent loss.

“This is a stark departure from what we would have expected historically, when our ancestors would have been more aware of the living things around them.”.

“That’s something we lost. And this is a first step toward regaining that understanding.”.

The list has a very long tail. About 52% of the species were recorded indoors just once.

The true total is almost certainly higher than 2,100, because 44% of the observations couldn’t be identified down to species.

Sources indicate that the authors also point out the dataset’s limits. Nobody controlled how hard each person looked, so large, eye-catching animals are probably overrepresented.

Industry observers note that and not every animal that ends up indoors actually lives there. Some had simply wandered in and become trapped.

The survey also shows how little is known about even the most common indoor animals.

“It could inform future research in many ways,” Dunn stated.

Industry observers note that “For example, house centipedes were the third most commonly found animals, and yet I’m not aware of anyone who is studying them. That’s worth exploring.”.

Some of these animals might even turn out to be useful.

“For example, we now know that camel crickets carry a microbe that can break down paper products. That could be useful. What else might be out there, in our own homes?”.

“Once we know what’s there, we can begin asking additional questions,” Dunn noted.

Sources indicate that “Why are these organisms there? What are they doing? Are they beneficial?”.

According to recent reports, “But knowing what’s there is the first step. And it’s exciting because these are the animals we’re around all the time, but we just overlook.”.

The scientists want to investigate how the climate outside shapes what turns up inside. They also plan to figure out which species have actually adapted to life in buildings.

Every record has a date and a location, so the dataset can also serve as a baseline for spotting fresh arrivals or disappearances in the future. The data are free for anyone to use.

The project is still running, and anyone with a phone can contribute.

“People can still submit observations to Never Home Alone. The more data the project collects, the more insight we’ll have on the unique and growing ecosystem of the great indoors,” Allf concluded.

The study is published in the journal Ecology.

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (909 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

In a West Texas rock shelter, archaeologists found a hunting kit that was left behind 6,500 years

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (909 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Archaeologists in Texas uncovered a roughly 6,500-year-old hunting kit with darts, an atlatl and a rare preserved pronghorn hide.
  • Deep inside San Esteban Rockshelter, south of Marfa, Texas, archaeologists recovered parts of a hunter’s weapon kit that someone left behind thousands of years ago.
  • The Center for Significant Bend Studies at Sul Ross State University presented the find in its spring 2025 newsletter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Archaeologists in Texas uncovered a roughly 6,500-year-old hunting kit with darts, an atlatl and a rare preserved pronghorn hide.

Deep inside San Esteban Rockshelter, south of Marfa, Texas, archaeologists recovered parts of a hunter’s weapon kit that someone left behind thousands of years ago.

The Center for Significant Bend Studies at Sul Ross State University presented the find in its spring 2025 newsletter. The center puts the kit’s age at about 6,500 years and calls it “potentially the oldest example of a full weapon system in North America.”.

It has been revealed that the kit as a whole has not yet been described in a peer-reviewed study. Only one of its pieces, a spear-thrower known as an atlatl, has been the subject of a journal paper.

The kit includes six stone-tipped dart foreshafts – the front section of a dart – and four self-tipped hardwood dart foreshafts.

There are also four dart nock-ends, the rear tips that fit against the atlatl. A broken hunting boomerang and a partial atlatl complete the weapons.

It has been revealed that the excavators also found a folded pronghorn hide. It had been tanned, and its hair was still intact.

Spaced holes ran around the hide’s perimeter so it could be tied to a frame, as Plains groups often did.

Sources indicate that “We just sat there and stared at it in wonder,” stated Bryon Schroeder, then director of the center. Someone had folded the hide and set it on top of a rock, he explained.

“And nobody touched it for 6,000 years,” Schroeder said.

It has been revealed that an atlatl is essentially a wooden stick with a handle on one end and a hook or socket on the other. It acts as an extension of the human arm, increasing leverage against the dart, the National Park Service explains.

The San Esteban atlatl is described in a 2023 atlatl paper by Schroeder and Devin Pettigrew, an assistant professor at the center.

It has been revealed that A radiocarbon date indicates that the atlatl is more than 6,000 years old. That made it the oldest directly dated atlatl in North America at the time, the authors reported in the Journal of Massive Bend Studies.

In a paper published in 2026, Pettigrew and other archaeologists at the center measured how fast modern throwers launch darts.

That research demonstrates that heavier darts, paired with strong and skilled throwers, become lethal to very large animals such as mammoths, the center remarked.

It has been revealed that “In most archeological sites in Texas, only things made of stone survive,” notes Texas Beyond History, a project of the University of Texas at Austin. The dry Lower Pecos rock shelters are an exception.

Recent findings suggest that those shelters have yielded hardwood dart foreshafts and rabbit sticks, as well as bow fragments and arrow foreshafts from the bow-and-arrow era. Complete atlatls are very rare even there.

Unique depositional conditions favored the preservation of the Schöningen wooden spears in Germany. A 2025 dating study placed them at about 200,000 years old.

Sources indicate that A mammoth-ivory boomerang from Poland is one of the oldest known in Europe, an Obłazowa Cave analysis concluded. A statistical model built on dated bones from the same layer places it between 42,290 and 39,280 years ago.

“We can use the wood to reconstruct the environment and learn more about the amount of time they spent working on tools,” Schroeder remarked.

Sources indicate that schroeder’s reading of the scene is that a person came to the back of the cave and sorted through the gear piece by piece. Some parts were judged good and others not, and then the person went on their way.

“But that one small act is going to have profound implications in understanding the environment,” he remarked.

Recent findings suggest that the shelter sits in Presidio County along Alamito Creek, a tributary of the Rio Grande. A spring-fed rock pool, or tinaja, lies in front of it.

The center has worked there since 2019 with the Odyssey Archaeological Research Fund at the University of Kansas. The partners were looking for traces of the region’s earliest people.

It has been revealed that the Odyssey fund was established in 2003 with an endowment from Joseph and Ruth Cramer. Its director is Rolfe Mandel, a distinguished professor of anthropology at the university.

In 2020, the excavators uncovered a hearth-like feature with burned and unburned bird eggshells dated to about 15,200 years ago.

Sources indicate that “Though this site was pot-hunted in the past, the many large boulders that spalled from the ceiling preserved pockets of shelter deposits,” the Kansas team’s site summary states. Pot-hunting means digging for artifacts to collect.

The atlatl foreshafts and darts came from intact deposits in an area the excavators call the Sandal Shaft. The Kansas team dates them to about 6,200 years ago, a little younger than the center’s figure.

The pronghorn hide lay about 2 inches (5 centimeters) above them, capped with a metate, a grinding stone.

Recent findings suggest that the hide yielded a raw radiocarbon age of 5,621 years, plus or minus 24, not yet converted to calendar years. That makes it about 600 years younger than some of the foreshafts and darts, the Kansas researchers report.

The information was obtained from the Center for Substantial Bend Studies.

Flightless kākāpō parrots from Fresh Zealand are genetically healthy despite 10,000 years of inbreeding

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (735 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists sequenced the DNA of Newly introduced Zealand's endangered kākāpō and found that 10,000 years of inbreeding actually helped natural selection clear out harmful genetic mutations.
  • On New Zealand’s Stewart Island, flightless parrots called kākāpō spent about 10,000 years cut off from the rest of their species, breeding with relatives.
  • A 2021 study of their DNA found the opposite: the island kākāpō carried fewer harmful mutations than mainland kākāpō, which have since died out.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists sequenced the DNA of Newly introduced Zealand's endangered kākāpō and found that 10,000 years of inbreeding actually helped natural selection clear out harmful genetic mutations.

On New Zealand’s Stewart Island, flightless parrots called kākāpō spent about 10,000 years cut off from the rest of their species, breeding with relatives. In theory, that should have left the birds with more and more harmful mutations.

A 2021 study of their DNA found the opposite: the island kākāpō carried fewer harmful mutations than mainland kākāpō, which have since died out.

In a recent development, the researchers wrote that the finding is evidence a small population can survive hundreds of generations of isolation. The species is still critically endangered, though, and many of its eggs fail to hatch.

Nicolas Dussex, a researcher at the Centre for Palaeogenetics in Stockholm, led the study. Few birds anywhere are as inbred or as endangered as the kākāpō, Dussex stated.

Kākāpō likely numbered in the hundreds of thousands before people reached Latest Zealand. Overhunting and predators introduced by people reduced them to 51 birds by 1995.

Sources indicate that fifty came from Stewart Island. The other was a mainland male named Richard Henry.

When the study came out, 201 kākāpō were alive, all on island sanctuaries.

For 49 kākāpō, Dussex’s team analyzed each bird’s complete set of DNA, called its genome. Thirty-five were Stewart Island birds.

The rest were mainland birds: Richard Henry and 13 museum specimens. Those specimens were collected between 1847 and 1924.

An inbred bird’s DNA has a recognizable pattern. A chick gets one copy of its genome from each parent. When the parents are related, long stretches of the two copies match.

In a recent development, in the Stewart Island birds, matching stretches made up 53% of the genome on average. In the mainland birds, matching stretches made up 15%.

In a recent development, so the island birds were far more inbred. The team then counted the most damaging kind of mutation, the kind predicted to stop a gene from working.

Sources indicate that mainland birds carried 34.1 of those mutations on average. Island birds carried 17.6 of them, about half as many.

It has been revealed that many of these mutations seem to do harm mainly when a bird inherits the same one from both parents. That happens more often when the parents are related.

According to recent reports, chicks that inherit the mutation from both parents are less likely to survive or breed, the team suggested. Over many generations, the mutation becomes rarer. Geneticists call that process purging.

The team tested the idea with computer simulations spanning 25,000 years. A simulated population that stayed small, like Stewart Island’s, ended up with fewer harmful mutations than a larger one like the mainland’s.

Industry observers note that but in a simulated population one-tenth as large as the island’s, the harm from mutations grew instead. So purging seems to need enough birds for natural selection to work.

After the kākāpō’s recent decline, the team wrote, the birds may now face the same growing harm as that smallest population.

Conservation managers have favored matings with Richard Henry and his offspring, to help the population keep its ability to adapt.

“We show that the single male survivor from the mainland, Richard Henry, has more harmful mutations than Stewart Island birds,” mentioned Love Dalén of the Swedish Museum of Natural History, who supervised the study.

“Therefore, there could be a risk that these harmful mutations spread in future generations.”.

Richard Henry was also genetically distinct, Dalén added, and may have carried useful genetic diversity. The team recommended weighing that benefit against the risk and, if necessary, limiting breeding between the two family lines.

Recent findings suggest that dussex’s team counted mutations in DNA and didn’t measure what they do to a living bird. Their effects on survival and breeding weren’t known.

The team called for research into the genetic causes of the kākāpō’s low fertility and hatching success.

Recent findings suggest that in some other shrinking species, harmful mutations increased as numbers fell, the authors wrote. In others, the mutations decreased.

Next, the team planned to examine other highly inbred birds and mammals, to learn whether the kākāpō is a rare exception.

The full study was published in the journal Cell Genomics.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • 23, 1221, Alfonso X was born in Spain, the son of King Ferdinand III of Castile and Leon.
  • Known as Alfonso the Wise, the king pioneered efforts to translate Arabic and Andalusian works of astronomy into the vernacular Castilian.
  • Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.

On Nov. 23, 1221, Alfonso X was born in Spain, the son of King Ferdinand III of Castile and Leon. By the time he succeeded his father in 1252, Alfonso was already known as a scholar – though he demonstrated his military might as well, putting down several revolts and annexing Murcia.

Known as Alfonso the Wise, the king pioneered efforts to translate Arabic and Andalusian works of astronomy into the vernacular Castilian. His multicultural court authored scholarly works and engineered scientific instruments, as well as collecting an extensive library of works on astrology and astronomy. Alfonso also commissioned the Alfosine Tables, astronomical tables based on Arabic sources and updated with new observations – facilitated by new astronomical instruments constructed at Alfonso’s orders. The work included stellar and planetary positions and became the standard for astronomy in Europe for the late medieval and early Renaissance periods.

Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.

Growing mountain ranges played a major role in sparking life on Earth

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1137 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Rocks once buried in mountain belts suggest Earth's ranges grew taller in two steps, each near a rise in oxygen and in complex life.
  • Picture the young Earth and you probably see mountains in your mind.
  • Sources indicate that rocks that were once buried deep inside mountain ranges suggest the ranges grew taller in two steps, a fresh study finds.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rocks once buried in mountain belts suggest Earth's ranges grew taller in two steps, each near a rise in oxygen and in complex life.

Picture the young Earth and you probably see mountains in your mind. For the planet’s first billion years or more, it may not have had any that would resemble the majestic mountain ranges our planet has today.

Sources indicate that rocks that were once buried deep inside mountain ranges suggest the ranges grew taller in two steps, a fresh study finds. The first step ended about 2.2 billion years ago and the second about 700 million years ago.

Each step came around the time Earth’s air gained oxygen and life grew more complex.

Matthijs Smit, an associate professor of earth sciences at the University of British Columbia, led the work.

The link to life is a match in timing, not a demonstrated cause. The authors call it a hypothesis that still has to be tested.

In a recent development, when two plates collide, rock gets shoved downward as well as up. Minerals that form under that squeeze keep a record of the pressure they felt, and pressure translates into depth.

According to recent reports, the deepest-buried rocks that later return to the surface mark roughly how thick a mountain belt’s crust had grown. Smit’s team gathered pressure and age estimates for such rocks from around the world.

The team relied on garnet, a mineral that forms during the burial itself and can be dated precisely. They also added new measurements from ancient rocks in Cameroon and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

In an interview with Earth.com, Smit noted the debate over the early Earth has run between two pictures.

“Some would argue that it was an almost alien world, with no emerged lands, whereas others would argue that it operated very much in the same way as the modern Earth, with large mountain chains, active tectonics and widespread emerged lands,” he said.

Before about 2.7 billion years ago, the rocks record burial no deeper than roughly 19 to 22 miles (30 to 35 kilometers). In the long middle era that followed, mountain belts buried rock to 34 to 37 miles (55 to 60 kilometers).

Recent findings suggest that the middle-era depth is roughly double the earlier one. In the current era, rocks have come back from about 56 miles (90 kilometers) down, about half again as deep.

The modern figure matches the crust under the Himalaya and Pamir today.

What surprised Smit was how steady the maximum depth stayed within each era, and how consistently it changed from one era to the next.

“There does seem to be a specific tectonic style for each episode in the tectonic evolution of the lithosphere, which dictates in a broad sense how thick (and tall) mountains could become,” he noted.

Thicker crust generally stands higher above sea level. Using the relationship between thickness, density, and elevation seen today, the team converted the depths into rough heights.

It has been revealed that before 3 billion years ago, the highest terrain comes out at sea level, within the error bars. Through the middle era, the highest peaks could have stood about 3.1 miles (5 kilometers) tall, roughly half the height of Everest.

Mountains of that era were real, then, but they were not the giants of today.

According to recent reports, for the modern era, the method gives about 5.5 miles (8.8 kilometers). That is the height of Everest, K2, and Kangchenjunga, to within the uncertainty.

Industry observers note that the authors note the sea-level comparison holds for recent geological time and probably for the middle era too. In the earliest era, the oceans were larger and the crust denser, so those early heights are rougher guesses.

Most of the sediment that rivers carry to the sea comes from mountains, and the amount depends on erosion above about 1.9 miles (3 kilometers) of altitude.

Taller mountains mean more rock washed into the oceans, and with it phosphorus, which limits how much marine life can grow.

In a recent development, both growth periods line up, broadly, with the two great rises in atmospheric oxygen. Each oxygen rise was followed by a Snowball Earth ice age and then by a jump in the amount and variety of life.

Strontium in ancient seawater, which tracks how much material was coming off the continents, also rose during both periods. Phosphorus would have behaved the same way, the authors argue, because it is held in similar minerals.

“It’s likely not a coincidence that life on Earth developed and diversified approximately during the same period that the two growth spurts occurred,” said co-author Ellen Kooijman of the Swedish Museum of Natural History.

Industry observers note that the match isn’t perfect, and the authors say so. Some records of oxygen and living matter don’t move in step with the mountains. That could mean the hypothesis is wrong, or that the planet responded to extra nutrients in thresholds and delays.

Industry observers note that why would mountains grow taller only at certain times? “We suspect that these increases are ultimately linked to the cooling of our planet,” Smit said. “As a result, the process that makes mountains changed, allowing mountains to grow taller.”.

In the authors’ reading, the first change was the arrival of plate tectonics as we know it, with one plate sliding beneath another and crust piling up.

The second came as the cooling mantle let continental margins be dragged deeper before snapping free. That is how the thickest mountain belts are built today.

According to recent reports, old, deeply buried rocks rarely survive. Such rocks are the most likely to be altered by later events or lost back into the mantle, so the record is thinnest exactly where the first step happened.

Smit told Earth.com that the first change is pinned down only to a window of several hundred million years, ending around 2 billion years ago.

“We don’t know precisely how this change occurred in time and whether it was even one continuous change or whether there were short bursts by which mountains were able to get higher and higher,” he noted.

Until that window narrows, the timing can’t be checked closely against the changes in the oceans and atmosphere, Smit stated.

Sources indicate that that work starts with more field research in ancient terrains, sampling rocks and measuring their pressures and ages. He also suggested Earth system models that include step-like, tectonically driven increases in phosphorus.

It has been revealed that the full study was published in the journal Science Advances. Co-authors are at Utrecht University, the Swedish Museum of Natural History, and the Geological Survey of Canada, among others.

  • Challenger Deep is the deepest valley in the deepest trench in the ocean, plunging to roughly 11,000 meters below sea level.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Challenger Deep is the deepest valley in the deepest trench in the ocean, plunging to roughly 11,000 meters below sea level.

Now, scientists have a new clue about how it got to be so … well, deep.

Challenger Deep is found within the Mariana Trench, a crescent-shaped gouge in the seafloor east of the Philippines in the Pacific Ocean. The trench is the scene of a slo-mo tectonic collision called a subduction zone: The Pacific plate is diving beneath the Mariana plate, bending downward as it sinks into the mantle, forming a steep trench on the ocean floor.

All subduction zones are deep, but “it’s interesting why this is the deepest spot in the Earth’s ocean,” indicates geoscientist Robert Stern, an emeritus professor at the University of Texas at Dallas and a visiting researcher at the University of California, Los Angeles.

Recent findings suggest that he and colleagues employed a remotely operated robot called ROV Jason/Medea to descend to more than 6,000 meters and explore the Mariana Trench seafloor around the edges of Challenger Deep. The rocks turned out to contain pyroclastic deposits, evidence of an erstwhile explosive volcanic eruption. Those deposits included platelike blocks that could indicate eruption pulses, and lobe-shaped rocks where the volcanic flows ended and swiftly cooled.

These are the deepest pyroclastic deposits found on Earth, the scientists report November 23 in Frontiers in Earth Science.

How explosive an eruption is at Earth’s surface depends on the chemical makeup of the magma. When the molten rock contains a high proportion of volatile gases, including water vapor, those gases suddenly expand when the magma reaches the surface, producing a violent explosion.

Such explosive volcanism shouldn’t be possible in the deep sea; the pressure is too high for any escaping gases to expand, Stern claims. Along with that mystery, the volcanic deposits were found unusually close to the trench, compared with what would be expected for a subduction zone.

Stern and his colleagues developed a hypothesis that incorporates these disparate pieces of evidence: The extreme depth of Challenger Deep, they say, may be at least partially due to an especially sharp bend in the Pacific Plate as it sinks into the mantle.

According to recent reports, that tighter bend would explain why volcanism is happening closer to the subduction zone than usual. The classic subduction zone scenario is that the sinking plate heats up and melts partially as it descends; the magma rises through the overhanging plate and erupts, forming volcanic island arcs several hundred kilometers from the collision zone. Here, the volcanic deposits were just a hundred kilometers or so from the trench — which makes sense if the plate is dipping more steeply.

It has been revealed that as for the pyroclastics, “we can’t answer if the eruptions were really explosive,” Stern indicates. But at those pressures, any gases such as water vapor contained in the magma wouldn’t be able to explosively expand as they would at the surface.

Instead, the pyroclastic rocks might have formed through a new version of deep-sea eruption, one in which water emerging from the magma is initially in a supercritical fluid state. That would minimize any explosive expansion during the eruption and could also produce fragmented, dense deposits like those seen by Jason/Medea.

According to recent reports, the discovery of deep-sea pyroclastics is “surprising and unprecedented,” says William Chadwick, a geologist at Oregon State University in Newport. Challenger Deep may be the only place on Earth “with the ingredients to produce explosive volcanism in the super-deep ocean,” he says. “Imagining this happening is … pretty mind-boggling.”.

Industry observers note that A lot more work remains to be done to evaluate all of these upcoming ideas, Stern notes. “But a lot of things are now coming together.”.

Breaking: In 1966, Buzz Aldrin took the first spacewalk selfies, and photos from Gemini flights like his helped inspire the revolutionary Landsat satellites

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that sixty years ago, Buzz Aldrin took the first spacewalk selfies on Gemini XII.
  • Recent findings suggest that sixty years ago this month, Buzz Aldrin opened the hatch of his Gemini spacecraft, looked outside and exclaimed, “Man!
  • Near the end of that spacewalk, on November 12, 1966, he mounted a camera on the edge of the hatch, pointed it at himself and took the first selfies ever taken during a spacewalk.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that sixty years ago, Buzz Aldrin took the first spacewalk selfies on Gemini XII. NASA says Gemini photos also helped make the case for satellites like Landsat.

Recent findings suggest that sixty years ago this month, Buzz Aldrin opened the hatch of his Gemini spacecraft, looked outside and exclaimed, “Man! Look at that!”.

Near the end of that spacewalk, on November 12, 1966, he mounted a camera on the edge of the hatch, pointed it at himself and took the first selfies ever taken during a spacewalk. NASA notes that it happened decades before the concept even existed.

Industry observers note that that flight, Gemini XII, is better known for something else. It finally demonstrated that astronauts could do useful work outside a spacecraft, a skill NASA needed before it could send anyone to the Moon.

And a NASA image article published on November 13 points to a quieter legacy: photos like the ones Aldrin and his commander took from orbit helped inspire the program that led to the Landsat satellites.

Sources indicate that aldrin and command pilot James A. Lovell released on November 11, 1966, on a four-day mission. It was the final flight of NASA’s Gemini program, which had to prove the techniques that Apollo would need to land on the Moon.

Those techniques included rendezvous and docking, spacewalking, and showing that spacecraft and astronauts could function for at least eight days, the minimum for a round trip to the Moon.

It has been revealed that spacewalks were the weak spot. Astronauts on the Gemini IX, X and XI missions had run into significant difficulties outside their spacecraft, and NASA looked for better ways to train.

On September 12, 1966, Aldrin became the first astronaut to train for his spacewalks underwater, using mockups of the Gemini and its target vehicle in a school swimming pool in Owings Mills, Maryland. Neutral buoyancy training, as it is called, is still in use today.

Gemini XII debuted about 90 minutes after an uncrewed Agena target vehicle. When the crew’s rendezvous radar proved erratic, Aldrin used backup methods and onboard calculations to guide them in.

Industry observers note that he had written his doctoral dissertation on orbital rendezvous. They docked on the third orbit.

A problem with the Agena’s engine stopped a planned boost to a higher orbit. Instead, Mission Control told the crew that a slight change would put them on the path of a solar eclipse the next morning.

On November 12, as they flew over the Galapagos Islands, the nearly total eclipse came into view, and Aldrin took several photographs and a short film clip.

Industry observers note that it was the first time a solar eclipse was photographed from Earth orbit, according to NASA. Gemini XII passed within 3.4 miles of the center of the eclipse’s path.

Recent findings suggest that later that day, Aldrin made his first spacewalk, a “standup” outing in which he stayed in the open hatch. He installed a handrail on the Agena for the next day, photographed stars in ultraviolet light and took his selfies. He spent two hours and 28 minutes outside.

The next day, tied to the spacecraft by a 30-foot umbilical, he moved along the handrail to the Agena and later worked at the back of the Gemini with his feet in restraints called “golden slippers.”.

Sources indicate that he completed 19 tasks in all, reporting no problems with keeping his body in position. At two hours and nine minutes, it was the longest umbilical spacewalk to that time.

According to recent reports, A third standup spacewalk brought his total to a then-record five hours and 48 minutes. Aldrin credited his underwater training and adequate restraint systems for his success.

Spacewalks have come a long way since then: in September 2024, the crew of SpaceX’s Polaris Dawn mission carried out the first civilian spacewalk.

Industry observers note that on November 14, 1966, Lovell and Aldrin also photographed the area around the Red Sea and the Nile River valley. NASA featured that image in its November 13 article.

According to the agency, the photos taken by Lovell, Aldrin and other Gemini astronauts demonstrated the value of orbital imagery for studying Earth’s surface, and helped scientists make the case for a dedicated Earth observation satellite program.

Industry observers note that one of the strongest advocates for Earth-observing satellites was William T. Pecora, director of the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) from 1965 to 1971.

In a 1969 statement, he noted the Earth Resources Observation Satellite program he championed, which later paved the way for Landsat, was “conceived in 1966 largely as a direct result of the demonstrated utility of Mercury and Gemini orbital photography to Earth resource studies.”.

For more than five decades, Landsat and other Earth-observing satellites have been used to monitor crops, wildfires, flooding, vegetation health and land use. In October, Landsat 9 captured autumn’s colors in the forests around Ripton, Vermont.

Sources indicate that lovell and Aldrin splashed down in the Atlantic Ocean on November 15, 1966, only three miles from the planned target. The flight lasted 94 hours and 34 minutes.

Industry observers note that gemini flew 10 crewed missions in 20 months, and all of the program’s major objectives were accomplished. Less than three years later, Aldrin walked on the Moon with Apollo 11. The Gemini XII spacecraft is on display at the Adler Planetarium in Chicago.

The information was obtained from NASA’s history of the Gemini XII mission, its account of eclipses seen from space and its image article on Gemini Earth photography.

Latest Update: The 2026 ozone hole grew to more than twice the size of the U.S., but a 1987 treaty kept it from getting even bigger

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the 2026 Antarctic ozone hole was the seventh largest in 48 years.
  • Recent findings suggest that this year’s ozone hole over Antarctica grew to cover an area more than twice the size of the United States.
  • In a recent development, that sounds like bad news, and in part it is.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the 2026 Antarctic ozone hole was the seventh largest in 48 years. But it would have been bigger without the Montreal Protocol.

Recent findings suggest that this year’s ozone hole over Antarctica grew to cover an area more than twice the size of the United States. NASA and NOAA scientists say it was the seventh largest in 48 years of monitoring.

In a recent development, that sounds like bad news, and in part it is. But the same scientists say the ozone layer is still on track to recover later this century, and that the hole would have been even bigger if the world had not cut back on the chemicals that destroy ozone.

According to recent reports, many of those chemicals came from everyday products like refrigerators, air conditioners and building insulation. Some of them are still around, which is one reason the recovery is taking so long.

During the peak ozone depletion season, from September 7 to October 13, the hole covered an average of about 9.6 million square miles (25 million square kilometers), according to NOAA and NASA, which reported the results on November 4.

Industry observers note that it reached its greatest extent for the year on September 18, at 10.5 million square miles (27.1 million square kilometers). That is about 90% as large as the largest ozone hole ever observed, on September 9, 2000.

“The 2026 ozone hole is large but could have been 1 to 2 million square miles (3.5 million square kilometers) larger if ozone-depleting substances were as prevalent in the atmosphere today as they were at their year 2000 peak,” said Paul Newman, a senior scientist at the University of Maryland, Baltimore County (UMBC), and longtime leader of NASA’s ozone research team at the Goddard Space Flight Center.

The word “hole” is not literal. No place is empty of ozone. Scientists use it to describe the area where ozone concentrations drop below 220 Dobson units, a level that had never been observed before 1979.

The stratospheric ozone layer works as Earth’s sunscreen. It absorbs ultraviolet light, which damages DNA in plants and animals and leads to sunburns and skin cancer in people.

This is not the same as ground-level ozone, an air pollutant that commonly results from human activities and that reached dangerous levels for billions of people in 2026.

Every southern spring, ozone thins over Antarctica. Human-made compounds containing chlorine and bromine rise into the stratosphere, where ultraviolet light breaks them down.

The freed chlorine and bromine atoms then interact with cloud particles in the frigid Antarctic stratosphere and destroy ozone.

It has been revealed that A ring of seasonal winds called the stratospheric polar vortex keeps that cold air in place. In 2026, the vortex was unusually powerful.

“The polar vortex was unusually large this year in part because planetary-scale weather systems that typically well up from the lower atmosphere and break up the vortex were especially weak in August and September,” said Amy Butler, a research scientist at the NOAA Chemical Sciences Laboratory.

That weak wave action kept the strongest winds several degrees of latitude farther from the South Pole, she stated, which created a larger area where ozone could be destroyed.

Size is only part of the picture. The 2026 hole was not as deep as the record-breaking holes of 10 or 20 years ago.

NOAA scientists launch balloons carrying instruments called ozonesondes from the South Pole Baseline Atmospheric Observatory.

They found that ozone directly overhead reached its lowest value of the year, 105 Dobson units, on October 17. The lowest value ever recorded over the South Pole was 92 Dobson units, in October 2006.

One hundred Dobson units of ozone, compressed at sea level, would make a layer 1 millimeter deep, about as thick as a dime.

“The annual ozone hole has been forming later in the season in recent years, which tells us the ozone layer is healing,” Newman remarked.

“But an unusually powerful polar vortex has extended ozone depletion in the Antarctic this season, allowing the hole to grow to proportions we haven’t seen in a decade.”.

The ozone hole was first reported in 1985 by British Antarctic Survey scientists, and NASA satellite instruments revealed its continental scale.

Scientists traced the damage to chlorofluorocarbons, or CFCs, which had been used in refrigerators and aerosol sprays since the 1930s.

That led to the Montreal Protocol in 1987, a treaty in which countries committed to phasing out ozone-depleting substances and replacing them with less harmful alternatives.

According to NOAA and NASA, the controls set by the treaty continue to drive the long-term recovery of the ozone layer.

Since their peak, chlorine levels in the Antarctic stratosphere from ozone-depleting substances have declined by about a third relative to the 1980s, remarked Stephen Montzka, senior scientist at NOAA’s Global Monitoring Laboratory.

Ozone recovery is also having unexpected effects, like the way it is changing life in Antarctica.

Recent findings suggest that the ozone hole forms over Antarctica, far from the United States. But the chemicals behind it came from ordinary products, and they do not go away rapidly.

Recent findings suggest that NOAA indicates CFCs and similar compounds can linger in the atmosphere, or leak out of old products and landfills, for many decades. As those older compounds break down, scientists estimate that the ozone hole will recover by the 2070s.

Recent findings suggest that that is why the way old appliances are thrown away still matters. Under the Clean Air Act, the Environmental Protection Agency requires refrigerant to be recovered when refrigeration and air conditioning equipment is disposed of, to keep it out of the air.

Household refrigerators and freezers, window air conditioners and car air conditioners usually reach the end of the line with their refrigerant still inside.

In those cases, the EPA states the final person in the disposal chain, such as a scrap metal recycler or a landfill owner, is responsible for making sure the refrigerant is recovered first.

The EPA also notes that reduced ozone means more UVB radiation reaching the ground. In Antarctica, the amount of UVB measured at the surface can double during the annual ozone hole.

The agency claims it is always crucial to protect yourself from UVB, even without ozone depletion, by wearing hats, sunglasses and sunscreen.

Satellites have tracked the ozone layer since 1979. This year, instruments on NASA’s Aura satellite, the NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 satellites and the Suomi National Polar-orbiting Partnership satellite, run jointly by NASA and NOAA, all contributed to the monitoring.

Weather can still make some years worse than others. Year-to-year changes in size and depth are caused by differences in stratospheric temperature and circulation, and colder conditions produce a larger hole, according to NASA’s Earth Observatory.

Without the cuts that began in 1987, this year’s unusually strong vortex would have had more chlorine to work with, and scientists say the hole would have been even larger.

The information was obtained from NOAA, NASA, NASA Earth Observatory and the Environmental Protection Agency’s pages on appliance disposal and the effects of ozone depletion.

The phenomenon of a Full Moon arises when our planet, Earth, is precisely sandwiched between the Sun and the Moon. This alignment ensures the entire side of the Moon that faces us gleams under sunlight. Thanks to the Moon’s orbit around Earth, the angle of sunlight hitting the lunar surface and being reflected back to our planet changes. That creates different lunar phases.

Industry observers note that the next Full Moon will be the November Beaver Moon, which occurs at 9:54 a.m. EST on Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026. It will also be a Super Moon.

We’ll revision this article multiple times each week with the latest moonrise, moonset, Full Moon schedule, and some of what you can see in the sky each week.

In a recent development, A few hours earlier, before dawn, the Full Moon passes through the Pleiades star cluster (M45) in Taurus, occulting several of its bright stars. This is an easy event to watch, visible to the naked eye — or you can get a closer view with binoculars or a telescope. The timing of the event will depend heavily on your location; note that it begins right around sunrise along the East Coast, so observers there may only see the Moon approaching the famous group of stars.

Recent findings suggest that the 5th-magnitude star Celaeno (16 Tauri) disappears behind the Moon’s leading edge just moments before 6 A.M. CST, followed minutes later by 4th-magnitude Taygeta (19 Tau). Next to vanish is 4th-magnitude Maia (20 Tau) just before 6:20 A.M. CST, followed quickly by Sterope (21 Tau) a few minutes later. Celaeno reappears around 6:40 A.M. CST, 15 minutes or so before sunrise.

For specific timings from your location, visit the International Occultation Timing Association at http://www.lunar-occultations.com/bobgraze/index.html.

The Moon then passes 5° north of Uranus, also in Taurus, at 2 P.M. EST.
